questions.q: Which description correctly gives the location of the pituitary gland and the names of its two lobes?
options: In the anterior neck; two lobes joined by an isthmus
In the sella turcica; cortex and medulla
In the posterior roof of the third ventricle; adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis
In the sella turcica; adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis
questions.why: The pituitary gland, or hypophysis, is about the size of a pea and sits in the sella turcica, the saddle-shaped pocket of the sphenoid bone. It hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk called the infundibulum. It has two lobes made of different tissues: the anterior lobe, or adenohypophysis, which is glandular, and the posterior lobe, or neurohypophysis, which is nervous tissue.
notes: The pituitary is in the skull, not the neck. An anterior neck gland with two lobes joined by an isthmus is the thyroid gland.
The location is right, but cortex and medulla are the two regions of the adrenal gland, not the lobes of the pituitary.
The lobe names are right, but the pituitary sits below the brain in the sella turcica. The posterior roof of the third ventricle is where the pineal gland sits.
Correct. The pituitary sits in the sphenoid's saddle and has an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis).
questions.answerText: In the sella turcica; adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares how the two pituitary lobes connect to the hypothalamus?
options: Both lobes by a nerve fiber tract
Anterior by a nerve fiber tract; posterior by portal blood vessels
Both lobes by the hypophyseal portal system
Anterior by portal blood vessels; posterior by a nerve fiber tract
questions.why: The type of tissue in each lobe tells you how it connects to the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium, so the hypothalamus reaches it through blood, using a set of vessels called the hypophyseal portal system. The posterior lobe is nervous tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus, so it is connected by a tract of nerve fibers running down through the infundibulum.
notes: Only the posterior lobe is linked by nerve fibers, because it is an extension of the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe is glandular and connects through blood vessels.
This reverses the two links. The posterior lobe is itself nervous tissue, so it is the one connected by nerve fibers.
Only the anterior lobe receives the portal vessels. Pick the portal system if the question asked about the anterior lobe alone.
Correct. Glandular tissue is linked by blood, and nervous tissue by nerve fibers.
questions.answerText: Anterior by portal blood vessels; posterior by a nerve fiber tract

questions.q: Which two cell types are found in the thyroid gland?
options: Follicular cells and parafollicular cells
Alpha cells and beta cells
Chief cells and follicular cells
Chromaffin cells and chief cells
questions.why: The thyroid gland is made of microscopic hollow spheres called follicles. Follicular cells form the wall of each follicle and surround the stored colloid. Parafollicular cells, also called C cells, are scattered in the spaces between the follicles.
notes: Correct. Follicular cells form the follicle walls, and parafollicular (C) cells sit between the follicles.
Alpha and beta cells are not in the thyroid. They are endocrine cells of the pancreatic islets in the abdomen.
Chief cells are the main hormone-making cells of the parathyroid glands, not the thyroid. Only the follicular cells in this pair belong to the thyroid.
Neither cell belongs to the thyroid. Chromaffin cells are in the adrenal medulla, and chief cells are in the parathyroid glands.
questions.answerText: Follicular cells and parafollicular cells

questions.q: How many parathyroid glands does a person usually have, and where are they?
options: Usually four, on the posterior surface of the thyroid
Usually two, on the anterior surface of the thyroid
Usually one, in the mediastinum behind the sternum
Usually four, one capping each kidney
questions.why: Most people have four small, round parathyroid glands, a superior and an inferior gland on the posterior surface of each thyroid lobe. Each one has its own thin capsule that separates it from the thyroid tissue. Because they are so small and sit right on the thyroid, surgeons must take care to spare them during thyroid surgery.
notes: Correct. Usually four small glands sit on the back of the thyroid lobes, two on each side.
Both the number and the side are wrong. The front of the thyroid is crossed by the isthmus, and the parathyroids are on the back, usually four of them.
The parathyroids are in the neck, not the chest. A single organ in the mediastinum behind the sternum is the thymus.
The parathyroids are in the neck, not on the kidneys. The glands on the superior pole of each kidney are the two adrenal glands.
questions.answerText: Usually four, on the posterior surface of the thyroid

questions.q: Which description gives the location of an adrenal gland and its two main regions?
options: On the posterior surface of the thyroid; outer cortex and inner medulla
Behind the stomach; islets and acini
On top of each kidney; outer cortex and inner medulla
On top of each kidney; anterior lobe and posterior lobe
questions.why: Each adrenal gland, also called a suprarenal gland, caps the superior pole of a kidney. It is really two glands in one: an outer adrenal cortex made of glandular tissue arranged in three zones, and an inner adrenal medulla made of modified nervous tissue that belongs to the sympathetic nervous system.
notes: The regions are right, but the back of the thyroid is where the parathyroid glands sit, not the adrenal glands.
Islets and acini belong to the pancreas, which lies behind the stomach. The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys and have a cortex and a medulla instead.
Correct. Each adrenal gland caps a kidney and is built as a cortex around a medulla.
The location is right, but anterior and posterior lobes describe the pituitary gland, not the adrenal gland.
questions.answerText: On top of each kidney; outer cortex and inner medulla

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex lies deepest, directly against the adrenal medulla?
options: Zona reticularis
Zona fasciculata
Zona glomerulosa
Adrenal medulla
questions.why: The adrenal cortex has three zones, in order from the surface inward: the zona glomerulosa, the zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis. The zona reticularis is the deepest, a branching network of cells lying against the medulla.
notes: Correct. The zona reticularis is the inner zone, bordering the medulla.
The zona fasciculata is the thick middle zone, the widest of the three. It would be the answer for the zone with cells in straight columns.
The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer zone, just beneath the capsule. Pick it for the most superficial zone.
The medulla is the inner core itself, made of modified nervous tissue, so it is not a zone of the cortex. Pick it if the question asked for the innermost part of the whole adrenal gland.
questions.answerText: Zona reticularis

questions.q: In a thyroid follicle, which cells form the wall around the colloid?
options: Chief cells
Parafollicular cells
Chromaffin cells
Follicular cells
questions.why: The thyroid is built of microscopic hollow spheres called follicles. A single layer of follicular cells, a simple cuboidal epithelium, forms the wall of each follicle, and the center is filled with colloid, a protein-rich fluid that stains pink. Parafollicular (C) cells sit between follicles or at the outer edge of a follicle wall, and they never touch the colloid.
notes: Chief cells are not in the thyroid at all. They are the main cells of the parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid.
Parafollicular (C) cells sit between follicles or at the outer edge of a follicle wall, and they never touch the colloid. The cells that line the colloid are the follicular cells.
Chromaffin cells are not in the thyroid. They make up the adrenal medulla, the inner core of the adrenal gland.
Correct. Follicular cells line each follicle and surround its colloid.
questions.answerText: Follicular cells

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the pancreatic islets and the acini?
options: Both release hormones directly into the blood
Islets release enzymes into ducts; acini release hormones into blood
Both release digestive enzymes through ducts
Islets release hormones into blood; acini release enzymes into ducts
questions.why: The pancreas is a mixed organ that sits behind the stomach. Most of its tissue is exocrine acini, clusters of cells that make digestive enzymes and send them through ducts to the small intestine. Scattered among them are the pancreatic islets, or islets of Langerhans, small clusters of endocrine cells that release hormones directly into the blood.
notes: Only the islets are endocrine. The acini are exocrine clusters that secrete enzymes through ducts.
This reverses the two roles. The islets are the scattered hormone-producing clusters, while the acini make digestive enzymes.
Only the acini are exocrine. The islets are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood.
Correct. The islets are the endocrine part, and the acini are the exocrine part.
questions.answerText: Islets release hormones into blood; acini release enzymes into ducts

questions.q: The hypothalamus is part of which division of the brain?
options: The cerebrum
The cerebellum
The brainstem
The diencephalon
questions.why: The hypothalamus lies in the diencephalon, below the thalamus, where it forms the floor and walls of the third ventricle. It links the nervous and endocrine systems and directs the pituitary gland, which hangs below it on the infundibulum. The pineal gland is also in the diencephalon, in the roof of the third ventricle.
notes: The cerebrum is the large upper part of the brain with its lobes and cortex. The hypothalamus lies below it, in the diencephalon.
The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and coordinates movement. It is a separate division, not the one that holds the hypothalamus.
The brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata) lies below the diencephalon. The hypothalamus sits just above it.
Correct. The hypothalamus forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle in the diencephalon.
questions.answerText: The diencephalon

questions.q: Where is the pituitary gland located?
options: In the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
In the mediastinum behind the sternum
Capping the superior pole of each kidney
On the posterior surface of the thyroid gland
questions.why: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped pocket in the body of the sphenoid bone in the middle of the base of the skull. It hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk, the infundibulum. Bone forms the floor and the front and back walls of the pocket, so a growing pituitary tumor usually expands upward toward the optic chiasm.
notes: Correct. The pituitary rests in the sphenoid's saddle and hangs from the hypothalamus.
The pituitary is in the skull, not the chest. The mediastinum behind the sternum is where the thymus lies.
The pituitary is in the skull, not the abdomen. The superior pole of each kidney is where the adrenal glands sit.
The pituitary is in the skull, not the neck. The posterior surface of the thyroid is where the parathyroid glands sit.
questions.answerText: In the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone

questions.q: Where is the thyroid gland located?
options: In the anterior neck, below the larynx
Scattered through the pancreas behind the stomach
In the pelvis on each side of the uterus
In the posterior roof of the third ventricle
questions.why: The thyroid gland lies in the anterior neck, just below the larynx. Its two lobes lie beside the trachea, and a bridge of tissue called the isthmus joins them across the front. Because it sits just under the skin, an enlarged thyroid can be seen and felt.
notes: Correct. The thyroid's lobes lie beside the trachea just below the larynx.
The thyroid is one gland in the neck, not tissue scattered in the abdomen. Clusters scattered through the pancreas are the pancreatic islets.
The thyroid is in the neck, not the pelvis. One on each side of the uterus describes the ovaries.
The thyroid is in the neck, not the brain. The posterior roof of the third ventricle is where the pineal gland sits.
questions.answerText: In the anterior neck, below the larynx

questions.q: What is the infundibulum?
options: The stalk connecting the pituitary to the hypothalamus
The bridge of tissue joining the two thyroid lobes
The fluid stored in the center of a thyroid follicle
The saddle-shaped pocket of the sphenoid bone
questions.why: The infundibulum is the slender stalk that connects the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus above it. A tract of nerve fibers runs down through it to the posterior lobe, and the vessels of the hypophyseal portal system run along it to the anterior lobe, so it is the physical link between brain and pituitary.
notes: Correct. The pituitary hangs from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.
That bridge is the isthmus of the thyroid in the neck. It joins the thyroid lobes and has no link to the pituitary.
That fluid is colloid, inside thyroid follicles. It is not a stalk and is not part of the pituitary.
That pocket is the sella turcica, the bone the pituitary sits in. The infundibulum is the soft stalk above it, not the bone.
questions.answerText: The stalk connecting the pituitary to the hypothalamus

questions.q: What is another name for the pituitary gland?
options: The hypophysis
The hypothalamus
The infundibulum
The pineal gland
questions.why: The pituitary gland is also called the hypophysis. That is why its lobes are called the adenohypophysis (anterior, glandular) and the neurohypophysis (posterior, nervous), and why the vessels that serve the anterior lobe are called the hypophyseal portal system.
notes: Correct. Hypophysis is another name for the pituitary gland.
The hypothalamus is the brain region above the pituitary that controls it. The names look alike, which is why students mix them up, but they are separate structures.
The infundibulum is the stalk connecting the pituitary to the hypothalamus, not the gland itself.
The pineal gland is a different endocrine gland, a small cone in the posterior roof of the third ventricle, not the pituitary.
questions.answerText: The hypophysis

questions.q: What is the isthmus of the thyroid gland?
options: The bridge of tissue connecting the two thyroid lobes
The microscopic hollow spheres that make up the gland
The protein-rich fluid stored inside each follicle
A small gland on the back of the thyroid
questions.why: The thyroid gland has two lateral lobes, one on each side of the trachea. The isthmus is the narrow bridge of thyroid tissue that crosses the front of the trachea and joins the two lobes, giving the gland its butterfly or H shape.
notes: Correct. The isthmus crosses the front of the trachea between the two lobes.
Those hollow spheres are the thyroid follicles, the microscopic units inside the gland. The isthmus is a visible bridge of tissue, not a microscopic unit.
That fluid is colloid, found inside each follicle. The isthmus is solid gland tissue joining the lobes.
A small gland on the back of the thyroid is a parathyroid gland. The isthmus is part of the thyroid itself and lies in front of the trachea.
questions.answerText: The bridge of tissue connecting the two thyroid lobes

questions.q: Where are the parathyroid glands located?
options: On the posterior surface of the thyroid gland
In the mediastinum behind the sternum
On the superior pole of each kidney
Inside the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are usually four small, round glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, two on each side. Each has its own thin capsule. Their name means beside the thyroid, and because they are tiny and sit right on the thyroid, they must be found and spared during thyroid surgery.
notes: Correct. The small parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid lobes.
The parathyroids are in the neck, not the chest. The mediastinum behind the sternum is where the thymus lies.
The parathyroids are in the neck, not the abdomen. The superior pole of each kidney is where the adrenal glands sit.
The parathyroids are in the neck, not the skull. The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland.
questions.answerText: On the posterior surface of the thyroid gland

questions.q: An adrenal gland has an outer region and an inner core. What is the outer region called?
options: The zona reticularis
The adrenal cortex
The adrenal capsule
The adrenal medulla
questions.why: Each adrenal gland is two glands in one. The outer adrenal cortex is glandular tissue that forms the bulk of the gland and is arranged in three zones. The inner adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue belonging to the sympathetic nervous system. The words cortex (bark or outer layer) and medulla (marrow or core) are used the same way in the kidney and brain.
notes: The zona reticularis is one zone of the cortex, the deepest one against the medulla. It is only part of the outer region, not its name.
Correct. The cortex is the outer region and the bulk of the gland.
The capsule is the thin connective tissue covering around the whole gland. It surrounds the cortex but is not glandular tissue itself.
The medulla is the inner core, made of modified nervous tissue. Pick it for the inner part of the adrenal gland.
questions.answerText: The adrenal cortex

questions.q: What term describes a gland that secretes its product directly into the surrounding fluid and blood, with no duct?
options: A follicular cell
A target cell
An endocrine gland
An exocrine gland
questions.why: An endocrine gland is a ductless gland that releases its product, a hormone, directly into the surrounding tissue fluid and blood. The blood then carries the hormone throughout the body. Exocrine glands are the contrast: they release their products through ducts onto a surface or into a cavity.
notes: A follicular cell is one specific cell type, forming the wall of a thyroid follicle. It would be the answer for the cells around the colloid.
A target cell is a cell that carries a receptor for a hormone and responds to it. It receives the hormone rather than secreting it.
Correct. Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood.
An exocrine gland secretes through a duct onto a surface, such as a sweat gland or the pancreatic acini. Pick it for a gland with a duct.
questions.answerText: An endocrine gland

questions.q: Where is the thymus located?
options: In the anterior neck below the larynx
On the superior pole of each kidney
In the mediastinum, behind the sternum
In the diencephalon of the brain
questions.why: The thymus lies in the mediastinum, the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, behind the sternum and above the heart. It is large in childhood and shrinks after puberty. It belongs to both the lymphatic and the endocrine systems.
notes: The thymus is in the chest, not the neck. The anterior neck below the larynx is where the thyroid gland sits.
The thymus is in the chest, not the abdomen. The superior pole of each kidney is where the adrenal glands sit.
Correct. The thymus lies in the mediastinum behind the sternum.
The thymus is in the chest, not the brain. The diencephalon holds the hypothalamus and the pineal gland.
questions.answerText: In the mediastinum, behind the sternum

questions.q: Where is the pineal gland located?
options: In the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
In the mediastinum behind the sternum
In the floor and walls of the third ventricle
In the posterior roof of the third ventricle
questions.why: The pineal gland is a small, cone-shaped gland in the posterior roof of the third ventricle. It is part of the epithalamus of the diencephalon. The hypothalamus lies below it in the floor of the same ventricle, which is why the two are easy to confuse by location.
notes: The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland, which hangs below the brain. The pineal gland is up in the roof of the third ventricle instead.
The pineal gland is in the brain, not the chest. The mediastinum behind the sternum is where the thymus lies.
The floor and lower walls of the third ventricle are formed by the hypothalamus. The pineal gland sits on the opposite side, in the roof.
Correct. The pineal gland projects from the posterior roof of the third ventricle.
questions.answerText: In the posterior roof of the third ventricle

questions.q: What are the thyroid follicles?
options: The connective tissue capsule around the gland
The four small glands behind the thyroid
The microscopic hollow spheres that make up the thyroid
The endocrine cell clusters of the pancreas
questions.why: The thyroid gland is built of thousands of microscopic hollow spheres called follicles. Each follicle has a wall of follicular cells around a center filled with colloid, the protein-rich fluid where the thyroid stores its product. Parafollicular cells sit in the spaces between follicles.
notes: The capsule is the outer covering of the thyroid, not its working units. It would be the answer for the gland's protective wrapping.
These are the parathyroid glands. Pick them for the glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid.
Correct. Follicles are the functional units of the thyroid.
These are the pancreatic islets. Pick them for the endocrine tissue of the pancreas.
questions.answerText: The microscopic hollow spheres that make up the thyroid

questions.q: Which gland is the largest purely endocrine gland in the body?
options: The thyroid gland
The pineal gland
The adrenal gland
The pituitary gland
questions.why: The thyroid gland is the largest gland in the body whose whole job is making hormones. Larger organs such as the pancreas contain endocrine tissue, but they are mixed organs with other jobs. The thyroid sits in the anterior neck just below the larynx, with a lobe on each side of the trachea.
notes: Correct. The thyroid is the largest gland whose only job is making hormones.
The pineal gland is tiny and cone-shaped, in the posterior roof of the third ventricle. It is far smaller than the thyroid.
Each adrenal gland is a small cap on a kidney, much smaller than the thyroid.
The pituitary is about the size of a pea. It is a major endocrine gland but far smaller than the thyroid.
questions.answerText: The thyroid gland

questions.q: A gland caps the superior pole of each kidney. Which gland is it?
options: The pancreas
The thyroid gland
The thymus
The adrenal gland
questions.why: Each adrenal gland caps the superior pole of a kidney, which is why it is also called the suprarenal gland (supra means above, renal means kidney). Inside, it has an outer cortex of glandular tissue and an inner medulla of modified nervous tissue.
notes: The pancreas lies behind the stomach. It is near the kidneys in the abdomen but does not cap them; pick it for the mixed exocrine and endocrine organ.
The thyroid is in the anterior neck, wrapped around the trachea. Pick it for the gland just below the larynx.
The thymus lies in the mediastinum behind the sternum. It would be the answer for the chest organ that shrinks after puberty.
Correct. Each adrenal gland sits on top of a kidney.
questions.answerText: The adrenal gland

questions.q: Which brain structure forms the floor of the third ventricle and directs the pituitary gland?
options: The pineal gland
The pituitary gland
The hypothalamus
The thalamus
questions.why: The hypothalamus is part of the diencephalon. It forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, and the pituitary hangs from it by the infundibulum. It links the nervous and endocrine systems, directing the pituitary through nerve fibers to the posterior lobe and through portal blood vessels to the anterior lobe.
notes: The pineal gland sits in the posterior roof of the third ventricle, not its floor, and it does not control the pituitary.
The pituitary is the gland being controlled, hanging below the hypothalamus in the sella turcica. It is not part of the third ventricle.
Correct. The hypothalamus forms the floor of the third ventricle and controls the pituitary.
The thalamus sits above the hypothalamus and forms the upper part of the side walls of the third ventricle. It does not form the floor or control the pituitary.
questions.answerText: The hypothalamus

questions.q: The anterior lobe of the pituitary is also known by which name?
options: The adenohypophysis
The hypophyseal portal system
The neurohypophysis
The infundibulum
questions.why: The anterior lobe of the pituitary is called the adenohypophysis. The prefix adeno means gland, which fits its glandular epithelial tissue. The posterior lobe is the neurohypophysis, with neuro pointing to its nervous tissue. Reading the prefixes is the fastest way to match each name to its lobe.
notes: Correct. Adeno means gland, matching the glandular anterior lobe.
This is the set of blood vessels linking the hypothalamus to the anterior lobe. It serves the anterior lobe but is not another name for it.
The neurohypophysis is the posterior lobe, made of nervous tissue. Pick it for the lobe connected by nerve fibers.
The infundibulum is the stalk connecting the pituitary to the hypothalamus. It would be the answer for the stalk, not a lobe.
questions.answerText: The adenohypophysis

questions.q: Which structure is nervous tissue that is a direct extension of the hypothalamus itself?
options: The posterior lobe of the pituitary
The adrenal medulla
The pineal gland
The anterior lobe of the pituitary
questions.why: The posterior lobe of the pituitary, the neurohypophysis, is nervous tissue that grows down from the hypothalamus itself. Axons from hypothalamic neurons run through the infundibulum and end in the posterior lobe, where their hormones are stored. That is why its link to the hypothalamus is a nerve tract rather than blood vessels.
notes: Correct. The posterior lobe, or neurohypophysis, is an extension of the hypothalamus.
The adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue too, but it sits on the kidney and belongs to the sympathetic nervous system. It is not part of the hypothalamus.
The pineal gland is in the roof of the third ventricle and belongs to the epithalamus, not the hypothalamus.
The anterior lobe is glandular epithelial tissue, linked to the hypothalamus by blood vessels rather than being part of it.
questions.answerText: The posterior lobe of the pituitary

questions.q: The parafollicular cells scattered between the thyroid follicles are also known by which name?
options: Acinar cells
Chief cells
Follicular cells
C cells
questions.why: The thyroid has two cell types. Follicular cells form the walls of the follicles, while parafollicular cells sit between the follicles or at the outer edge of a follicle wall, never touching the colloid. Parafollicular cells are also called C cells. They are larger and paler than follicular cells.
notes: Acinar cells are not in the thyroid. They form the exocrine acini of the pancreas, which make digestive enzymes.
Chief cells are the main hormone-making cells of the parathyroid glands. Chief and C cells both start with C, which is why students mix them up, but chief cells belong to a different gland.
Follicular cells form the wall of each follicle around the colloid. Parafollicular cells are a separate type that sit between follicles.
Correct. Parafollicular cells are also called C cells.
questions.answerText: C cells

questions.q: A slide of the pancreas shows pale, rounded clusters of cells surrounded by many darker-staining glandular clusters. What are the pale clusters?
options: The pancreatic islets
The acini
The thyroid follicles
The chief cells
questions.why: On a pancreas slide, most of the tissue is acini, exocrine clusters whose cells stain darkly. Scattered among them are the pancreatic islets, also called the islets of Langerhans, which stain more lightly and look like pale islands in a dark sea. The islets are the endocrine portion of the pancreas.
notes: Correct. The islets appear as pale islands among the darker acini.
The acini are the darker-staining exocrine clusters that make up most of the pancreas. Pick them for the surrounding tissue that makes digestive enzymes.
Thyroid follicles are hollow spheres of follicular cells filled with colloid, found in the neck, not the pancreas. They would be the answer on a thyroid slide.
Chief cells make up most of a parathyroid gland. They are not found in the pancreas.
questions.answerText: The pancreatic islets

questions.q: The adrenal medulla, the inner core of the adrenal gland, is modified tissue of which system?
options: The somatic nervous system
The parasympathetic nervous system
The sympathetic nervous system
The lymphatic system
questions.why: The adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue that belongs to the sympathetic nervous system. It develops from the neural crest, the same embryonic tissue that forms the sympathetic ganglia. Its chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic neurons with no axons or dendrites, and they are supplied by preganglionic sympathetic fibers, so the medulla works like a sympathetic ganglion.
notes: The somatic nervous system controls skeletal muscle. It has no tissue in the adrenal gland.
The parasympathetic division is the other branch of the autonomic nervous system. The adrenal medulla belongs to the sympathetic branch instead.
Correct. The adrenal medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue.
The lymphatic system includes the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. The adrenal medulla is nervous tissue, not lymphatic tissue.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic nervous system

questions.q: Chief cells are the main hormone-producing cells of which gland?
options: The thyroid gland
The pineal gland
The parathyroid glands
The adrenal cortex
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are usually four small glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid. Their main hormone-producing cells are called chief cells. The thyroid beside them has a different pair of cells, follicular cells and parafollicular cells, so the cell name tells you which of the two neighboring glands you are looking at.
notes: The thyroid's cells are follicular cells and parafollicular (C) cells, not chief cells. Chief cells belong to the small glands on its back.
The pineal gland is a small cone in the roof of the third ventricle. It is not built of chief cells.
Correct. Chief cells are the main hormone-making cells of the parathyroids.
The adrenal cortex is glandular tissue in three zones (glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis), not chief cells.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid glands

questions.q: The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine organ. Which part of it is the endocrine tissue?
options: The follicular cells
The colloid
The pancreatic islets
The acini
questions.why: The pancreas is a mixed organ. Most of it is exocrine acini, which make digestive enzymes, but scattered through it are the pancreatic islets, or islets of Langerhans. These small clusters of endocrine cells release hormones such as insulin and glucagon directly into the blood.
notes: Follicular cells form the walls of thyroid follicles, in the neck. They would be the answer for the thyroid.
Colloid is the protein-rich fluid stored inside thyroid follicles. It is not found in the pancreas.
Correct. The islets are the hormone-producing part of the pancreas.
The acini are the exocrine clusters that make digestive enzymes and send them through ducts. Pick them for the exocrine tissue.
questions.answerText: The pancreatic islets

questions.q: Which structure carries hypothalamic signals to the anterior lobe of the pituitary?
options: A tract of nerve fibers through the infundibulum
The cerebrospinal fluid of the third ventricle
The sella turcica
The hypophyseal portal system
questions.why: The anterior lobe is glandular tissue, so the hypothalamus reaches it through the blood. The hypophyseal portal system is a set of vessels in which blood passes through capillaries in the hypothalamus, then travels down to a second capillary bed in the anterior lobe. This carries hypothalamic signals straight to the anterior pituitary without first passing through the rest of the body.
notes: This is the link to the posterior lobe, which is nervous tissue. Pick it if the question asked how the hypothalamus connects to the neurohypophysis.
The third ventricle sits above the pituitary, but its fluid does not carry the hypothalamus's signals to the gland. This choice comes from confusing location with connection.
The sella turcica is the bony saddle that holds the pituitary. It protects the gland but carries no signals.
Correct. These blood vessels carry hypothalamic signals to the anterior lobe.
questions.answerText: The hypophyseal portal system

questions.q: Besides being reproductive organs, what else are the ovaries and testes?
options: Lymphatic organs
Parts of the urinary system
Endocrine glands
Organs of the digestive system
questions.why: The ovaries and testes, the gonads, are mixed organs. They make the sex cells for reproduction, and they are also endocrine glands that secrete hormones into the blood: estrogen and progesterone from the ovaries, and testosterone from the testes.
notes: Lymphatic organs include the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. Pick this group for organs that house immune cells.
The urinary system includes the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra. The gonads are nearby in the pelvis but belong to the reproductive system.
Correct. The gonads secrete sex hormones into the blood.
Digestive organs include the stomach and intestines, which do contain scattered endocrine cells. The gonads, though, are not digestive organs.
questions.answerText: Endocrine glands

questions.q: Which organ contains hormone-producing cells in the wall of its atria?
options: The kidneys
The heart
The skin
The placenta
questions.why: Many organs whose main job is something else still contain endocrine tissue. The heart is one of them: cells in the wall of its atria release a hormone into the blood. Atria are the two upper chambers of the heart, so the clue in the question points straight to it.
notes: The kidneys do contain endocrine cells, in the renal cortex, including the juxtaglomerular cells. Kidneys have no atria.
Correct. Cardiac muscle cells in the atrial walls of the heart release a hormone.
The skin's endocrine cells are keratinocytes of the epidermis, which begin making a hormone in sunlight. Skin has no atria.
The placenta is a temporary organ of pregnancy that contains endocrine cells. It has no atria.
questions.answerText: The heart

questions.q: Which structure is the saddle-shaped pocket of the sphenoid bone that cradles and protects the pituitary gland?
options: The foramen magnum
The sella turcica
The infundibulum
The third ventricle
questions.why: The sella turcica, Latin for Turkish saddle, is a depression on the superior surface of the sphenoid bone. The pituitary gland sits in it, protected by bone below, in front, and behind. That bony enclosure is why a pituitary tumor tends to grow upward toward the optic chiasm.
notes: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the occipital bone where the spinal cord joins the brainstem. It does not hold the pituitary.
Correct. The sella turcica is the bony seat of the pituitary.
The infundibulum is the soft stalk connecting the pituitary to the hypothalamus. Pick it for the stalk, not the bony pocket.
The third ventricle is a fluid-filled space in the diencephalon, above the pituitary. It would be the answer for the space bordered by the hypothalamus and thalamus.
questions.answerText: The sella turcica

questions.q: Which organs have scattered endocrine cells in the lining of the digestive tract?
options: Adipose tissue
The stomach and small intestine
The thymus
The kidneys
questions.why: The stomach and small intestine are organs of digestion, but their lining contains scattered endocrine cells. These cells release hormones into the blood that help coordinate digestion. They are an example of endocrine tissue inside an organ whose main job is something else.
notes: Adipose tissue does contain endocrine cells (the adipocytes), but it is fat tissue, not the lining of the digestive tract.
Correct. Enteroendocrine cells are scattered through the mucosa of the stomach and small intestine.
The thymus is in the mediastinum behind the sternum and is not part of the digestive tract.
The kidneys contain endocrine cells in the renal cortex, but they are urinary organs, not part of the digestive tract.
questions.answerText: The stomach and small intestine

questions.q: A gland lies in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, hanging from a stalk below the hypothalamus. Which gland is it?
options: The pineal gland
The pituitary gland
The hypothalamus
The thyroid gland
questions.why: The pituitary gland is identified by its position. It sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone and hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk called the infundibulum. No other endocrine gland lies in the skull base, so the sella turcica alone points to the pituitary.
notes: The pineal gland is in the brain too, but it sits in the posterior roof of the third ventricle, not in the sphenoid bone. Pick it for that location.
Correct. The sella turcica and the stalk below the hypothalamus identify the pituitary.
The hypothalamus is the structure above, from which the gland hangs. It forms the floor of the third ventricle and is not in the sella turcica.
The thyroid is in the anterior neck, around the trachea. It would be the answer for a gland with two lobes joined by an isthmus.
questions.answerText: The pituitary gland

questions.q: A gland wraps around the trachea just below the larynx and has two lateral lobes joined across the front. Which gland is described?
options: The adrenal glands
The parathyroid glands
The thymus
The thyroid gland
questions.why: The thyroid gland sits in the anterior neck, just below the larynx. Its two lateral lobes lie against the trachea, and the isthmus joins them across the front. The parathyroid glands are on its posterior surface, and the thymus is lower down, in the chest.
notes: The adrenal glands are in the abdomen, on top of the kidneys, not in the neck.
The parathyroids are small glands on the back of the thyroid, not two large lobes beside the trachea.
The thymus is lower, in the mediastinum behind the sternum, not wrapped around the trachea below the larynx.
Correct. The lobes beside the trachea and the isthmus across the front identify the thyroid.
questions.answerText: The thyroid gland

questions.q: A pituitary lobe is made of glandular epithelial tissue and is linked to the hypothalamus by a set of blood vessels. Which lobe is it?
options: The posterior lobe
The infundibulum
The anterior lobe
The neurohypophysis
questions.why: The anterior lobe, or adenohypophysis, is glandular epithelial tissue. Because it is not nervous tissue, the hypothalamus cannot reach it with nerve fibers; it reaches it through blood, using the hypophyseal portal system. The tissue type and the type of link always go together.
notes: The posterior lobe is nervous tissue linked by a tract of nerve fibers. Pick it for the lobe that is an extension of the hypothalamus.
The infundibulum is the stalk joining the pituitary to the hypothalamus, not a lobe. It would be the answer for the connecting stalk.
Correct. The glandular anterior lobe connects to the hypothalamus through portal blood vessels.
The neurohypophysis is another name for the posterior lobe. Its name points to nervous tissue, the opposite of glandular epithelium.
questions.answerText: The anterior lobe

questions.q: An adrenal cortex zone is the thick middle zone, with its cells arranged in straight columns. Which zone is it?
options: Adrenal medulla
Zona reticularis
Zona fasciculata
Zona glomerulosa
questions.why: The adrenal cortex has three zones. The zona fasciculata is the middle zone and the widest of the three, and its cells line up in long straight columns, which is what fasciculata (bundled) describes. It sits between the thin outer zona glomerulosa and the inner zona reticularis.
notes: The medulla is the inner core of modified nervous tissue, not a zone of the cortex. Pick it for the part made of chromaffin cells.
The zona reticularis is the inner zone, a branching network against the medulla. It would be the answer for the deepest zone.
Correct. Fasciculata means bundled, describing its straight columns of cells.
The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer zone just beneath the capsule. Pick it for the most superficial zone.
questions.answerText: Zona fasciculata

questions.q: The pineal gland belongs to which part of the diencephalon?
options: The thalamus
The midbrain
The epithalamus
The hypothalamus
questions.why: The diencephalon has three parts named by position: the thalamus in the middle, the hypothalamus below (hypo means under), and the epithalamus above and behind (epi means upon). The pineal gland projects from the posterior roof of the third ventricle as part of the epithalamus.
notes: The thalamus is the large central mass of the diencephalon that relays sensory information to the cerebrum. It forms the upper walls of the third ventricle but does not include the pineal gland.
The midbrain is the top part of the brainstem, below the diencephalon. It would be the answer for structures such as the cerebral peduncles, not the pineal gland.
Correct. The pineal gland is part of the epithalamus, the roof region of the diencephalon.
The hypothalamus is the floor region of the diencephalon, below the third ventricle. Pick it for the structure that directs the pituitary.
questions.answerText: The epithalamus

questions.q: A part of the adrenal gland is modified nervous tissue forming the inner core. Which part is it?
options: The adrenal cortex
The adrenal medulla
The adrenal capsule
The zona glomerulosa
questions.why: Each adrenal gland is two glands in one. The outer adrenal cortex is glandular epithelial tissue arranged in three zones, and the inner adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue belonging to the sympathetic nervous system. The medulla is made of chromaffin cells, large cells in clusters around blood vessels that are modified sympathetic neurons.
notes: The cortex is the outer region, made of glandular tissue in three zones. Pick it for the bulk of the gland.
Correct. The medulla is the nervous tissue core of the adrenal gland.
The capsule is the connective tissue covering around the outside of the gland. It would be the answer for the outer wrapping.
The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer zone of the cortex, just beneath the capsule. It is glandular tissue at the surface, the opposite of the core.
questions.answerText: The adrenal medulla

questions.q: A pituitary lobe is nervous tissue connected to the hypothalamus by a tract of nerve fibers running down through the infundibulum. Which lobe is it?
options: The infundibulum
The adenohypophysis
The anterior lobe
The posterior lobe
questions.why: The posterior lobe, or neurohypophysis, is nervous tissue that extends down from the hypothalamus. Axons of hypothalamic neurons form a tract that runs through the infundibulum and ends in the posterior lobe, where their hormones are stored and released. Nervous tissue goes with a nerve connection, and glandular tissue goes with a blood connection.
notes: The infundibulum is the stalk that the nerve tract runs through on its way down. It is the route of the tract, not the lobe where the fibers end; pick it for the pituitary stalk.
The adenohypophysis is another name for the anterior lobe. Its prefix adeno, meaning gland, signals glandular tissue rather than nervous tissue.
The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium linked by portal blood vessels. Pick it for the lobe served by the hypophyseal portal system.
Correct. The nervous posterior lobe is linked by a nerve fiber tract.
questions.answerText: The posterior lobe

questions.q: Small round glands, usually four of them, sit on the posterior surface of a larger neck gland. Which glands are these?
options: The pancreatic islets
The adrenal glands
The thyroid follicles
The parathyroid glands
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are usually four small, round glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, two on each side, each in its own thin capsule. Their main hormone-making cells are chief cells. Their position on the back of the thyroid is why surgeons must take care to spare them during thyroid surgery.
notes: The pancreatic islets are microscopic clusters scattered through the pancreas in the abdomen, not glands in the neck.
The adrenal glands are two glands on top of the kidneys in the abdomen, not four glands in the neck.
Thyroid follicles are microscopic hollow spheres inside the thyroid, not separate glands on its surface.
Correct. The parathyroids sit on the back of the thyroid lobes.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid glands

questions.q: An adrenal cortex zone is made of cells arranged in a branching network. Which zone is it?
options: Zona glomerulosa
Zona fasciculata
Adrenal medulla
Zona reticularis
questions.why: The names of the three cortical zones describe how their cells are arranged. The zona glomerulosa has rounded clusters, the zona fasciculata has straight columns, and the zona reticularis has a branching network (reticulum means little net). The zona reticularis is also the deepest zone, lying against the medulla.
notes: The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer zone, with cells in rounded clusters. Pick it for the zone just beneath the capsule.
The zona fasciculata has cells in straight columns, not a network. It would be the answer for the thick middle zone.
The medulla is the core of modified nervous tissue, not a zone of the cortex. Pick it for the part made of chromaffin cells.
Correct. Reticularis means network, describing its branching cords of cells.
questions.answerText: Zona reticularis

questions.q: A soft gland lies behind the stomach and does both an exocrine and an endocrine job. Which organ is it?
options: The pancreas
The thymus
The liver
The adrenal gland
questions.why: The pancreas is a soft, elongated gland that lies behind the stomach. It is a mixed organ: most of it is exocrine acini, which make digestive enzymes and send them through ducts, and scattered among them are the endocrine pancreatic islets, which release hormones into the blood.
notes: Correct. The pancreas lies behind the stomach and has both exocrine acini and endocrine islets.
The thymus is in the mediastinum behind the sternum, not in the abdomen. Pick it for the organ that shrinks after puberty.
The liver is a large organ in the upper right abdomen, under the diaphragm, not tucked behind the stomach. Pick it for the organ that makes bile.
The adrenal gland caps the kidney and is purely endocrine. It would be the answer for a gland with a cortex and a medulla.
questions.answerText: The pancreas

questions.q: Which paired endocrine organs lie in the female pelvis, one on each side of the uterus?
options: The ovaries
The testes
The placenta
The adrenal glands
questions.why: The ovaries are the paired female gonads. They lie in the female pelvis, one on each side of the uterus. Like the testes, they are mixed organs, producing sex cells and also acting as endocrine glands that secrete estrogen and progesterone.
notes: Correct. The ovaries are the female gonads, beside the uterus.
The testes are the male gonads, located in the scrotum. Pick them if the question asked about the male gonads.
The placenta is a single temporary organ of pregnancy attached to the uterine wall, not a pair beside the uterus. It would be the answer for the organ that releases hormones supporting pregnancy.
The adrenal glands are paired too, but they cap the kidneys in the upper abdomen. Pick them for the suprarenal glands.
questions.answerText: The ovaries

questions.q: Which temporary organ of pregnancy releases hormones that support the pregnancy?
options: The placenta
Adipose tissue
The uterus
The ovaries
questions.why: The placenta is a temporary organ that forms during pregnancy, attached to the uterine wall. Besides exchanging materials between mother and fetus, it contains endocrine tissue that releases hormones supporting the pregnancy. It is delivered after the baby, which is why it is called temporary.
notes: Correct. The placenta exists only during pregnancy and contains endocrine cells.
Adipose tissue does contain endocrine cells (the adipocytes), but it is a permanent tissue found all over the body, not a temporary organ of pregnancy.
The uterus is the permanent muscular organ where the fetus develops. The placenta attaches to its wall, but the uterus itself is not the temporary organ.
The ovaries are permanent paired gonads in the pelvis, present long before and after any pregnancy.
questions.answerText: The placenta

questions.q: Which sequence orders these endocrine glands from most superior to most inferior in the body: adrenal gland, thyroid gland, pineal gland?
options: Adrenal, thyroid, pineal
Pineal, thyroid, adrenal
Thyroid, pineal, adrenal
Pineal, adrenal, thyroid
questions.why: Order these glands by body region. The pineal gland is in the brain, in the roof of the third ventricle, so it is the most superior. The thyroid is in the anterior neck, below the larynx. The adrenal glands cap the kidneys in the abdomen, so they are the most inferior of the three.
notes: This is the correct order run backward, from inferior to superior. It would be right if the question asked for the lowest gland first.
Correct. Brain, then neck, then abdomen.
This places the thyroid above the pineal gland. The pineal gland is inside the brain, so it is higher than any gland in the neck.
This places the adrenal gland above the thyroid. The adrenals sit on the kidneys in the abdomen, well below the neck.
questions.answerText: Pineal, thyroid, adrenal

questions.q: Which sequence orders the three zones of the adrenal cortex from the most superficial, just under the capsule, to the deepest, against the medulla?
options: Glomerulosa, reticularis, fasciculata
Fasciculata, glomerulosa, reticularis
Glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis
Reticularis, fasciculata, glomerulosa
questions.why: The adrenal cortex has three zones in order from the surface inward. The zona glomerulosa is a thin outer layer just under the capsule. The zona fasciculata is the thick middle zone, the widest of the three. The zona reticularis is the inner zone, a branching network of cells against the medulla.
notes: This swaps the last two zones. The reticularis is the deepest zone, against the medulla, so it must come last.
This swaps the first two zones. The thin glomerulosa lies just under the capsule, above the thick fasciculata.
Correct. Outer, middle, and inner zones in order.
This is the correct order run backward, from deep to superficial. It would be right if the question started at the medulla.
questions.answerText: Glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis

questions.q: An endocrine organ in the mediastinum behind the sternum is large in childhood and shrinks after puberty. Which organ is it?
options: The pineal gland
The thyroid gland
The thymus
The parathyroid glands
questions.why: The thymus lies in the mediastinum, behind the sternum. It is large and active in childhood, when T cells are maturing, and it shrinks after puberty as much of it is replaced by fat. It belongs to both the lymphatic and the endocrine systems.
notes: The pineal gland is in the brain, in the roof of the third ventricle. It would be the answer for the gland of the epithalamus.
The thyroid is in the anterior neck, around the trachea, above the mediastinum. Pick it for the largest purely endocrine gland.
Correct. The thymus is large in children and shrinks after puberty.
The parathyroids are small glands on the back of the thyroid, in the neck. Pick them for the glands with chief cells.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: The adrenal glands are also called by which other name?
options: The suprarenal glands
The hypophysis
The pancreatic islets
The parathyroid glands
questions.why: The adrenal glands are also called the suprarenal glands. Both names describe location: ad-renal means toward the kidney and supra-renal means above the kidney. Each gland caps the superior pole of a kidney and has an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
notes: Correct. Supra means above and renal means kidney, describing where they sit.
The hypophysis is another name for the pituitary gland. It would be the answer for the gland in the sella turcica.
The pancreatic islets are the endocrine clusters of the pancreas, also called islets of Langerhans. They are not on the kidneys.
The parathyroids are the small glands on the back of the thyroid. Their name means beside the thyroid, so pick them for that location.
questions.answerText: The suprarenal glands

questions.q: Which sequence orders these structures of the pituitary region from superior to inferior: anterior pituitary lobe, hypothalamus, infundibulum?
options: Hypothalamus, infundibulum, anterior pituitary lobe
Infundibulum, hypothalamus, anterior pituitary lobe
Anterior pituitary lobe, infundibulum, hypothalamus
Hypothalamus, anterior pituitary lobe, infundibulum
questions.why: The hypothalamus forms the floor of the third ventricle. The infundibulum is a slender stalk that hangs down from it, and the pituitary gland, with its anterior and posterior lobes, hangs from the bottom of the stalk in the sella turcica. So from top to bottom the order is hypothalamus, infundibulum, pituitary.
notes: Correct. The gland hangs from the hypothalamus by the stalk.
This places the stalk above the hypothalamus. The infundibulum hangs down from the hypothalamus, so it must come second.
This is the correct order run backward, from inferior to superior. It would be right if the question started at the gland.
This places the gland above its own stalk. The infundibulum connects the two, so it lies between them.
questions.answerText: Hypothalamus, infundibulum, anterior pituitary lobe

questions.q: Which organ is not an endocrine gland, but has cells in its epidermis that begin making a hormone when exposed to sunlight?
options: Adipose tissue
The skin
The liver
The kidneys
questions.why: The skin is one of several organs whose main job is something else but that still contain endocrine cells. Its endocrine cells are keratinocytes, the main cells of the epidermis, and they begin making a hormone when the skin is exposed to sunlight. Only the skin has an epidermis, so that clue points straight to it.
notes: Adipose tissue has endocrine cells too, but they are the adipocytes (fat cells), not cells of an epidermis.
Correct. Keratinocytes of the epidermis begin making a hormone in sunlight.
The liver's endocrine cells are its hepatocytes. The liver has no epidermis.
The kidneys' endocrine cells are in the renal cortex, including the juxtaglomerular cells. The kidneys have no epidermis.
questions.answerText: The skin

questions.q: What is an endocrine gland?
options: A cell that carries the receptor for a hormone
A chemical messenger carried in the blood
A ductless gland that secretes into the blood
A gland that secretes through a duct onto a surface
questions.why: An endocrine gland is a ductless gland. It secretes its product, a hormone, straight into the tissue fluid around it, and from there the hormone enters the blood. Exocrine glands are the contrast, because they use ducts to deliver their products onto a surface.
notes: This defines a target cell, the cell that responds to a hormone. It receives a signal rather than making one.
This defines a hormone, the product of an endocrine gland. The gland is the organ that makes it.
Correct. No duct is involved; the blood carries the product away.
This defines an exocrine gland, such as a sweat gland or the pancreatic acini. Pick it if the question asked about exocrine glands.
questions.answerText: A ductless gland that secretes into the blood

questions.q: Why can a clinician feel the thyroid gland during a neck exam, and why is an enlarged thyroid often visible?
options: It rests on the superior pole of the kidney
It lies just under the skin of the anterior neck
It lies deep in the mediastinum behind the sternum
It sits inside a bony pocket of the sphenoid bone
questions.why: The thyroid gland sits in the anterior neck, just below the larynx and just under the skin. Because it is so superficial, a clinician can palpate it, and an enlarged thyroid, called a goiter, can often be seen as a swelling at the front of the neck. The same position makes thyroid surgery accessible.
notes: This is the position of the adrenal gland, deep in the abdomen. Pick it for the gland often found by chance on kidney imaging.
Correct. Its superficial position makes it easy to see and palpate.
This is the position of the thymus, which is hidden behind bone. A structure in that location could not be felt in a neck exam.
This is the position of the pituitary gland, deep in the skull. It would be the answer for the gland whose tumors press on the optic chiasm.
questions.answerText: It lies just under the skin of the anterior neck

questions.q: Where are the adrenal glands located?
options: On the back of the thyroid
Behind the stomach
In the sella turcica
Capping the superior pole of each kidney
questions.why: The adrenal glands are paired glands, one capping the superior pole of each kidney. That position is why they are also called the suprarenal glands. Each has an outer cortex of glandular tissue and an inner medulla of modified nervous tissue.
notes: The back of the thyroid is in the neck, where the parathyroid glands sit. The adrenal glands are in the abdomen.
Behind the stomach is where the pancreas lies. The adrenal glands sit higher and farther back, on the kidneys.
The sella turcica is in the skull and holds the pituitary gland, not the adrenal glands.
Correct. Each adrenal gland sits on top of a kidney.
questions.answerText: Capping the superior pole of each kidney

questions.q: What is the slender stalk connecting the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus called?
options: The infundibulum
The sella turcica
The isthmus
The colloid
questions.why: The infundibulum, a name meaning funnel, is the slender stalk that connects the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus. A nerve fiber tract runs through it to the posterior lobe, and portal blood vessels run along it to the anterior lobe.
notes: Correct. The infundibulum is the pituitary stalk.
The sella turcica is the bony saddle that holds the pituitary. It would be the answer for the pocket of the sphenoid bone.
The isthmus is the bridge of tissue joining the two thyroid lobes. Pick it for the thyroid.
Colloid is the fluid inside thyroid follicles. Pick it for the stored product of the thyroid.
questions.answerText: The infundibulum

questions.q: What is the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland also called?
options: The neurohypophysis
The infundibulum
The epithalamus
The adenohypophysis
questions.why: The posterior lobe of the pituitary is called the neurohypophysis because it is made of nervous tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe is the adenohypophysis, from adeno meaning gland. Together the two lobes make up the hypophysis, the pituitary gland.
notes: Correct. Neuro points to the nervous tissue of the posterior lobe.
The infundibulum is the stalk that connects the pituitary to the hypothalamus. It would be the answer for the stalk.
The epithalamus is the roof region of the diencephalon that contains the pineal gland. It is not part of the pituitary.
The adenohypophysis is the anterior lobe, made of glandular tissue. Pick it for the anterior lobe.
questions.answerText: The neurohypophysis

questions.q: What type of tissue makes up the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland?
options: Nervous tissue
Glandular epithelial tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Smooth muscle tissue
questions.why: The posterior lobe is nervous tissue. It is made largely of the axon endings of hypothalamic neurons and their supporting cells, which is why it is called the neurohypophysis and why its link to the hypothalamus is a nerve tract. The anterior lobe, by contrast, is glandular epithelium.
notes: Correct. The posterior lobe is an extension of the hypothalamus.
Glandular epithelium makes up the anterior lobe. Pick it for the adenohypophysis.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments. It would be the answer for a structure built to resist pulling in one direction.
Smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs and vessels. It is not found in the pituitary lobes.
questions.answerText: Nervous tissue

questions.q: What is the bridge of thyroid tissue that connects the two thyroid lobes called?
options: The follicle
The infundibulum
The colloid
The isthmus
questions.why: The isthmus is the narrow bridge of thyroid tissue that crosses the front of the trachea and connects the right and left lobes. The word isthmus means a narrow strip joining two larger parts, the same idea as a land isthmus joining two land masses.
notes: A follicle is one microscopic hollow sphere of the thyroid. Pick it for the gland's microscopic unit.
The infundibulum is the stalk joining the pituitary to the hypothalamus. Pick it for the pituitary stalk.
Colloid is the protein-rich fluid inside each follicle. It would be the answer for the thyroid's stored product.
Correct. The isthmus crosses the front of the trachea.
questions.answerText: The isthmus

questions.q: What is the protein-rich fluid stored in the center of each thyroid follicle called?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid
Plasma
Colloid
Synovial fluid
questions.why: Each thyroid follicle is a hollow sphere whose wall is made of follicular cells. The center is filled with colloid, a thick protein-rich fluid in which the thyroid stores the material it uses to make its hormones. The thyroid is unusual among endocrine glands for storing its product outside its cells like this.
notes: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles of the brain and surrounds the CNS. It is not found in the thyroid.
Plasma is the liquid part of blood. Pick it for the fluid in which blood cells are suspended.
Correct. Colloid fills the center of each follicle.
Synovial fluid fills the cavity of a synovial joint and lubricates it. It would be the answer for joints, not glands.
questions.answerText: Colloid

questions.q: What are the two main regions of an adrenal gland?
options: An outer cortex and an inner medulla
An anterior lobe and a posterior lobe
A head and a tail
Two lateral lobes joined by an isthmus
questions.why: An adrenal gland has two main regions that are really two glands in one. The outer adrenal cortex is glandular tissue arranged in three zones, and the inner adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue of the sympathetic nervous system.
notes: Correct. The adrenal gland is a cortex wrapped around a medulla.
These are the two lobes of the pituitary gland. Pick this pair for the pituitary.
Head and tail are regions of the pancreas. It would be the answer for that organ.
This describes the thyroid gland. Pick it for the gland around the trachea.
questions.answerText: An outer cortex and an inner medulla

questions.q: How many zones make up the adrenal cortex?
options: Two
Three
Five
Four
questions.why: The adrenal cortex has three zones. From the surface inward they are the zona glomerulosa, the thin outer zone; the zona fasciculata, the thick middle zone; and the zona reticularis, the inner zone against the medulla. The medulla itself is a separate region, not a fourth zone.
notes: Two is the number of main regions of the whole adrenal gland, the cortex and the medulla. Students mix up that count with the zones of the cortex.
Correct. The zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis.
Five comes from counting the capsule and the medulla along with the three zones, but neither one is a zone of the cortex. The capsule is the covering and the medulla is the core.
Four is the usual number of parathyroid glands. It does not describe the adrenal cortex.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.q: What are the exocrine clusters of the pancreas that make digestive enzymes called?
options: The follicles
The chief cells
The pancreatic islets
The acini
questions.why: The pancreas is mostly made of acini, small clusters of exocrine cells that make digestive enzymes and release them into ducts leading to the small intestine. The acini are not endocrine tissue. The endocrine tissue is the scattered pancreatic islets.
notes: Follicles are the hollow spheres of the thyroid gland. They would be the answer for the thyroid's microscopic units.
Chief cells are the main cells of the parathyroid glands. Pick them for the parathyroids.
The islets are the endocrine clusters of the pancreas, which release hormones into the blood. Pick them for the endocrine tissue.
Correct. The acini are the enzyme-making exocrine clusters.
questions.answerText: The acini

questions.q: What is the main hormone-producing cell of the parathyroid glands called?
options: The parafollicular cell
The follicular cell
The chief cell
The acinar cell
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are usually four small glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid. Their main hormone-producing cell is the chief cell. The thyroid next door has follicular cells and parafollicular cells instead, so the cell names separate the two glands.
notes: Parafollicular cells, or C cells, lie between thyroid follicles. They would be the answer for the cells scattered between follicles.
Follicular cells form the walls of thyroid follicles. Pick them for the thyroid.
Correct. Chief cells are the main cells of the parathyroids.
Acinar cells make up the exocrine acini of the pancreas. Pick them for the cells that make digestive enzymes.
questions.answerText: The chief cell

questions.q: A small, cone-shaped endocrine gland sits in the posterior roof of the third ventricle. Which gland is it?
options: The pituitary gland
An adrenal gland
The thyroid gland
The pineal gland
questions.why: The pineal gland is a small, cone-shaped gland, named for its likeness to a pine cone. It sits in the posterior roof of the third ventricle as part of the epithalamus of the diencephalon. The hypothalamus lies below it, in the floor of the same ventricle.
notes: The pituitary hangs below the brain in the sella turcica, not in the roof of a ventricle.
The adrenal glands cap the kidneys in the abdomen, nowhere near the brain.
The thyroid is in the anterior neck below the larynx, not in the brain.
Correct. The pineal gland is the cone-shaped gland in the roof of the third ventricle.
questions.answerText: The pineal gland

questions.q: Which structure links the nervous and endocrine systems and directs the pituitary gland?
options: The pineal gland
The thymus
The hypothalamus
The thyroid gland
questions.why: The hypothalamus is a region of the diencephalon that acts as a bridge between the nervous and endocrine systems. Its neurosecretory cells send signals to the anterior pituitary through portal blood vessels and send axons into the posterior pituitary. This control is why the hypothalamus is called a neuroendocrine organ.
notes: The pineal gland is in the brain too, in the roof of the third ventricle, but it does not control the pituitary.
The thymus sits in the mediastinum behind the sternum. It is not part of the brain and does not control the pituitary.
Correct. The hypothalamus is the neuroendocrine link that controls the pituitary.
The thyroid is a gland in the anterior neck. It is not part of the brain and does not control the pituitary.
questions.answerText: The hypothalamus

questions.q: The hypophyseal portal system carries hypothalamic signals to which part of the pituitary gland?
options: The sella turcica
The infundibulum only
The posterior lobe
The anterior lobe
questions.why: The hypophyseal portal system is a set of blood vessels running from capillaries in the hypothalamus down to a second capillary bed in the anterior lobe of the pituitary. It carries hypothalamic signals directly to the anterior lobe, which is glandular and cannot be reached by nerve fibers. The posterior lobe is linked by a nerve tract instead.
notes: The sella turcica is the bony pocket around the gland, not a part of the pituitary. It would be the answer for the gland's protective seat.
The portal vessels run along the infundibulum, but their destination is the anterior lobe. The stalk is the route, not the target.
The posterior lobe receives a tract of nerve fibers, not portal vessels. Pick it for the lobe linked by axons.
Correct. The portal vessels serve the glandular anterior lobe.
questions.answerText: The anterior lobe

questions.q: Which adrenal cortex zone lies just beneath the connective tissue capsule?
options: Zona reticularis
Zona glomerulosa
Zona fasciculata
Adrenal medulla
questions.why: The adrenal gland is wrapped in a connective tissue capsule. Just beneath it is the zona glomerulosa, the thin outer zone of the cortex, whose cells form rounded clusters. Below it come the zona fasciculata and then the zona reticularis, which borders the medulla.
notes: The zona reticularis is the deepest zone, against the medulla. It would be the answer for the zone with a branching network of cells.
Correct. The glomerulosa is the thin outer zone under the capsule.
The zona fasciculata is the thick middle zone, with cells in straight columns. Pick it for the widest zone.
The medulla is the inner core of modified nervous tissue, as far from the capsule as possible. Pick it for the part made of chromaffin cells.
questions.answerText: Zona glomerulosa

questions.q: Viewing a slide of the adrenal cortex from the capsule inward, which zone do you reach immediately after the zona glomerulosa?
options: Zona fasciculata
Adrenal medulla
Adrenal capsule
Zona reticularis
questions.why: The adrenal cortex is layered in a fixed order from outside in: capsule, zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis, then the medulla. The zona fasciculata comes right after the glomerulosa and is the thickest of the three zones, with its cells lined up in straight columns.
notes: Correct. The fasciculata is the middle zone, directly under the glomerulosa.
The medulla is reached only after passing all three cortical zones. It would be the answer for the inner core.
The capsule is the outer covering, found before the zona glomerulosa, not after it. Pick it for the first layer at the surface.
The zona reticularis comes after the fasciculata, as the deepest zone against the medulla. Pick it for the zone reached last.
questions.answerText: Zona fasciculata

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the tissue of the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla?
options: Both are glandular tissue arranged in zones
Both are modified nervous tissue
Cortex is modified nervous tissue; medulla is glandular tissue in three zones
Cortex is glandular in three zones; medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue
questions.why: The adrenal gland is two glands in one because its two regions are made of different tissues. The outer cortex is glandular tissue, organized into the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis. The inner medulla is modified nervous tissue belonging to the sympathetic nervous system, made of chromaffin cells.
notes: Only the cortex is zoned glandular tissue. The medulla is modified nervous tissue with chromaffin cells.
Only the medulla is nervous tissue. The cortex is glandular, which is why the adrenal gland is described as two glands in one.
This reverses the two regions. The zones belong to the outer cortex, and the nervous tissue is in the core.
Correct. The two regions come from different tissues.
questions.answerText: Cortex is glandular in three zones; medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue

questions.q: What runs down through the infundibulum to connect the hypothalamus with the posterior lobe of the pituitary?
options: A lymphatic duct
Portal blood vessels
Cerebrospinal fluid
A tract of nerve fibers
questions.why: The posterior lobe of the pituitary is nervous tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus. Neurons in the hypothalamus send their axons down through the infundibulum as a tract of nerve fibers, and these axons end in the posterior lobe. Hormones made in the hypothalamus travel down these axons and are stored in the posterior lobe until release.
notes: Lymphatic ducts return lymph to the veins in the neck and chest. They play no part in connecting the hypothalamus to the pituitary.
Portal vessels link the hypothalamus to the anterior lobe, not the posterior lobe. Pick them for the hypophyseal portal system.
Cerebrospinal fluid fills the third ventricle above the pituitary but does not run down the stalk to the posterior lobe. This choice mixes up nearby space with a physical connection.
Correct. Hypothalamic axons run through the stalk and end in the posterior lobe.
questions.answerText: A tract of nerve fibers

questions.q: The pancreas does an endocrine job. What is its other major role?
options: It is an organ that makes bile
It is an exocrine organ that makes digestive enzymes
It is a lymphatic organ that filters blood
It is an organ that absorbs nutrients
questions.why: The pancreas is a mixed organ. Its endocrine part is the pancreatic islets, which release hormones into the blood. Its exocrine part, which makes up most of the organ, is the acini, clusters of cells that make digestive enzymes and send them through ducts into the small intestine.
notes: Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. It would be the answer for the liver.
Correct. The acini make digestive enzymes and send them through ducts.
Filtering blood as a lymphatic organ is the role of the spleen, which lies near the pancreas. Pick the spleen for that job.
Absorbing nutrients is the main job of the small intestine. Pick the small intestine for that role.
questions.answerText: It is an exocrine organ that makes digestive enzymes

questions.q: The kidneys are not endocrine glands, but they contain endocrine cells. Where in the kidney are these cells found?
options: In the renal cortex, including the juxtaglomerular cells
In the adrenal medulla that caps the kidney
In the renal pelvis, where urine collects
In the fibrous renal capsule around the kidney
questions.why: The kidneys are urinary organs, but they are one of several organs that also contain endocrine cells. These cells sit in the renal cortex, the outer region of the kidney, and include the juxtaglomerular cells in the walls of the afferent arterioles. The adrenal gland rests on top of the kidney, but it is a separate gland and not part of the kidney.
notes: Correct. The kidney's endocrine cells are in the renal cortex, including the juxtaglomerular cells in the walls of the afferent arterioles.
The adrenal gland sits on the superior pole of the kidney, but it is a separate endocrine gland with its own capsule, not part of the kidney. Its medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue.
The renal pelvis is the funnel inside the kidney that collects urine and passes it to the ureter. It drains urine and is not where the kidney's endocrine cells are.
The renal capsule is the fibrous connective tissue covering of the kidney. It protects the organ and does not hold its endocrine cells.
questions.answerText: In the renal cortex, including the juxtaglomerular cells

questions.q: What are the male gonads called?
options: The prostate glands
The testes
The ovaries
The adrenal glands
questions.why: The testes are the paired male gonads, located in the scrotum. Like the ovaries, they are mixed organs: they produce sperm and also act as endocrine glands, secreting testosterone into the blood.
notes: The prostate is a single accessory gland of the male reproductive system below the bladder, not a gonad. Pick it for the gland around the urethra.
Correct. The testes are the male gonads, in the scrotum.
The ovaries are the female gonads, in the pelvis beside the uterus. Pick them for the female gonads.
The adrenal glands cap the kidneys. They would be the answer for the suprarenal glands.
questions.answerText: The testes

questions.q: A pituitary tumor enlarges and presses upward on the optic chiasm, causing loss of peripheral vision. What anatomical feature forces the tumor to expand upward?
options: The gland lies in the third ventricle
The gland has two lobes of different tissues
The gland hangs from the infundibulum
The gland is boxed inside the bony sella turcica
questions.why: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica, a pocket of the sphenoid bone with a bony floor and bony front and back walls. When a pituitary tumor grows, that bone holds it in below, in front, and behind, so it usually expands upward. Just above the pituitary lies the optic chiasm, and pressure there can cause a loss of peripheral vision.
notes: The pituitary does not lie in the third ventricle; the third ventricle is above it, bordered by the hypothalamus. This choice confuses the pituitary's position with that of the hypothalamus.
The two lobes explain how each connects to the hypothalamus, not the direction a tumor grows. This would be the answer for why the lobes link by different routes.
The infundibulum is a soft stalk and does not restrict growth in any direction. Pick it for what connects the pituitary to the hypothalamus.
Correct. Bone surrounds the gland on most sides, so growth goes upward.
questions.answerText: The gland is boxed inside the bony sella turcica

questions.q: A patient develops a goiter, a swelling visible at the front of the neck. Which gland has enlarged?
options: The thyroid gland
The thymus
The adrenal gland
The pituitary gland
questions.why: The thyroid gland lies in the anterior neck just under the skin, below the larynx and wrapped around the trachea. Because it is so superficial, an enlarged thyroid, called a goiter, shows as a visible and palpable swelling at the front of the neck.
notes: Correct. A goiter is an enlarged thyroid.
The thymus is behind the sternum in the mediastinum, hidden by bone. It would be the answer for the organ that shrinks after puberty.
The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys deep in the abdomen. An adrenal mass is usually found on imaging, not seen.
The pituitary is deep in the skull, in the sella turcica, so its enlargement cannot be seen in the neck. Pick it for a tumor that affects vision.
questions.answerText: The thyroid gland

questions.q: An imaging study ordered to view a kidney also shows a mass sitting on top of it. Which endocrine gland was imaged by chance?
options: The thyroid gland
The pineal gland
The adrenal gland
The thymus
questions.why: Each adrenal gland rests on the superior pole of a kidney. Because the two organs are so close, imaging ordered for the kidney usually captures the adrenal too, and an adrenal mass is sometimes discovered by accident this way.
notes: The thyroid is in the neck, far from the kidney. Pick it for a swelling at the front of the neck.
The pineal gland is in the brain, in the roof of the third ventricle. It would be the answer for a brain image.
Correct. The adrenal gland rests on the superior pole of the kidney.
The thymus is in the mediastinum behind the sternum. Pick it for chest imaging, not kidney imaging.
questions.answerText: The adrenal gland

questions.q: During thyroid surgery, the surgeon carefully spares several tiny glands on the back surface of the thyroid. Which glands are they?
options: The pancreatic islets
The adrenal glands
The thyroid follicles
