The parathyroid glands
questions.why: The parathyroid glands, usually four, are tiny glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, each in its own thin capsule. The thyroid's position just under the skin of the anterior neck makes surgery on it accessible, but because the parathyroids sit on its back, the surgeon must find and protect them.
notes: The pancreatic islets are scattered inside the pancreas in the abdomen, not on the thyroid.
The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys, far from the neck.
The thyroid follicles are inside the thyroid itself, the organ being operated on. They are microscopic units, not separate glands on its surface.
Correct. The parathyroids sit on the back of the thyroid lobes.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid glands

questions.q: A gland sits below the hypothalamus in a bony saddle and has one lobe of glandular epithelium and one lobe of nervous tissue. Which gland is it?
options: The thyroid gland
The adrenal gland
The pineal gland
The pituitary gland
questions.why: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, below the hypothalamus. It has an anterior lobe of glandular epithelial tissue, the adenohypophysis, and a posterior lobe of nervous tissue, the neurohypophysis. The adrenal gland also combines glandular and nervous tissue, but as a cortex around a medulla rather than as two lobes.
notes: The thyroid has two lobes, but both are glandular and it sits in the neck, not in a bony saddle. Pick it for the gland joined by an isthmus.
The adrenal gland also has a glandular part and a nervous part, but they are an outer cortex and inner medulla, and the gland sits on the kidney. Pick it for that layout.
The pineal gland is in the brain but sits in the roof of the third ventricle and has no lobes. It would be the answer for the cone-shaped gland of the epithalamus.
Correct. The sella turcica and the two different lobes identify the pituitary.
questions.answerText: The pituitary gland

questions.q: Endocrine glands release their hormones into the blood rather than through ducts. Why does this suit hormones that must reach organs far from the gland?
options: Hormones act only on the gland that makes them
The blood carries the hormone throughout the body
Hormones reach only cells touching the gland
Ducts would carry hormones to every organ faster
questions.why: An endocrine gland has no duct. It secretes its hormone into the tissue fluid around it, the hormone enters nearby capillaries, and the circulating blood carries it to nearly every part of the body. This is how a gland in the neck or the skull can signal target cells in organs far away.
notes: A hormone that acted only on its own gland would not need the blood at all. This misconception ignores that hormones signal distant target cells.
Correct. Circulating blood reaches nearly every tissue.
Signals limited to neighboring cells are local signals, not hormones. Hormones are defined by traveling in the blood.
Ducts deliver a product to one place, such as a surface or a cavity. That is how exocrine glands work, and it would not spread a hormone to distant organs.
questions.answerText: The blood carries the hormone throughout the body

questions.q: Hormones travel in the blood to nearly every cell, yet each hormone affects only certain cells. What makes a cell a target cell for a hormone?
options: It has a duct leading to the bloodstream
It makes the same hormone itself
It carries the receptor for that hormone
It is the cell closest to the gland
questions.why: A hormone in the blood passes nearly every cell, but only target cells respond to it. A target cell is one that carries the receptor for that particular hormone. Cells without the receptor are exposed to the hormone but do not react, which is how one hormone can have very specific effects.
notes: Ducts belong to exocrine glands, and no duct leads to the blood. This choice mixes up gland structure with how cells respond.
Making a hormone describes an endocrine cell, not a target cell. A target cell responds to the hormone rather than producing it.
Correct. Only cells with the matching receptor respond.
Distance from the gland does not decide a response, because the blood carries hormones everywhere. This misconception treats hormones like local signals.
questions.answerText: It carries the receptor for that hormone

questions.q: One part of the adrenal gland is supplied by preganglionic sympathetic nerve fibers and works like a sympathetic ganglion. Which part is it, and what explains its tie to the sympathetic system?
options: The adrenal medulla, modified sympathetic nervous tissue
The adrenal cortex, glandular tissue in three zones
The adrenal capsule, the connective tissue covering
The zona glomerulosa, the outer zone of the cortex
questions.why: The adrenal medulla is the inner core of the adrenal gland, and it is modified nervous tissue that develops from the neural crest, the same embryonic tissue that forms the sympathetic ganglia. Its chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic neurons with no axons or dendrites. Preganglionic sympathetic fibers reach them directly, and they release their product straight into the blood.
notes: Correct. The medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue made of chromaffin cells.
The cortex is the outer region, made of glandular epithelial tissue from mesoderm in three zones. It is not nervous tissue and does not work like a ganglion.
The capsule is the connective tissue covering of the gland. It is not nervous tissue.
The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer zone of the cortex, made of glandular tissue just under the capsule. It is the part farthest from the nervous core.
questions.answerText: The adrenal medulla, modified sympathetic nervous tissue

questions.q: A blockage in the main pancreatic duct means pancreatic juice cannot reach the small intestine. Which part of the pancreas still delivers its product normally, and why?
options: The islets, because they release hormones into the blood
The acini, because they bypass the duct through capillaries
Neither part, because both depend on the duct
The acini, because they release enzymes into the blood
questions.why: The pancreas has two kinds of tissue with two delivery routes. The exocrine acini make digestive enzymes and send them through the pancreatic ducts to the small intestine, so a blocked duct stops that flow. The endocrine pancreatic islets are ductless and release hormones directly into the blood, so the blockage does not affect them.
notes: Correct. The islets do not use ducts, so a duct blockage does not stop them.
Acini have no route around the ducts; their enzymes must travel through them. This misconception gives exocrine tissue an endocrine pathway.
Only the exocrine acini depend on the duct. The endocrine islets are ductless and keep delivering hormones to the blood.
The acini send their digestive enzymes through ducts, so they are the part blocked here. Pick the acini for the exocrine tissue affected by the obstruction.
questions.answerText: The islets, because they release hormones into the blood

questions.q: Unlike most endocrine glands, the thyroid stores its product in bulk outside its cells. Where is it stored?
options: In the parathyroid glands on its back surface
In the isthmus that joins the two lobes
Inside the parafollicular cells
In the colloid at the center of each follicle
questions.why: Each thyroid follicle is a hollow sphere of follicular cells surrounding a central space filled with colloid. The thyroid stores the material it uses to make its hormones in this colloid, outside the cells, which is unusual among endocrine glands. This store lets the gland hold a large reserve.
notes: The parathyroids are separate glands with their own chief cells. They do not store thyroid products.
The isthmus is just a bridge of ordinary thyroid tissue across the trachea. It would be the answer for the part connecting the two lobes.
Parafollicular cells, or C cells, lie between follicles and are not the thyroid's storage site. Pick them for the cells scattered in the spaces between follicles.
Correct. The follicle's center is the thyroid's storage space.
questions.answerText: In the colloid at the center of each follicle

questions.q: Adipose tissue is not an endocrine gland, but it contains endocrine cells. Which cells are they?
options: Juxtaglomerular cells
Keratinocytes
Adipocytes (fat cells)
Enteroendocrine cells
questions.why: Many organs and tissues whose main job is something else still contain endocrine cells. In adipose tissue, the endocrine cells are the adipocytes, the same fat cells that store fat, so one cell type does both jobs. Other examples are the keratinocytes of the skin, the enteroendocrine cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney.
notes: Juxtaglomerular cells are endocrine cells of the kidney, in the walls of the afferent arterioles in the renal cortex. They are not part of adipose tissue.
Keratinocytes are the endocrine cells of the skin, in the epidermis, which begin making a hormone when exposed to sunlight. They are not found in adipose tissue.
Correct. In adipose tissue the endocrine cells are the adipocytes themselves.
Enteroendocrine cells are scattered in the mucosa of the stomach and small intestine. They belong to the digestive lining, not to fat tissue.
questions.answerText: Adipocytes (fat cells)

questions.q: Which of these is a pure endocrine gland, rather than a mixed organ with another major role?
options: The pancreas
The ovary
The thyroid gland
The testis
questions.why: Pure endocrine glands do nothing but make hormones; examples are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, and adrenal glands. Mixed organs do an endocrine job alongside another role, so only part of the organ is endocrine tissue. The pancreas also makes digestive enzymes, and the gonads also make sex cells.
notes: The pancreas is mixed, with exocrine acini that make digestive enzymes alongside its endocrine islets. Pick it for a mixed organ in the abdomen.
The ovary is mixed, producing eggs as well as hormones. It would be the answer for a female gonad.
Correct. The thyroid's whole job is making hormones.
The testis is mixed, producing sperm as well as testosterone. Pick it for a male gonad.
questions.answerText: The thyroid gland

questions.q: On a kidney model, a small cap-shaped gland sits on the superior pole of each kidney. What is it?
options: The spleen
The liver
The pancreas
The suprarenal (adrenal) gland
questions.why: The suprarenal glands, also called adrenal glands, sit like caps on the superior pole of each kidney. Supra means above and renal means kidney, and ad-renal means near the kidney, so both names describe the location. They are endocrine glands, but they are identified on the kidney model in the urinary lab.
notes: The spleen is a lymphatic organ in the upper left abdomen, beside the left kidney, not on top of either kidney. It would be the answer for the organ near the left kidney that filters blood.
The liver fills the upper right abdomen above the right kidney and is the reason the right kidney sits lower. It is a large organ, not a small cap on each kidney.
The pancreas lies across the posterior abdomen in front of the kidneys, with its tail reaching toward the spleen. Pick it if the question asked for the gland that sits behind the stomach.
Correct. The suprarenal (adrenal) gland caps the superior pole of each kidney.
questions.answerText: The suprarenal (adrenal) gland

questions.q: The ovaries are listed both with the reproductive organs and with the endocrine glands. Which statement explains why?
options: They produce oocytes and also produce milk
They house the embryo and also secrete hormones
They store sperm and also secrete hormones
They produce oocytes and also secrete hormones
questions.why: The ovaries are the female gonads, so they make the gametes (oocytes), which places them in the reproductive system. They also secrete sex hormones directly into the blood, which makes them endocrine glands as well. The testes have the same double role in males.
notes: Milk is made by the mammary glands, not the ovaries. Pick milk production for the mammary glands.
The embryo is housed in the uterus, not the ovary. Pick this role for the uterus, which holds the developing embryo and fetus.
The ovaries do not store sperm. Sperm are stored in the male epididymis. Pick sperm storage for a question about the epididymis.
Correct. The ovaries make oocytes and secrete hormones.
questions.answerText: They produce oocytes and also secrete hormones

questions.q: Which is the largest purely endocrine gland in the body?
options: The adrenal gland
The pancreas
The thyroid gland
The pituitary gland
questions.why: A purely endocrine gland is one whose only job is to make hormones. Among those, the thyroid gland is the largest, with two lobes lying against the trachea in the anterior neck. Larger organs such as the pancreas contain endocrine tissue, but they also have other jobs, so they are not purely endocrine.
notes: The adrenal glands are purely endocrine but much smaller than the thyroid. Pick them if the question asked which gland has an outer cortex and an inner medulla.

The pancreas is larger than the thyroid, but it is a mixed gland. Most of it is exocrine tissue that makes digestive enzymes, and only its scattered islets are endocrine, so it is not purely endocrine.
Correct. The thyroid is the largest gland whose only job is making hormones.
The pituitary is purely endocrine but only about the size of a pea. Choose it if the question asked which gland sits in the sella turcica.
questions.answerText: The thyroid gland

questions.q: A patient's first sign of a pituitary tumor is a loss of peripheral vision. Which fact about the gland's location best explains this?
options: Its bony pocket forces it to grow up into the optic chiasm
It sits behind the eye, pressing directly on the retina
It lies in the occipital lobe, next to the visual cortex
It sits inside the orbit, right beside the optic nerve
questions.why: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica, a pocket of the sphenoid bone with a bony floor and bony front and back walls. A growing tumor is held in by that bone, so it usually expands upward, and just above the gland lies the optic chiasm, where the optic nerves cross. Pressure on the chiasm can cause a loss of peripheral vision, and that can be the first sign the gland has enlarged.
notes: Correct. Trapped by the sella turcica, the growing gland pushes up on the optic chiasm.
The retina lines the back of the eyeball, far from the pituitary. A problem there would point to the eye itself, not a gland in the skull base.

The occipital lobe of the cerebrum holds the visual cortex, but it is at the back of the head, far above and behind the pituitary. Pick the occipital lobe if the question asked where visual information is processed.
The pituitary lies in the middle of the cranial floor, not in the orbit. The optic nerve does run through the orbit, so this would describe a tumor of the eye socket rather than the pituitary.
questions.answerText: Its bony pocket forces it to grow up into the optic chiasm

questions.q: Which slender stalk connects the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus?
options: The optic chiasm
The sella turcica
The infundibulum
The mammillary body
questions.why: The infundibulum is the slender stalk that hangs from the floor of the hypothalamus and attaches to the pituitary gland below it. Nerve fibers to the posterior lobe and the portal blood vessels to the anterior lobe both run along this stalk. The word means funnel, and the same name is used for the funnel-shaped end of the uterine tube.
notes: The optic chiasm is where the optic nerves cross, just in front of and above the infundibulum. Choose it if the question asked what structure a pituitary tumor presses on to cause vision loss.

The sella turcica is the saddle-shaped pocket of the sphenoid bone that cradles the pituitary. It holds the gland from below rather than connecting it to the brain; pick it if the question asked what bony pocket protects the pituitary.
Correct. The infundibulum is the stalk joining the hypothalamus and the pituitary.

The mammillary bodies are two small round bumps on the underside of the hypothalamus, just behind the infundibulum. Pick them if the question asked which paired bumps lie on the floor of the hypothalamus.
questions.answerText: The infundibulum

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the anterior and posterior pituitary lobes by tissue type?
options: Both lobes are glandular epithelium, joined by a stalk of nerve fibers
Both lobes are nervous tissue that grew down from the hypothalamus
Anterior lobe is glandular epithelium; posterior lobe is nervous tissue
Anterior lobe is nervous tissue; posterior lobe is glandular epithelium
questions.why: The two lobes of the pituitary come from two different tissues. The anterior lobe, or adenohypophysis (adeno means gland), is glandular epithelial tissue. The posterior lobe, or neurohypophysis (neuro means nerve), is nervous tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus itself.
notes: Only the anterior lobe is glandular epithelium. The posterior lobe is itself nervous tissue, continuous with the nerve fibers in the stalk.
Only the posterior lobe is an extension of the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium, which is why it needs blood vessels rather than nerve fibers to receive signals.
Correct. The adenohypophysis is glandular and the neurohypophysis is nervous tissue.
This swaps the lobes. The prefixes in the other names give it away: the neurohypophysis is the nervous lobe, and it is the posterior one.
questions.answerText: Anterior lobe is glandular epithelium; posterior lobe is nervous tissue

questions.q: How does the hypothalamus connect to each lobe of the pituitary gland?
options: Anterior lobe by portal blood vessels; posterior lobe by a nerve fiber tract
Both lobes by nerve fiber tracts running through the optic chiasm
Anterior lobe by a nerve fiber tract; posterior lobe by portal blood vessels
Both lobes by portal blood vessels running through the sella turcica
questions.why: The tissue of each lobe tells you its link. The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium, so the hypothalamus reaches it through blood vessels, the hypophyseal portal system that runs down the infundibulum. The posterior lobe is nervous tissue, so the hypothalamus reaches it through a tract of nerve fibers that runs down the same stalk.
notes: Correct. Blood vessels serve the glandular anterior lobe, and nerve fibers serve the nervous posterior lobe.
Only the posterior lobe is linked by nerve fibers, and they run down the infundibulum, not through the optic chiasm. The optic chiasm is the crossing of the optic nerves just in front of the stalk.
This swaps the two links. The posterior lobe is the nervous lobe, so it is the one connected by nerve fibers, and the glandular anterior lobe is reached by blood vessels.

Only the anterior lobe is linked by the portal vessels, and those vessels run down the infundibulum, not through the bone of the sella turcica. Pick the portal system if the question asked how the anterior lobe receives hypothalamic signals.
questions.answerText: Anterior lobe by portal blood vessels; posterior lobe by a nerve fiber tract

questions.q: Which part of the thyroid gland is the bridge of tissue crossing the front of the trachea that connects the two lobes?
options: The thyroid follicle
The infundibulum
The isthmus
The parathyroid gland
questions.why: The thyroid has two lateral lobes, one on each side of the trachea. The isthmus is the narrow band of thyroid tissue that crosses the front of the trachea and joins them, giving the gland its butterfly or H shape. The word isthmus means a narrow strip connecting two larger parts, which is why the uterine tube also has an isthmus.
notes: A thyroid follicle is a microscopic hollow sphere of cells that stores colloid. It is far too small to bridge the two lobes; choose it if the question asked which units make up the gland under the microscope.
The infundibulum is the stalk that connects the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus. Pick it if the question asked what links the pituitary to the brain.
Correct. The isthmus is the bridge of tissue connecting the two thyroid lobes.
The parathyroid glands are tiny separate glands on the back of the thyroid lobes, not a bridge across the front. Pick them if the question asked which glands sit on the posterior thyroid surface.
questions.answerText: The isthmus

questions.q: Where are the parathyroid glands, and how many are there usually?
options: On the posterior surface of the thyroid; usually four
On the anterior surface of the thyroid; usually two
On the posterior surface of the thyroid; usually two
In the mediastinum behind the sternum; usually one
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are small, round glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes. Most people have four, a superior and an inferior gland on each lobe, and each has its own thin capsule. Because they are so small and sit right on the back of the thyroid, surgeons must take care to spare them during thyroid surgery.
notes: Correct. There are usually four parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid.
The front of the thyroid is covered by the isthmus and the lobes, not by the parathyroids. Students who choose this know the glands are tied to the thyroid but forget they sit behind it.
The location is right, but the usual number is four, two on each lobe. Picking two comes from counting one gland per lobe instead of two.
This describes the thymus, a single gland in the chest behind the sternum. Pick it if the question asked which gland is large in childhood and shrinks after puberty.
questions.answerText: On the posterior surface of the thyroid; usually four

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes thyroid follicles and colloid?
options: Follicles hold developing oocytes; colloid is the fluid that fills a mature follicle
Follicles are the four small glands; colloid is the tissue joining them together
Follicles are solid cords of cells; colloid is the fluid between those cords
Follicles are hollow spheres of cells; colloid is the fluid stored in their centers
questions.why: Under the microscope, the thyroid is made of many small hollow spheres called thyroid follicles. Each follicle is a ring of follicular cells around a central space filled with colloid, a thick, protein-rich fluid where the thyroid's hormone material is stored. Parafollicular cells (C cells) sit scattered between the follicles.
notes: This describes ovarian follicles in the ovary, which hold oocytes, and the fluid inside a mature ovarian follicle is not called colloid. The word follicle means a small sac in both organs, which is the source of the mix-up.
The four small glands are the parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid. Follicles are microscopic units inside the thyroid, and colloid is a fluid, not a connecting tissue.
Thyroid follicles are hollow, not solid cords, and the colloid sits inside them, not between them. Packed cords of cells with no colloid describe parathyroid tissue.
Correct. Follicles are hollow spheres of cells, and colloid fills their centers.
questions.answerText: Follicles are hollow spheres of cells; colloid is the fluid stored in their centers

questions.q: Which statement correctly names the two regions of an adrenal gland and the tissue of each?
options: Outer cortex and inner medulla, both of glandular tissue
Outer cortex of glandular tissue; inner medulla of nervous tissue
Outer cortex of nervous tissue; inner medulla of glandular tissue
Outer medulla of nervous tissue; inner cortex of glandular tissue
questions.why: Each adrenal gland is really two glands in one. The outer adrenal cortex forms most of the gland and is glandular tissue arranged in three zones. The inner adrenal medulla is modified nervous tissue that belongs to the sympathetic nervous system, so it is built from a different tissue than the cortex around it.
notes: Only the cortex is glandular tissue. The medulla is modified nervous tissue, which is why the adrenal is described as two glands in one.
Correct. The cortex is outer glandular tissue, and the medulla is inner modified nervous tissue.
The positions are right, but the tissues are swapped. The medulla is the part that belongs to the sympathetic nervous system, so it is the nervous tissue.
This puts the medulla on the outside. As in the kidney, cortex means the outer layer and medulla means the inner core.
questions.answerText: Outer cortex of glandular tissue; inner medulla of nervous tissue

questions.q: Which list names only organs whose main job is not endocrine but that still contain endocrine tissue?
options: Heart, thyroid, kidneys
Thyroid, adrenal glands, pituitary
Pineal gland, parathyroids, skin
Heart, kidneys, stomach
questions.why: Many organs whose main job is something else still contain endocrine cells. The heart has hormone-making cells in the muscle of its atrial walls, the kidneys have endocrine cells in the renal cortex, and the stomach and small intestine have enteroendocrine cells scattered in their mucosa. The liver, skin, adipose tissue, and placenta also belong to this group.
notes: The heart and kidneys fit, but the thyroid is a purely endocrine gland, the largest one in the body. One pure gland in the list makes it wrong.
These are all pure endocrine glands, whose only job is making hormones. Pick this list if the question asked for glands that do nothing but make hormones.
The skin fits, but the pineal gland and parathyroid glands are purely endocrine glands. Choose them if the question asked for small glands whose only job is making hormones.
Correct. The heart, kidneys, and stomach each have other main jobs but contain endocrine tissue.
questions.answerText: Heart, kidneys, stomach

questions.q: A pituitary tumor grows upward out of the sella turcica. Which structure, lying just above and in front of the gland, is it most likely to press on?
options: The hypophyseal portal veins.
The optic chiasm.
The body of the sphenoid bone.
The nasal cavity.
questions.why: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped pocket of the sphenoid bone. The bone forms the floor and the front and back walls of the pocket, so the open side faces up. The optic chiasm lies just above and in front of the gland. A tumor that grows up out of the pocket meets the optic chiasm first.
notes: The portal veins run down along the infundibulum to the anterior lobe. They are part of the gland's own connection, not the structure above and in front of it.
Correct. The optic chiasm lies just above and in front of the pituitary, so an upward-growing tumor reaches it.
The sphenoid bone forms the floor and walls of the sella turcica, below and around the gland. A tumor growing upward moves away from it.
The nasal cavity lies below the sphenoid bone, whose body forms the floor of the sella turcica (the sphenoid also helps form the roof of the nasal cavity). A tumor growing upward moves away from it.
questions.answerText: The optic chiasm.

questions.q: On a pituitary slide, one lobe looks pale and fibrous, with scattered nuclei of glial cells among many axons. Which lobe is it, and how is it linked to the hypothalamus?
options: The posterior lobe, linked by the hypophyseal portal system.
The anterior lobe, linked by the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract.
The anterior lobe, linked by the hypophyseal portal system.
The posterior lobe, linked by the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract.
questions.why: The slide tells you the tissue type. Pale, fibrous-looking tissue of axons with scattered pituicyte nuclei is nervous tissue, so it is the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), an extension of the hypothalamus. Because it is nervous tissue, it connects by nerve fibers, the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract, which runs down through the infundibulum. The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium linked by the hypophyseal portal system.
notes: The lobe is right, but the portal system links the hypothalamus to the anterior lobe. The posterior lobe connects by nerve fibers.
The tract runs to the posterior lobe, and the anterior lobe on a slide is packed gland cells, not pale fibrous tissue.
The anterior lobe is glandular epithelium, densely packed gland cells in cords, and it is linked by blood vessels. The pale, fibrous lobe is the posterior lobe.
Correct. Pale, fibrous tissue of axons and pituicytes is the posterior lobe, linked to the hypothalamus by nerve fibers through the infundibulum.
questions.answerText: The posterior lobe, linked by the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract.

questions.q: A head injury tears the infundibulum completely. Which links between the hypothalamus and the pituitary are cut?
options: Both the nerve tract to the posterior lobe and the portal veins to the anterior lobe.
Only the nerve tract to the posterior lobe; the anterior lobe has no link there.
Neither link, since both lobes connect through the sella turcica instead.
Only the portal veins to the anterior lobe; the posterior lobe links elsewhere.
questions.why: The infundibulum is the stalk that hangs the pituitary from the hypothalamus. The posterior lobe connects by nerve fibers, the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract, which runs down through the stalk. The anterior lobe connects by blood vessels: the hypophyseal portal veins carry blood down along the stalk from the primary capillary plexus to the secondary plexus in the anterior lobe. A complete tear of the stalk cuts both links.
notes: Correct. The tract runs down through the infundibulum and the portal veins run down along it, so tearing the stalk cuts both.
The anterior lobe is linked by the hypophyseal portal veins, which run down along the infundibulum, so they are torn as well.
The sella turcica is the bony pocket that holds the gland. The links to the hypothalamus run through and along the infundibulum.
The posterior lobe is linked by the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract, which runs through the infundibulum, so it is torn as well.
questions.answerText: Both the nerve tract to the posterior lobe and the portal veins to the anterior lobe.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the chief cells and the oxyphil cells of the parathyroid glands?
options: Chief cells are larger and stain dark pink; oxyphil cells are small and make up most of the gland.
Chief cells and oxyphil cells look alike, but only oxyphil cells make the gland's hormone.
Chief cells form the walls of follicles; oxyphil cells sit in the colloid at the center.
Chief cells are small and numerous; oxyphil cells are larger, fewer, and stain dark pink.
questions.why: Parathyroid tissue is packed cords and clusters of cells with capillaries between them. Chief cells (principal cells) are the small, numerous cells with round nuclei and pale cytoplasm that make up most of the gland, and they are its hormone-making cells. Oxyphil cells are larger and much fewer, and their cytoplasm is packed with mitochondria, so it stains dark pink. Oxyphil cells become more common with age.
notes: This swaps the two. The small, numerous cells are chief cells, and the larger dark pink cells are oxyphil cells.
The two look different on a slide, and the chief cells are the hormone-making cells. The function of oxyphil cells is not fully understood.
Follicles and colloid belong to the thyroid. Parathyroid tissue has no follicles and no colloid, only packed cords of cells.
Correct. Chief cells make up most of the gland, while oxyphil cells are larger, fewer, and packed with mitochondria that stain dark pink.
questions.answerText: Chief cells are small and numerous; oxyphil cells are larger, fewer, and stain dark pink.

questions.q: A slide shows packed cords of small cells with capillaries between them, no follicles, and no colloid. A few larger cells with dark pink, granular cytoplasm are scattered among them. Which gland is this, and what are the larger cells?
options: The parathyroid gland; the larger cells are oxyphil cells.
The parathyroid gland; the larger cells are chief cells.
The thyroid gland; the larger cells are follicular cells.
The thyroid gland; the larger cells are parafollicular cells.
questions.why: First identify the gland. Follicles and colloid mean thyroid, so packed cords of cells with no colloid mean parathyroid. Then identify the cells. On a parathyroid slide the small, plentiful cells are chief cells, and the larger cells with dark pink, granular cytoplasm (packed with mitochondria) are oxyphil cells.
notes: Correct. Packed cords with no colloid mean parathyroid, and the larger dark pink cells are oxyphil cells.
The gland is right, but chief cells are the small, numerous cells that make up most of the tissue. The larger dark pink cells are oxyphil cells.
Follicular cells are simple cuboidal cells lining each follicle around the colloid. A slide with no follicles is not thyroid.
Parafollicular cells are larger and paler, but they sit between thyroid follicles. This slide has no follicles or colloid, so it is not thyroid.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid gland; the larger cells are oxyphil cells.

questions.q: During neck surgery, a surgeon removes tissue from the back surface of the right thyroid lobe only. Which glands are most at risk, and how many of them usually sit on that one lobe?
options: The parathyroid glands; usually four, all on the right lobe.
The parafollicular cells; usually two clusters, each in a capsule.
The parathyroid glands; usually two, a superior and an inferior.
The thyroid isthmus; one bridge that crosses behind the lobe.
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are small, round glands, each about the size of a grain of rice. Most people have four: a superior and an inferior gland on the posterior surface of each thyroid lobe, each in its own thin capsule. Surgery on the back of one lobe puts the two glands on that lobe at risk. Their number and exact position vary from person to person.
notes: The glands are right, but most people have four in total, two on each lobe. Only the superior and inferior glands on the right lobe are at risk here.
Parafollicular cells (C cells) sit alone or in small groups between the thyroid follicles, inside the thyroid. They do not form separate glands with their own capsules.
Correct. Most people have a superior and an inferior parathyroid gland on the posterior surface of each thyroid lobe, so two sit on the right lobe.
The isthmus is thyroid tissue, not a separate gland, and it crosses in front of the upper trachea in the midline, not behind a lobe.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid glands; usually two, a superior and an inferior.

questions.q: On a thyroid slide, you find a large, pale cell tucked at the outer edge of a follicle wall. It does not touch the pink material in the center. What is the pink material, and what is the cell?
options: The pink material is cytoplasm; the cell is a chief cell.
The pink material is colloid; the cell is a follicular cell.
The pink material is cytoplasm; the cell is an oxyphil cell.
The pink material is colloid; the cell is a parafollicular cell.
questions.why: Each thyroid follicle is a ring of cells around a center filled with colloid, a thick, protein-rich fluid that stains pink. The wall is a single layer of simple cuboidal follicular cells that sit around the colloid. Parafollicular cells (C cells) are larger and paler, sit between the follicles or at the outer edge of a follicle wall, and do not touch the colloid.
notes: Chief cells are the small, numerous cells of the parathyroid, which has no follicles. The pink center of a thyroid follicle is colloid.
Follicular cells form the single cuboidal layer that lines the colloid, so they touch it. The pale cell that does not touch the colloid is a parafollicular cell.
Oxyphil cells belong to the parathyroid, which has no follicles. The pink center of a thyroid follicle is colloid.
Correct. The pink center is colloid, and a larger, pale cell at the edge of the wall that does not touch it is a parafollicular cell (C cell).
questions.answerText: The pink material is colloid; the cell is a parafollicular cell.

questions.q: Moving inward from the capsule on an adrenal slide, you pass a thin band of rounded clusters, then a thick band of pale, foamy cells in straight columns. Which layer comes next, and what lies beyond it?
options: The zona reticularis, then the medulla with its chromaffin cells.
The zona reticularis, then the capsule of dense connective tissue.
The zona glomerulosa, then the medulla with its chromaffin cells.
The medulla, then the zona reticularis around the central vessels.
questions.why: From the capsule inward, the cortex has three zones: the thin zona glomerulosa of rounded clusters, the thick zona fasciculata of pale, foamy columns, and the thin zona reticularis of cells in a branching network. The reticularis sits against the medulla, the inner core made of chromaffin cells clustered around blood vessels. GFR, then the medulla, gives the order.
notes: Correct. After the glomerulosa and fasciculata comes the zona reticularis, and the medulla of chromaffin cells lies inside it.
The zone is right, but the capsule is the outer covering. Inside the zona reticularis lies the medulla.
The zona glomerulosa is the thin band of rounded clusters just under the capsule, which you have already passed.
The zona reticularis lies between the fasciculata and the medulla, so you reach it before the medulla, not after.
questions.answerText: The zona reticularis, then the medulla with its chromaffin cells.

questions.q: During dissection, you find a crescent-shaped gland on the superior pole of a kidney, behind the peritoneum. Which side of the body is it on, and what cells make up its inner core?
options: The left side; zona reticularis cells in a branching network.
The left side; chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic neurons.
The right side; chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic neurons.
The right side; glandular epithelial cells in three zones.
questions.why: Each adrenal gland sits on the superior pole of a kidney, behind the peritoneum. The right gland is shaped like a pyramid and the left like a crescent, so a crescent-shaped gland is the left adrenal. Its outer cortex is glandular epithelium in three zones. Its inner core, the medulla, is made of chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic neurons with no axons or dendrites.
notes: The side is right, but the zona reticularis is the inner zone of the cortex. The inner core, the medulla, is made of chromaffin cells.
Correct. The left adrenal gland is crescent-shaped, and its medulla is made of chromaffin cells, modified sympathetic neurons.
The core is right, but the right adrenal gland is shaped like a pyramid. The crescent-shaped gland is on the left.
The right gland is pyramid-shaped, and the three zones of glandular epithelium form the outer cortex, not the inner core.
questions.answerText: The left side; chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic neurons.

questions.q: A slide of a testis shows clusters of cells in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules. What are these cells, and what kind of tissue are they?
options: Islet cells, the endocrine tissue of the testis.
Corpus luteum cells, the endocrine tissue of the testis.
Interstitial (Leydig) cells, the endocrine tissue of the testis.
Interstitial (Leydig) cells, the gamete-making tissue of the testis.
questions.why: The gonads are mixed organs: they make gametes, and they also contain endocrine cells. The testes sit in the scrotum, and their endocrine tissue is the interstitial cells (Leydig cells), which lie in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules. In the ovaries, the endocrine tissue is the cells of the developing follicles and the corpus luteum.
notes: Islet cells form the pancreatic islets, scattered among the acini of the pancreas. They are not found in the testis.
The corpus luteum forms in the ovary after ovulation. It is endocrine tissue of the female gonad, not the testis.
Correct. The interstitial cells between the seminiferous tubules are the endocrine tissue that makes the testis a mixed organ.
The cells are named correctly, but they are endocrine cells. Gametes are made inside the seminiferous tubules, not in the spaces between them.
questions.answerText: Interstitial (Leydig) cells, the endocrine tissue of the testis.

questions.q: A surgeon removes the tail of the pancreas, near the spleen. What happens to the pancreatic islets?
options: No islets are removed, since they are all in the head of the gland.
Some islets are removed, since they are scattered throughout the gland.
All the islets are removed, since they are all in the tail of the gland.
No islets are removed, since they lie outside the gland in the duodenum.
questions.why: The pancreas lies behind the stomach, with its head in the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaching toward the spleen. About 1 to 2 million pancreatic islets are scattered among the acini throughout the whole gland, not gathered in one region. Removing the tail removes the islets in the tail, while the islets in the head and body remain.
notes: The islets are not collected in the head. They are scattered throughout the pancreas, including the tail.
Correct. The islets are scattered throughout the pancreas, so removing any part of it removes the islets in that part.
The islets are not gathered in the tail. They are scattered throughout the pancreas, so the head and body still hold islets.
The islets lie inside the pancreas, scattered among the acini. The duodenal mucosa has its own enteroendocrine cells, which are different.
questions.answerText: Some islets are removed, since they are scattered throughout the gland.

questions.q: From what precursor molecule are all steroid hormones synthesized?
options: Cholesterol
Tyrosine
A ribosomal peptide chain
Arachidonic acid
questions.why: Every steroid hormone starts as cholesterol and is modified by a series of enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, which is why the steroids all share a similar four ring core. Tyrosine is the precursor for the amine hormones, including thyroid hormone and the catecholamines. A ribosomal peptide chain is how peptide hormones begin, and arachidonic acid gives rise to eicosanoids, which are local paracrines rather than steroid hormones.
questions.answerText: Cholesterol

questions.q: Where does synthesis of a peptide hormone begin in the endocrine cell?
options: In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria
On ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytosol from cholesterol
questions.why: Peptide hormones are proteins, so they are translated on rough ER ribosomes as a preprohormone and then trimmed in the ER and Golgi before packaging. The smooth ER and the mitochondria are the sites where steroid synthesis enzymes work. Cholesterol in the cytosol is a steroid precursor, not a template for a peptide sequence.
questions.answerText: On ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum

questions.q: How is a peptide hormone handled between synthesis and secretion?
options: It is stored in the nucleus bound to DNA
It diffuses out of the cell as fast as it is made, with no storage
It is stored in secretory vesicles until a signal causes exocytosis
It is bound to cholesterol and held in lipid droplets in the cytosol
questions.why: Because peptides are water soluble they cannot cross the membrane, so the cell packages them in vesicles and releases a preformed pool by exocytosis, which allows a fast burst of secretion. Immediate diffusion out of the cell describes steroid release, since steroids are lipid soluble. Lipid droplets store cholesterol esters as raw material, not finished peptide, and hormones are not stored on DNA.
questions.answerText: It is stored in secretory vesicles until a signal causes exocytosis

questions.q: How much steroid hormone does a steroid secreting cell keep in storage?
options: A week of supply bound to intracellular receptors in the cell
A pool held in the Golgi until a neural signal arrives
A large vesicle pool that is released by exocytosis on demand
Almost none, since steroids leave as fast as they are made
questions.why: Steroids are lipid soluble, so they cross the plasma membrane the moment they are made and cannot be held in a vesicle. Secretion rate therefore tracks synthesis rate, and the controlled step is the enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. Vesicle pools and Golgi storage are features of peptide hormones, and intracellular receptors are in target cells, not storage sites in the gland.
questions.answerText: Almost none, since steroids leave as fast as they are made

questions.q: Where is the receptor for a peptide hormone located?
options: On the outer surface of the target cell plasma membrane
On the inner face of the mitochondrial membrane
In the nucleus bound to a response element
Free in the cytosol
questions.why: A peptide hormone is water soluble and cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so its receptor must face the extracellular fluid and pass the message inward through a second messenger. Nuclear and cytosolic receptors belong to the lipid soluble hormones that can enter the cell. The mitochondrial membrane is not a hormone receptor site in this scheme.
questions.answerText: On the outer surface of the target cell plasma membrane

questions.q: Where is the receptor for a steroid hormone located?
options: In the extracellular matrix next to the cell
Inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus
On the plasma membrane coupled to a G protein
On the plasma membrane with tyrosine kinase activity
questions.why: Steroids are lipid soluble and diffuse through the bilayer, so the receptor waits inside and the hormone receptor complex acts on DNA to change transcription. G protein coupled and tyrosine kinase receptors sit in the membrane and serve water soluble hormones such as epinephrine and insulin. Nothing in the extracellular matrix serves as a hormone receptor here.
questions.answerText: Inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus

questions.q: Amine hormones are synthesized by modifying which amino acid?
options: Glycine
Tryptophan
Tyrosine
Glutamate
questions.why: Both families of amine hormones taught here, the thyroid hormones and the catecholamines, are built from tyrosine, which is why the two look chemically related despite behaving very differently. Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin and melatonin, which are amines but not the endocrine examples used for this competency. Glycine and glutamate act as neurotransmitters and are not hormone precursors.
questions.answerText: Tyrosine

questions.q: Insulin, cortisol, and epinephrine belong to which classes, in that order?
options: Amine, steroid, peptide
Peptide, amine, steroid
Steroid, peptide, amine
Peptide, steroid, amine
questions.why: Insulin is a chain of amino acids, cortisol is built from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex, and epinephrine is a small molecule made from tyrosine in the adrenal medulla. Calling insulin a steroid misses that it is destroyed by digestion and must be injected. Swapping cortisol and epinephrine confuses the adrenal cortex, which makes steroids, with the adrenal medulla, which makes catecholamines.
questions.answerText: Peptide, steroid, amine

questions.q: A hormone binds a receptor inside the nucleus and changes the rate of transcription of specific genes. Which class is it most likely to be?
options: Steroid
Catecholamine
Prostaglandin
Peptide
questions.why: Only a lipid soluble hormone can reach an intranuclear receptor, and steroid is the class defined by that route, so the response is a change in the amount of new protein made. Peptides and catecholamines act at surface receptors and change the activity of proteins already present. Prostaglandins are local eicosanoids and are not part of the three class hormone scheme.
questions.answerText: Steroid

questions.q: A drug blocks all new gene transcription in a target cell. Which hormone response is blocked first?
options: Epinephrine activating existing glycogen phosphorylase
Cortisol raising the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme
Insulin causing existing glucose transporters to move to the membrane
Glucagon raising cyclic AMP in a liver cell
questions.why: A steroid works by making new messenger RNA and new protein, so blocking transcription removes its whole mechanism. The other three act through second messengers on proteins the cell already has, which is why their effects appear within seconds and survive a transcription block. Those responses would eventually fade if the cell could never replace worn proteins, but that is a much slower effect.
questions.answerText: Cortisol raising the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme

questions.q: Why must insulin be injected rather than swallowed?
options: It binds an intracellular receptor that the gut lining does not have
It is a steroid and would be stored in fat before reaching the blood
It is a peptide and would be digested into amino acids in the gut
It is an amine and would be destroyed by stomach acid into cholesterol
questions.why: Peptide hormones are proteins, and the digestive tract breaks proteins into amino acids, so an oral dose never arrives intact at the target. Steroids are the class that survives the gut and can be taken as a pill, which is why prednisone works orally. Insulin is not an amine, and the reason has nothing to do with receptor location, since insulin receptors are on the cell surface.
questions.answerText: It is a peptide and would be digested into amino acids in the gut

questions.q: A newly described hormone is lipid soluble, is not stored in the gland, and can be taken as a tablet. Which class fits best?
options: Glycoprotein
Peptide
Catecholamine
Steroid
questions.why: Lipid solubility explains all three observations at once: the molecule leaves the cell as soon as it is made, so there is no storage pool, and it crosses the gut lining intact, so it survives an oral dose. Peptides and glycoproteins are water soluble, stored in vesicles, and digested if swallowed. Catecholamines are water soluble as well and act at surface receptors with a very short life in plasma.
questions.answerText: Steroid

questions.q: Thyroid hormone is built from tyrosine, yet it uses an intracellular receptor. Which property explains that?
options: It is lipid soluble, so it can cross the plasma membrane
It is a large glycoprotein that is taken in by endocytosis
It is made from cholesterol despite its name
It is stored in vesicles like a peptide
questions.why: Receptor location follows solubility, not the precursor, and thyroid hormone is lipid soluble enough to enter the cell and act on nuclear receptors like a steroid. That is why its effects are slow to start and long lasting. It is not a glycoprotein, and it is built from tyrosine and iodine rather than from cholesterol. Its storage is unusual, held extracellularly in thyroid colloid rather than in secretory vesicles.
questions.answerText: It is lipid soluble, so it can cross the plasma membrane

questions.q: Two hormones reach a cell at the same instant. One acts within seconds, the other over hours. What most likely accounts for the difference?
options: The fast one is carried bound to plasma protein, the slow one travels free
The fast one changes existing proteins, the slow one makes new protein
The fast one is present at a higher concentration in blood
The fast one is larger, so it binds its receptor more tightly
questions.why: A surface receptor and a second messenger can phosphorylate enzymes that are already in the cell, which takes seconds, while transcription, translation, and protein accumulation take hours. Binding to plasma protein changes half life and free fraction, not the speed of the intracellular step. Concentration and molecular size shift potency and clearance but do not explain a difference measured in hours.
questions.answerText: The fast one changes existing proteins, the slow one makes new protein

questions.q: A gland is treated with a drug that blocks exocytosis. Secretion of which hormone is affected least?
options: Insulin from the pancreatic beta cell
Growth hormone from the anterior pituitary
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary
questions.why: Cortisol is a steroid, so it leaves by simple diffusion through the membrane as soon as it is synthesized and never enters a vesicle. Insulin, growth hormone, and antidiuretic hormone are all peptides held in secretory vesicles, so blocking exocytosis traps them inside the cell. Steroid secretion is instead limited by the enzymes that convert cholesterol into the hormone.
questions.answerText: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex

questions.q: An enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone is inhibited in the adrenal cortex. Predict the effect on stored hormone available for immediate release and on the plasma level over the next hour.
options: Plasma cortisol rises because the blocked precursor is diverted to hormone
Plasma cortisol is unchanged because cortisol is recycled from target cells
A vesicle pool sustains normal plasma levels for several hours
There is no stored pool, so plasma cortisol falls as synthesis stops
questions.why: Steroid secreting cells store almost no finished hormone, so output equals synthesis and a block early in the pathway shows up in the blood within minutes to an hour. A vesicle buffer of several hours is what you would see if you blocked synthesis of a peptide hormone instead. Blocking a step cannot increase product downstream of the block, and hormones are cleared by the liver and kidney rather than recycled back to the gland.
questions.answerText: There is no stored pool, so plasma cortisol falls as synthesis stops

questions.q: A researcher labels an endocrine cell and finds abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, a large Golgi, and many dense secretory granules. The hormone it makes acts on target cells within seconds. Where is its receptor and why?
options: On the cell surface, because a water soluble peptide cannot cross the membrane
In the cytosol, because the hormone is lipid soluble
On the target cell surface, because the hormone is a steroid released by exocytosis
In the nucleus, because rapid effects require new transcription
questions.why: Heavy protein synthesis machinery plus dense granules identifies a peptide hormone, and a water soluble peptide has to signal from outside, which also fits the response within seconds. New transcription is the slow route and would not give a seconds long latency. Cytosolic receptors require lipid solubility, and steroids are never released by exocytosis because they are not packaged.
questions.answerText: On the cell surface, because a water soluble peptide cannot cross the membrane

questions.q: A patient is given a drug that inhibits protein synthesis in liver cells. Predict the effect on the immediate glucose releasing action of glucagon and on the slower glucose raising action of cortisol.
options: Both effects are lost, since both hormones act on the liver
The glucagon effect is preserved and the cortisol effect is lost
The cortisol effect is preserved and the glucagon effect is lost
Both effects are preserved, since the drug acts only in the gland
questions.why: Glucagon works through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A on enzymes the liver cell already contains, so it does not need the ribosome, while cortisol raises glucose by increasing the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme, which requires new protein. Losing both would only happen if the drug also blocked second messenger signaling. Reversing the two mixes up surface receptor speed with nuclear receptor speed.
questions.answerText: The glucagon effect is preserved and the cortisol effect is lost

questions.q: Iodine is removed from the diet of an experimental animal. Trace the effect through synthesis to the class of hormone affected.
options: Catecholamine synthesis in the adrenal medulla falls, because epinephrine contains iodine
Steroid synthesis falls, because iodine is needed to convert cholesterol to pregnenolone
Amine synthesis in the thyroid falls, because iodine is added to tyrosine
Peptide hormone synthesis falls, because iodine is a required amino acid
questions.why: Thyroid hormone is a tyrosine based amine whose activity depends on the iodine atoms attached to it, so no iodine means no functional hormone. Steroid synthesis uses cholesterol and needs no iodine. Iodine is not an amino acid and does not limit peptide synthesis, and the catecholamines, though also built from tyrosine, contain no iodine.
questions.answerText: Amine synthesis in the thyroid falls, because iodine is added to tyrosine

questions.q: Which fraction of a circulating hormone is able to bind target cell receptors?
options: The fraction bound to albumin only
The total of bound plus free
The fraction bound to carrier protein
The free, unbound fraction
questions.why: Only unbound hormone can leave the capillary and reach a receptor, so the free fraction sets the biological effect no matter how large the total is. Hormone held by a carrier, including albumin, is chemically shielded and inactive until it dissociates. Total hormone is what most simple blood tests report, which is exactly why total and activity can disagree.
questions.answerText: The free, unbound fraction

questions.q: Which hormone classes travel through plasma mostly bound to carrier proteins?
options: Steroid and thyroid hormones
Only the catecholamines
Only the glycoprotein hormones
Peptide and catecholamine hormones
questions.why: Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid soluble and poorly soluble in water, so they need a protein carrier to stay dissolved and to travel any distance in plasma. Peptides and catecholamines are water soluble and dissolve directly in plasma, circulating mostly free. Glycoproteins such as TSH are large water soluble peptides, so they too need no carrier.
questions.answerText: Steroid and thyroid hormones

questions.q: What is the approximate plasma half life of a typical peptide hormone?
options: A few seconds
A few minutes
About one day
About one week
questions.why: Peptides circulate free, are filtered at the kidney, and are cleaved by plasma and tissue peptidases, which gives them a half life on the order of minutes and lets their levels change quickly. A few seconds is closer to the catecholamines, which are cleared even faster. A day to a week describes the protein bound hormones, with thyroxine at the long end.
questions.answerText: A few minutes

questions.q: Which hormone has the longest plasma half life of these four?
options: Epinephrine
Insulin
Thyroxine, T4
Antidiuretic hormone
questions.why: Thyroxine is almost entirely bound to thyroxine binding globulin and other plasma proteins, so it is protected from clearance and lasts about a week, which is why thyroid hormone levels change slowly. Epinephrine lasts seconds, and insulin and antidiuretic hormone last minutes, since all three circulate free and are cleared rapidly. Binding, not gland size, is the reason for the difference.
questions.answerText: Thyroxine, T4

questions.q: Which plasma protein carries the largest share of cortisol?
options: Sex hormone binding globulin
Hemoglobin
Thyroxine binding globulin
Corticosteroid binding globulin
questions.why: Corticosteroid binding globulin, also called transcortin, is the high affinity carrier for cortisol, with albumin taking a smaller share. Thyroxine binding globulin carries thyroid hormone and sex hormone binding globulin carries testosterone and estradiol, each named for its cargo. Hemoglobin is inside red cells and carries respiratory gases, not hormones.
questions.answerText: Corticosteroid binding globulin

questions.q: How does binding to a plasma carrier protein change the clearance of a hormone?
options: It slows clearance by hiding hormone from filtration and enzymes
It speeds clearance by delivering the hormone to the liver faster
It has no effect, since only total hormone matters
It speeds clearance by making the hormone easier to filter
questions.why: A hormone bound to a large protein cannot pass the glomerular filter and is hidden from degrading enzymes, so it persists and the carrier acts as a circulating reservoir. Carriers do not target hormone to the liver for destruction. Total hormone does not set activity, and the bound complex is too large to filter, which is the opposite of easier filtration.
questions.answerText: It slows clearance by hiding hormone from filtration and enzymes

questions.q: Besides prolonging half life, what is the main transport reason a lipid soluble hormone needs a carrier protein?
options: It would otherwise be too large to enter a capillary
It is poorly soluble in the watery plasma on its own
It would otherwise bind its receptor before reaching the target
It carries a strong negative charge that plasma cannot buffer
questions.why: Plasma is water, and a lipid soluble molecule will not stay dissolved in it at useful concentrations, so the carrier keeps the hormone in solution while it travels. Steroids are small molecules, so size is not the barrier. Receptors are on target tissues rather than floating in blood, and steroids are not strongly charged.
questions.answerText: It is poorly soluble in the watery plasma on its own

questions.q: What relationship links free hormone and bound hormone in plasma?
options: Free hormone can only be replaced by new secretion from the gland
Binding is irreversible, so bound hormone is permanently lost
They are in reversible equilibrium, so bound hormone replaces free
Bound hormone converts to a different hormone before release
questions.why: Carrier binding obeys mass action, so as target tissues take up free hormone the complex dissociates and buffers the free concentration, smoothing out swings between secretory bursts. Irreversible binding would make the bound pool useless as a reserve. No chemical conversion happens on the carrier, and the reserve means the gland is not the only source of replacement over the short term.
questions.answerText: They are in reversible equilibrium, so bound hormone replaces free

questions.q: A drug displaces cortisol from corticosteroid binding globulin. What happens to the free cortisol concentration immediately after the drug is given?
options: It falls
It is unchanged
It falls, then total cortisol falls with it
It rises
questions.why: Displacement moves hormone from the bound reserve into the free pool, so free cortisol rises at once and biological activity increases before feedback has time to respond. It cannot fall, because nothing is being removed from the plasma. Saying it is unchanged confuses total hormone, which barely moves at first, with the free fraction that actually acts.
questions.answerText: It rises

questions.q: Pregnancy raises thyroxine binding globulin in plasma. What happens to total thyroxine in a woman whose thyroid gland is healthy?
options: Total T4 rises while free T4 stays near normal
Both total and free T4 fall
Both total and free T4 rise well above normal
Total T4 falls while free T4 rises
questions.why: More carrier binds more hormone, so the total measured in plasma goes up, but feedback adjusts secretion until the free level is back where it started, which is what the hypothalamus and pituitary actually sense. Total falling would require fewer carriers, not more. If free hormone also rose and stayed high, the woman would be thyrotoxic, and negative feedback prevents that in a healthy gland.
questions.answerText: Total T4 rises while free T4 stays near normal

questions.q: Liver disease lowers the plasma concentration of hormone binding proteins. Predict the effect on the half life of a highly bound steroid hormone.
options: The half life lengthens, because less hormone reaches the tissues
The half life shortens
The half life lengthens
The half life is unchanged, since half life depends only on the gland
questions.why: Fewer carriers means a larger share of hormone is free and therefore exposed to filtration and enzymatic breakdown, so it disappears from plasma faster. Lengthening would require more binding, not less. Half life is a property of clearance, not of secretion rate, and free hormone reaches tissues more readily rather than less.
questions.answerText: The half life shortens

questions.q: Two hormones are secreted in equal amounts. Hormone A is 99 percent protein bound, hormone B circulates free. Which shows the more rapid swings in plasma level between secretory bursts?
options: Neither swings, because plasma volume dilutes both
Hormone A, because bound hormone dissociates unpredictably
Hormone B, because nothing buffers or protects it
Both swing equally, since the secretion rate is the same
questions.why: A free hormone is cleared quickly and has no reservoir, so its level tracks each burst of secretion and falls just as quickly, which suits hormones that must signal minute to minute. The bound pool of hormone A dissociates in a graded way that buffers the free level rather than making it erratic. Equal secretion rates do not equalize clearance, and plasma dilution applies to both alike.
questions.answerText: Hormone B, because nothing buffers or protects it

questions.q: A laboratory reports a normal total thyroxine but the patient has clear signs of thyroid hormone excess. What is the most useful next measurement to explain the discrepancy?
options: Plasma albumin, since albumin sets total hormone
Urine cholesterol, since thyroxine is made from cholesterol
Total triiodothyronine bound to protein
Free thyroxine, since only the free fraction acts on tissues
questions.why: Total hormone lumps the active free fraction together with the much larger inactive bound pool, so a change in carrier protein can hide a real change in what tissues see. Measuring another total value repeats the same problem. Albumin is only a minor carrier for thyroxine, and thyroid hormone is built from tyrosine and iodine, not cholesterol.
questions.answerText: Free thyroxine, since only the free fraction acts on tissues

questions.q: Which hormone would you expect to be measurable in the urine of a healthy person in the largest proportion of what was secreted?
options: A small water soluble hormone that circulates free
Thyroxine bound to thyroxine binding globulin
A hormone bound to sex hormone binding globulin
A steroid that is 98 percent bound to globulin
questions.why: Free hormone is small enough to be filtered at the glomerulus, so an unbound water soluble hormone appears in urine, while carrier bound hormone stays in plasma because the protein cannot cross the filter. The three bound options all describe hormones shielded from filtration. This is the same protection that gives bound hormones their long half lives.
questions.answerText: A small water soluble hormone that circulates free

questions.q: A patient starts a drug that competes with thyroxine for binding sites on thyroxine binding globulin. Trace what happens to free T4 immediately and then to total T4 after several days of intact feedback.
options: Free T4 falls at first, then total T4 rises as the gland compensates
Free T4 rises at first, then feedback lowers total T4 and free T4 returns to normal
Free and total T4 both rise and stay high, since carrier binding cannot be regulated
Neither value changes, since the carrier only transports hormone
questions.why: Displacement shifts hormone into the free pool, and because the hypothalamus and pituitary sense free hormone, TSH falls and secretion drops until free T4 is back near its set point, leaving a lower total in a smaller bound pool. Free T4 cannot fall first, since the drug releases hormone rather than trapping it. Persistent elevation would require the feedback loop to be broken, and a change in binding clearly does change measured values.
questions.answerText: Free T4 rises at first, then feedback lowers total T4 and free T4 returns to normal

questions.q: Hormone X is 99 percent bound with a half life of 7 days. Hormone Y circulates free with a half life of 5 minutes. Which is better suited to controlling a variable that must be corrected within a minute, and why?
options: Hormone Y, because a long half life allows finer control
Hormone X, because a long half life keeps its concentration reliably high
Hormone Y, because a short half life lets its level rise and fall quickly
Hormone X, because bound hormone is delivered to tissues faster
questions.why: Fast control requires that the signal can be turned off as quickly as it was turned on, and only a rapidly cleared hormone can do that, which is why minute to minute regulators such as insulin and epinephrine are short lived. A steady high level is the profile you want for a background setting such as metabolic rate, not for fast correction. Binding slows delivery rather than speeding it, and the choice that credits hormone Y with finer control because it is long lived contradicts its 5 minute half life.
questions.answerText: Hormone Y, because a short half life lets its level rise and fall quickly

questions.q: After a bolus injection, hormone P disappears from plasma in about 10 minutes while hormone Q takes days. Both are secreted by the same person. What can you conclude about their transport and class?
options: Both must be peptides, since half life depends only on molecular size
P must have a larger secretion rate, which is why it disappears faster
P is likely a steroid carried on globulin, and Q is likely a peptide
P travels free as a water soluble hormone, Q is lipid soluble and bound
questions.why: Clearance rate is driven mainly by whether the hormone is shielded by a carrier, so minutes points to a free water soluble hormone and days points to an extensively bound lipid soluble one. Calling P a bound steroid and Q a peptide reverses the two, since steroid binding is what makes a hormone long lived. Size alone does not predict half life, and secretion rate sets concentration rather than the rate of disappearance after injection.
questions.answerText: P travels free as a water soluble hormone, Q is lipid soluble and bound

questions.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of plasma protein in the urine, including hormone binding globulins. Predict the effect on total cortisol and on free cortisol once feedback has adjusted.
options: Total cortisol falls while free cortisol is held near normal by feedback
Both total and free cortisol fall to very low levels
Both total and free cortisol rise, since less hormone is filtered
Total cortisol rises while free cortisol falls
questions.why: Losing carriers shrinks the bound reserve, so the total measured value drops, but the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis senses free cortisol and adjusts ACTH until the free level is back at its set point. Total cannot rise when the protein that holds hormone is being lost. A fall in free cortisol to very low levels would require the adrenal gland itself to fail, and protein loss increases rather than decreases filtration of hormone.
questions.answerText: Total cortisol falls while free cortisol is held near normal by feedback

questions.q: What determines whether a given cell responds to a hormone circulating in the blood?
options: Whether the cell is close to the gland that made the hormone
Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone
Whether the hormone is present at a high enough total concentration
Whether the cell has an open channel for the hormone to enter
questions.why: Blood carries hormone to every cell, so the receptor is what selects the target and gives endocrine signaling its specificity. Distance from the gland does not matter once a hormone is in the circulation. Concentration changes how strong the response is in cells that already have receptors, and hormones do not enter through channels.
questions.answerText: Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone

questions.q: What decides the nature of the response a target cell makes to a hormone?
options: The gland that secreted the hormone
The chemical structure of the hormone molecule by itself
The receptor and signaling machinery of the target cell
The distance the hormone traveled in the blood
questions.why: The hormone is only a key, and the response depends on what the cell it unlocks is equipped to do, which is why one molecule can trigger opposite effects in two tissues. The hormone structure determines which receptors it fits, not what those receptors then do. Travel distance and gland of origin have no bearing on the target cell's machinery.
questions.answerText: The receptor and signaling machinery of the target cell

questions.q: What does down regulation of a receptor mean?
options: The gland decreases its secretion of the hormone
The receptor moves from the membrane into the nucleus instead
The hormone is broken down faster in the liver
The target cell reduces the number of receptors for a hormone
questions.why: Down regulation is a change in the target cell, which internalizes and degrades receptors so the same hormone concentration produces a smaller effect. Reduced secretion is a change in the gland and is a separate mechanism. Receptors do not migrate between the membrane and the nucleus, and faster hepatic breakdown changes hormone level rather than receptor number.
questions.answerText: The target cell reduces the number of receptors for a hormone

questions.q: Chronically elevated hormone levels usually produce which change in target cell receptors?
options: Down regulation, so the cell becomes less sensitive
No change, since receptor number is fixed at birth
Conversion of surface receptors into intracellular receptors
Up regulation, so the cell becomes more sensitive
questions.why: Persistent high hormone drives receptor internalization and degradation, which protects the cell from overstimulation and is a common route into hormone resistance. Up regulation is the opposite response and follows chronically low hormone. Receptor number is continually adjusted rather than fixed, and receptor type does not switch locations.
questions.answerText: Down regulation, so the cell becomes less sensitive

questions.q: Chronically low hormone levels usually produce which change in the target cell?
options: Down regulation, a decrease in receptor number
Up regulation, an increase in receptor number
Loss of the second messenger system
Permanent loss of the ability to respond
questions.why: When a signal is scarce the cell adds receptors so that whatever hormone does arrive produces a larger effect, which raises sensitivity. Down regulation is the response to excess rather than to scarcity. The second messenger system remains intact, and the change is reversible rather than permanent.
questions.answerText: Up regulation, an increase in receptor number

questions.q: If a target cell increases its number of receptors for a hormone, what happens to its sensitivity?
options: Sensitivity is unchanged, since sensitivity depends only on hormone level
Sensitivity increases only if the hormone is lipid soluble
Sensitivity increases, so a lower hormone concentration produces a given response
Sensitivity decreases, so more hormone is needed for a given response
questions.why: More binding sites means more receptors are occupied at any given hormone concentration, so the dose response curve shifts left and less hormone is needed. Needing more hormone describes fewer receptors, not more. Sensitivity is a property of the target cell, and it responds to receptor number regardless of hormone class.
questions.answerText: Sensitivity increases, so a lower hormone concentration produces a given response

questions.q: Epinephrine constricts vessels in the skin and dilates vessels in skeletal muscle. What accounts for the opposite results?
options: Epinephrine is chemically altered on its way to muscle
Muscle vessels have no receptors for epinephrine
Skin vessels receive a higher concentration of epinephrine
The two beds express different adrenergic receptor subtypes
questions.why: Skin arterioles are rich in alpha1 receptors that raise intracellular Ca2+ and constrict, while skeletal muscle arterioles carry beta2 receptors that raise cyclic AMP and relax the smooth muscle. Both beds see the same circulating concentration, since one blood supply serves both. The hormone is not modified en route, and muscle vessels clearly do respond, so they cannot lack receptors.
questions.answerText: The two beds express different adrenergic receptor subtypes

questions.q: A cell has no receptor for a hormone at all. What is its response to a high blood level of that hormone?
options: No response, no matter how high the concentration goes
A response only if the hormone is lipid soluble
A delayed response after receptors diffuse in from neighbors
A weak response that grows with concentration
questions.why: Without a receptor there is nothing for the hormone to bind, so the signal is never transduced and raising the concentration adds nothing. A weak but growing response would require at least a few low affinity receptors. Lipid solubility lets a hormone enter the cell but it still needs an intracellular receptor, and receptors are not shared between cells.
questions.answerText: No response, no matter how high the concentration goes

questions.q: A person has had very high insulin levels for years. Predict the change in insulin receptor number and in target cell sensitivity.
options: Receptor number rises and sensitivity increases
Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases
Receptor number falls and sensitivity increases
Receptor number is unchanged and sensitivity decreases
questions.why: Sustained excess hormone triggers internalization and degradation of receptors, so fewer remain and a given insulin level does less, which is the core of insulin resistance. Rising receptor number is the answer to chronic hormone deficiency. A fall in receptors cannot raise sensitivity, and resistance in this setting is driven by the receptor change rather than occurring with receptor number held constant.
questions.answerText: Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle. Predict the effect of a fixed dose of epinephrine on heart rate in a person with excess thyroid hormone.
options: A fall in heart rate, since the receptors are saturated
A smaller increase in heart rate than normal
A larger increase in heart rate than normal
No change in heart rate at all
questions.why: More beta receptors means more of them are occupied at the same epinephrine concentration, so the cell is more sensitive and the chronotropic response is exaggerated, which is why thyroid excess produces palpitations. A smaller response would follow receptor down regulation. Adding receptors cannot abolish the response, and beta receptor activation raises heart rate rather than lowering it.
questions.answerText: A larger increase in heart rate than normal

questions.q: A drug blocks only the beta2 receptor. Predict its effect on the response to epinephrine in skeletal muscle arterioles and in skin arterioles.
options: Skin constriction is blocked and muscle dilation is preserved
Neither response changes, since the hormone is unchanged
Both dilation and constriction are blocked
Muscle dilation is blocked and skin constriction is preserved
questions.why: A subtype selective blocker removes only the response that runs through that subtype, so beta2 mediated dilation in muscle is lost while alpha1 mediated constriction in skin continues.
