Blocking both would require a nonselective drug. Reversing the two mixes up which bed carries which subtype, and blocking a receptor changes the response even though the hormone level is normal.
questions.answerText: Muscle dilation is blocked and skin constriction is preserved

questions.q: Two cells are exposed to the same concentration of a hormone. Cell A responds strongly, cell B barely responds. Both have the same second messenger system. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Cell A has more receptors for that hormone than cell B
Cell A binds more of the hormone to carrier protein
Cell A is exposed to the hormone for a shorter time
Cell A is closer to the gland of origin
questions.why: With the same hormone concentration and the same downstream machinery, the number of binding sites is what sets how much signal gets in, so receptor density explains the difference in sensitivity. Distance from the gland is irrelevant once the hormone is in the blood. Carrier binding happens in plasma, not on target cells, and a shorter exposure would weaken rather than strengthen the response.
questions.answerText: Cell A has more receptors for that hormone than cell B

questions.q: A tumor secretes a large excess of a peptide hormone for many months, then is removed. Immediately after removal, target cells are likely to be
options: more sensitive than normal, because receptors were up regulated
less sensitive than normal, because receptors were down regulated
unchanged, because receptor number responds only to hormone class
unable to respond ever again, because receptors were permanently lost
questions.why: Months of excess hormone leave the cells with a reduced receptor population, so once hormone levels fall the tissue underresponds until receptor number recovers over days. Up regulation follows deficiency, not excess. Receptor number tracks hormone exposure rather than hormone class, and the change reverses as the cell synthesizes new receptors.
questions.answerText: less sensitive than normal, because receptors were down regulated

questions.q: Glucagon raises cyclic AMP in a liver cell and epinephrine raises cyclic AMP in the same liver cell. Both produce glucose release. What does this show about specificity?
options: The liver cell can only respond to one hormone at a time
The two hormones must bind the same receptor
Different receptors can converge on one second messenger
Cyclic AMP is specific to a single hormone in each cell
questions.why: Specificity lives at the receptor, but several receptors in one cell can feed the same amplifier, so two hormones with different receptors produce the same end result. They cannot share a receptor, since a receptor is selective for one hormone shape. Cyclic AMP is a general purpose messenger, and a cell can carry receptors for many hormones at once.
questions.answerText: Different receptors can converge on one second messenger

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone contracts vascular smooth muscle through V1 receptors and inserts water channels in the collecting duct through V2 receptors. What is the best summary of why one hormone does two different things?
options: The kidney receives the hormone at a much lower concentration
The two tissues receive the hormone by different routes
The hormone changes shape when it enters the kidney
Each tissue expresses a different receptor subtype and pathway
questions.why: Receptor subtype selects which intracellular pathway is opened, so the same molecule raises Ca2+ in smooth muscle and cyclic AMP in the collecting duct cell. The hormone itself is unchanged from tissue to tissue. Concentration alters the size of a response, not its nature, and both tissues are reached by the same blood.
questions.answerText: Each tissue expresses a different receptor subtype and pathway

questions.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes has a fasting insulin level well above normal but a high blood glucose. Explain the combination in terms of receptors.
options: Target cells have down regulated insulin receptors, so high insulin does little
Insulin receptors are up regulated, which makes cells oversensitive to glucose
Insulin is bound to carrier protein, so none of it reaches target cells
The pancreas is secreting an inactive form of insulin, so glucose stays high
questions.why: High hormone with a weak effect is the signature of reduced target sensitivity, and years of elevated insulin drive receptor down regulation, so glucose stays up even as the pancreas works harder. An inactive hormone would not be measured as insulin in the usual assay. Up regulation would lower glucose rather than raise it, and insulin circulates free rather than carrier bound.
questions.answerText: Target cells have down regulated insulin receptors, so high insulin does little

questions.q: A researcher gives a low dose of epinephrine to a person at rest and measures a fall in total peripheral resistance. The same dose during a massive sympathetic discharge produces a rise. Which receptor idea best explains the reversal?
options: Epinephrine changes into norepinephrine during sympathetic discharge
Low doses mainly occupy beta2 receptors, while more agonist recruits alpha1
Receptors are down regulated within seconds of the first dose
The blood carries epinephrine to different organs at rest than during stress
questions.why: Both receptor subtypes are present in the circulation wide vascular bed, and which effect wins depends on how many of each are occupied, so a small amount of agonist reveals the more easily occupied beta2 dilation while a flood recruits enough alpha1 to constrict. Epinephrine is not converted to norepinephrine in plasma. Down regulation takes hours, not seconds, and the distribution of blood flow does not change which receptors a vessel carries.
questions.answerText: Low doses mainly occupy beta2 receptors, while more agonist recruits alpha1

questions.q: A cell line is engineered to express the receptor for a hormone it normally ignores, with no other change. Predict what happens when the hormone is applied, and what that shows.
options: The cell secretes the hormone itself, since receptor and secretion are linked
The cell still ignores the hormone, since the gland did not send it a signal
The cell now responds, showing that receptor expression is what makes a cell a target
The cell responds only if the hormone is lipid soluble
questions.why: Adding the receptor is sufficient to make a nontarget cell responsive, which is the clearest demonstration that targeting comes from the receptor rather than from anything about the hormone or the gland. There is no separate permission signal from the gland. Lipid solubility determines where the receptor must sit, not whether the experiment works, and receptor expression does not confer the ability to make the hormone.
questions.answerText: The cell now responds, showing that receptor expression is what makes a cell a target

questions.q: Cortisol is given at a high dose for two months and then stopped abruptly. Beyond the well known suppression of the axis, predict the receptor level change in target tissues and its effect during the first days after stopping.
options: Receptor number is unchanged, since steroid receptors are not regulated
Receptors are converted to membrane receptors, which respond faster
Up regulated receptors make tissues oversensitive, causing signs of excess
Down regulated glucocorticoid receptors leave the tissue underresponsive
questions.why: Two months of excess hormone reduces receptor number in the target tissue, so when the drug stops the tissue is doubly short changed, once by low hormone from the suppressed axis and again by reduced sensitivity. Up regulation would follow deficiency rather than months of excess. Intracellular receptors are regulated like surface receptors, and receptors do not change location or class.
questions.answerText: Down regulated glucocorticoid receptors leave the tissue underresponsive

questions.q: What does synergism between two hormones mean?
options: Their combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects
One hormone must be present for the other to act at all
One hormone opposes the effect of the other
Their combined effect is exactly the sum of their separate effects
questions.why: Synergism means the two together produce more than simple addition, usually because they act at different points of the same pathway and amplify one another. Requiring one hormone to be present for the other is permissiveness. Opposition is antagonism, and exact addition is an additive effect, which is the baseline that synergism exceeds.
questions.answerText: Their combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects

questions.q: What does permissiveness between two hormones mean?
options: The two hormones together produce more than the sum of their effects
One hormone must be present for the second to exert its full effect
The two hormones cancel each other out completely
The two hormones bind the same receptor with equal affinity
questions.why: A permissive hormone does little on its own but sets the stage, often by increasing the number of receptors or enzymes the second hormone needs. More than additive effect describes synergism, in which both hormones produce an effect on their own. Cancellation is antagonism, and permissiveness does not require the two to share a receptor.
questions.answerText: One hormone must be present for the second to exert its full effect

questions.q: What does antagonism between two hormones mean?
options: The two hormones produce a greater than additive effect
The two hormones are secreted by the same gland
One hormone opposes or reduces the effect of the other
The two hormones must both be present for any effect
questions.why: In antagonism the net effect on a variable is smaller than what either hormone would produce alone, either because they drive it in opposite directions or because one blunts the other's receptor. Requiring both for any effect is permissiveness. Greater than additive is synergism, and being secreted by the same gland says nothing about how the effects combine.
questions.answerText: One hormone opposes or reduces the effect of the other

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta receptors so that epinephrine can raise heart rate normally. Which interaction is that?
options: Antagonism
Additive effect
Synergism
Permissiveness
questions.why: Thyroid hormone does not itself produce the catecholamine response but is required for the full response to occur, which is the definition of a permissive hormone, and it works here by raising receptor number. Synergism would require thyroid hormone to produce the same effect on its own and for the pair to exceed addition. Antagonism would reduce the epinephrine effect, and an additive effect requires two independent contributions.
questions.answerText: Permissiveness

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose while glucagon raises it. Which interaction do the two show?
options: Antagonism
Additive effect
Permissiveness
Synergism
questions.why: The two hormones move the same variable in opposite directions, so the net blood glucose reflects their ratio rather than either level alone, which is the essence of antagonism. Permissiveness would mean one enables the other. Synergism and an additive effect both require the two to push in the same direction.
questions.answerText: Antagonism

questions.q: Glucagon, cortisol, and epinephrine together raise blood glucose far more than the sum of what each raises alone. Which interaction is that?
options: Additive effect
Synergism
Antagonism
Permissiveness
questions.why: Exceeding the sum of the separate effects is the defining test for synergism, and it happens here because the three hormones act on different steps of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis at once. Antagonism would predict a smaller combined effect. Permissiveness applies when one hormone alone does nothing, and an additive effect stops exactly at the sum.
questions.answerText: Synergism

questions.q: Cortisol is required for vascular smooth muscle to constrict normally in response to norepinephrine, though cortisol itself is not a vasoconstrictor. What is cortisol acting as here?
options: A trophic hormone
A synergistic hormone
A permissive hormone
An antagonistic hormone
questions.why: Cortisol produces no constriction on its own but the response to norepinephrine is weak without it, which is the classic permissive pattern and part of why cortisol deficiency causes low blood pressure. Synergism requires both partners to produce the effect independently. Antagonism would weaken the constriction, and a trophic hormone is one that stimulates another endocrine gland.
questions.answerText: A permissive hormone

questions.q: Estrogen increases the number of progesterone receptors in the uterus so that progesterone can act. What does this illustrate?
options: An antagonistic effect achieved by blocking receptors
A synergistic effect on the same receptor
A direct additive effect on endometrial growth
A permissive effect achieved by up regulating receptors
questions.why: Priming a tissue by raising receptor number is one of the commonest mechanisms of permissiveness, since the second hormone cannot act until the receptors exist. Blocking receptors would be antagonism, the opposite of what estrogen does here. Synergism would require both hormones to act through one shared pathway beyond addition, and this is an enabling step rather than an independent contribution.
questions.answerText: A permissive effect achieved by up regulating receptors

questions.q: Hormone A alone raises a measured response by 10 units, hormone B alone by 10 units, and the two together by 45 units. Which interaction is this?
options: Synergism
Permissiveness
Antagonism
Additive effect
questions.why: Addition would predict 20 units, and 45 is far above that, so the two hormones amplify each other rather than simply summing. Permissiveness would show one hormone producing little or nothing alone, but here each produces 10 units. Antagonism would give a combined value below 20.
questions.answerText: Synergism

questions.q: Hormone C alone raises a response by 0 units, hormone D alone by 5 units, and the two together by 30 units. Which interaction is this?
options: Additive effect
Permissiveness
Synergism
Antagonism
questions.why: Hormone C does nothing on its own yet the response to hormone D is six times larger in its presence, which is the signature of a permissive hormone that prepares the tissue. Antagonism would lower the combined response below 5 units. An additive effect would give 5 units, and synergism is usually reserved for pairs that each produce a measurable effect alone.
questions.answerText: Permissiveness

questions.q: A patient cannot make cortisol and has a dangerously low blood pressure that responds poorly to injected norepinephrine. Which interaction explains the poor response?
options: Synergism between cortisol and aldosterone on the kidney
Down regulation of cortisol receptors by norepinephrine
Loss of the permissive action of cortisol on vascular responsiveness
Antagonism between cortisol and norepinephrine at the same receptor
questions.why: Cortisol is required for vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines, so when it is absent the same dose of norepinephrine produces far less constriction. If the two were antagonists, removing cortisol would improve rather than worsen the response. The aldosterone pairing is a different interaction and does not explain the failure of injected norepinephrine, and norepinephrine does not regulate cortisol receptors here.
questions.answerText: Loss of the permissive action of cortisol on vascular responsiveness

questions.q: Parathyroid hormone raises plasma Ca2+ and calcitonin lowers it. Which term describes this pair?
options: Synergists
Trophic partners
Permissive partners
Antagonists
questions.why: The two hormones act on the same variable in opposite directions, so plasma Ca2+ settles where their opposing effects balance. Permissiveness would require one to enable the other. Synergism means pushing the same way beyond addition, and neither hormone stimulates the other's gland, which is what trophic would mean.
questions.answerText: Antagonists

questions.q: In an animal with no thyroid hormone, growth hormone alone produces almost no growth, but growth hormone plus thyroid hormone produces normal growth. Which interaction is shown?
options: Permissiveness of thyroid hormone for growth hormone
Synergism in which each hormone alone produces normal growth
Additive growth from two independent pathways
Antagonism of growth hormone by thyroid hormone
questions.why: Growth hormone cannot act fully unless thyroid hormone has prepared the tissues, so removing thyroid hormone leaves growth hormone almost ineffective, which is permissiveness. Antagonism would predict better growth without thyroid hormone. The synergism option contradicts the data, since growth hormone alone did almost nothing, and independent additive pathways would still give partial growth.
questions.answerText: Permissiveness of thyroid hormone for growth hormone

questions.q: A drug blocks the glucagon receptor in the liver of a fasting person. Predict the effect on blood glucose and name the interaction that is disturbed.
options: Blood glucose rises, because insulin action is also blocked
Blood glucose falls, because the antagonism that balanced insulin is removed
Blood glucose is unchanged, because cortisol replaces glucagon exactly
Blood glucose falls, because glucagon and insulin are synergists
questions.why: Glucose sits where the opposing actions of insulin and glucagon balance, so removing glucagon action lets insulin dominate and glucose drops. Blocking the glucagon receptor does not block insulin. Cortisol contributes to glucose production but slowly and not in exact replacement, and calling the pair synergists misnames a relationship in which they push in opposite directions.
questions.answerText: Blood glucose falls, because the antagonism that balanced insulin is removed

questions.q: An animal without adrenal glands is given epinephrine and shows a weak rise in blood glucose. It is then given cortisol for two days, and the same epinephrine dose now produces a large rise. Identify the interaction and its likely mechanism.
options: Additive effect, with each hormone contributing an independent share
Antagonism, with cortisol competing for the adrenergic receptor
Permissiveness, with cortisol raising the enzymes epinephrine needs
Synergism, with both hormones acting on the same receptor at once
questions.why: Cortisol pretreatment did not itself produce the glucose surge but made the epinephrine response much larger, which is the permissive pattern, and cortisol accomplishes it by increasing gluconeogenic enzymes and adrenergic receptor number. Antagonism would blunt the response after cortisol. Synergism requires both hormones to raise glucose on their own, and an additive effect would not multiply the epinephrine response the way this experiment shows.
questions.answerText: Permissiveness, with cortisol raising the enzymes epinephrine needs

questions.q: During a long fast, glucagon, cortisol, growth hormone, and epinephrine all rise while insulin falls. Explain what the two arrangements of interaction accomplish for blood glucose.
options: The four hormones are permissive for insulin, which is what raises glucose
The four hormones antagonize each other, which is why glucose stays constant
All five hormones are synergists whose effects sum to a stable glucose level
The four raise glucose synergistically while their antagonist insulin falls
questions.why: Glucose is defended by two moves at once, more of the hormones that mobilize fuel and less of the hormone that stores it, and the mobilizers together exceed the sum of their individual effects. Insulin cannot be grouped with the other four, since it lowers glucose. Insulin does not raise glucose, and calling the four mutual antagonists would predict no net rise during a fast.
questions.answerText: The four raise glucose synergistically while their antagonist insulin falls

questions.q: Two hormones each raise heart rate. Given alone, hormone E raises rate by 12 beats per minute and hormone F by 8. Together they raise it by 20. A student calls this synergism. What is the correct label and why?
options: An additive effect, because the total equals the sum of the two rises
Permissiveness, because both hormones were required for the full effect
Antagonism, because the increase is smaller than either hormone alone
Synergism, because two hormones acting together is always more than one
questions.why: Synergism requires the combination to exceed the sum, and 20 is exactly 12 plus 8, so these hormones simply add through independent routes. The number of hormones present does not by itself make an interaction synergistic. Permissiveness would show one hormone producing little alone, and antagonism would give a combined value below 12.
questions.answerText: An additive effect, because the total equals the sum of the two rises

questions.q: A patient on a drug that blocks estrogen receptors is given progesterone and the uterine response is much smaller than expected. Trace why, and identify the interaction that was interrupted.
options: Blocking estrogen removed an antagonist, so progesterone should have acted more strongly
Blocking estrogen prevented up regulation of progesterone receptors, a permissive effect
Progesterone and estrogen are synergists at a shared receptor that the drug blocked
The drug lowered plasma progesterone by displacing it from its carrier protein
questions.why: Estrogen primes the endometrium by increasing progesterone receptor number, so with estrogen receptors blocked there are too few progesterone receptors and the same hormone level does much less. If estrogen were an antagonist here, blocking it would have amplified the progesterone effect. The two hormones use separate receptors rather than one shared site, and a receptor blocker does not change plasma carrier binding.
questions.answerText: Blocking estrogen prevented up regulation of progesterone receptors, a permissive effect

questions.q: What defines a humoral stimulus for hormone release?
options: A stretch receptor in a hollow organ is activated
A nerve fiber releases neurotransmitter directly onto the gland cells
A change in the blood level of an ion or nutrient acts on the gland
Another hormone binds receptors on the gland
questions.why: Humoral refers to the body fluids, so the stimulus is the concentration of something dissolved in blood, such as glucose or Ca2+, sensed by the endocrine cell itself. Neurotransmitter release onto a gland is a neural stimulus, and another hormone acting on the gland is a hormonal stimulus. A stretch receptor generates a neural signal rather than a humoral one.
questions.answerText: A change in the blood level of an ion or nutrient acts on the gland

questions.q: What defines a neural stimulus for hormone release?
options: A rise in plasma K+ acts on the gland
A pituitary trophic hormone acts on the gland
The gland responds to a fall in blood pressure entirely by itself
A neuron releases neurotransmitter onto the endocrine cells
questions.why: In a neural stimulus the gland is innervated and the action potential arriving at the nerve ending triggers secretion, which gives the fastest possible endocrine response. A rise in plasma K+ is a humoral stimulus sensed by the cell itself. A trophic hormone is a hormonal stimulus, and a gland detecting a blood variable on its own is humoral.
questions.answerText: A neuron releases neurotransmitter onto the endocrine cells

questions.q: What defines a hormonal stimulus for hormone release?
options: One hormone stimulates an endocrine gland to release a second hormone
A sympathetic nerve fires onto the gland
The gland releases hormone at a fixed rate regardless of signals
A blood ion level changes and the gland responds
questions.why: A hormonal stimulus is hormone acting on hormone, the arrangement that builds the three tier axes of the hypothalamus and pituitary. Ion driven release is humoral and nerve driven release is neural. Constant unregulated release is not one of the three categories and is not how endocrine glands behave.
questions.answerText: One hormone stimulates an endocrine gland to release a second hormone

questions.q: A rise in blood glucose triggers insulin secretion from the pancreatic beta cell. Which type of stimulus is that?
options: Neural
Humoral
Hormonal
Trophic
questions.why: The beta cell senses glucose directly from the blood, so the nutrient itself is the stimulus, which is the definition of humoral. A neural stimulus would require nerve fibers to drive the secretion, and although autonomic nerves modulate the islet, glucose is the primary signal. There is no intervening hormone, so it is not hormonal or trophic.
questions.answerText: Humoral

questions.q: A fall in plasma Ca2+ triggers parathyroid hormone release. Which type of stimulus is that?
options: Hormonal
Neural
Humoral
Neuroendocrine reflex
questions.why: The parathyroid chief cell carries a calcium sensing receptor and reads plasma Ca2+ directly, so the ion in the blood is the stimulus. No other hormone stands between the change and the secretion, which rules out a hormonal stimulus. Nothing neural is involved, so neither of the nerve based options fits.
questions.answerText: Humoral

questions.q: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto adrenal medullary cells, which then secrete epinephrine. Which type of stimulus is that?
options: Paracrine
Humoral
Hormonal
Neural
questions.why: The medulla is effectively a modified sympathetic ganglion, and its secretory cells fire in response to neurotransmitter from a preganglionic neuron, which is a neural stimulus and explains the near instant catecholamine surge. No blood borne ion or nutrient triggers it, so it is not humoral, and no other hormone acts on the gland. Paracrine signaling is local diffusion between neighboring cells rather than a neural pathway.
questions.answerText: Neural

questions.q: ACTH from the anterior pituitary triggers cortisol release from the adrenal cortex. Which type of stimulus is that?
options: Hormonal
Humoral
Neural
Mechanical
questions.why: One hormone acting on another endocrine gland is a hormonal stimulus, and ACTH is the trophic hormone that drives the adrenal cortex. Humoral would require the cortex to be sensing an ion or nutrient. Nerve fibers do not drive cortisol secretion, and there is no mechanical trigger in this pathway.
questions.answerText: Hormonal

questions.q: Which stimulus type produces the fastest hormone secretion after the trigger appears?
options: Hormonal
Neural
All three act at the same speed
Humoral
questions.why: A neural stimulus travels by action potential and releases a preformed vesicle pool within seconds, which is why the adrenal medulla can respond to a startle almost immediately. A humoral stimulus waits for a blood level to change enough for the gland to sense it. A hormonal stimulus adds an entire extra gland and transit time, making it the slowest of the three.
questions.answerText: Neural

questions.q: Plasma K+ rises and the adrenal cortex secretes more aldosterone. Classify the stimulus.
options: Hormonal, because K+ acts through renin
Neural, because K+ depolarizes nerve endings on the gland
Humoral, because the ion acts on the gland directly
Hormonal, because K+ acts through ACTH
questions.why: Zona glomerulosa cells are depolarized directly by extracellular K+, which is why potassium is one of the strongest aldosterone stimuli and needs no intermediary. The depolarization happens in the endocrine cell rather than in a nerve. ACTH has only a permissive role for aldosterone, and while renin drives the angiotensin route, potassium acts on the gland without it.
questions.answerText: Humoral, because the ion acts on the gland directly

questions.q: Suckling at the breast leads to oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary. Classify the stimulus.
options: Hormonal, since prolactin release triggers oxytocin release from the gland
Humoral, since the fall in plasma volume triggers it
Humoral, since milk components enter the blood
Neural, since sensory nerves drive the hypothalamic neurons
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors in the nipple send action potentials to the hypothalamus, and the hypothalamic neurons release oxytocin from their endings in the posterior pituitary, so the whole loop is neural. Nothing dissolved in blood is being sensed, which rules out both humoral options. Prolactin is released by the same reflex but does not itself trigger oxytocin.
questions.answerText: Neural, since sensory nerves drive the hypothalamic neurons

questions.q: TSH from the pituitary raises thyroid hormone output. Classify the stimulus acting on the thyroid gland.
options: Hormonal
Neurohumoral
Neural
Humoral
questions.why: The thyroid follicular cell is responding to a hormone from another endocrine gland, which is the hormonal category by definition. It is not sensing an ion or nutrient in the blood, so humoral does not apply, even though iodine availability limits how much hormone it can make. No nerve fiber drives thyroid hormone secretion.
questions.answerText: Hormonal

questions.q: A student says that a hormone circulating in the blood makes any stimulus that reaches a gland through blood a humoral stimulus. Why is that wrong?
options: Humoral applies only to stimuli sensed in the hypothalamus
Humoral covers blood levels of ions and nutrients, not hormone on gland
Humoral applies only to stimuli that arrive through lymph rather than blood
Humoral applies only when the gland is also innervated
questions.why: The three categories are defined by what kind of signal reaches the gland, not by the route it traveled, so a hormone arriving through blood is still a hormonal stimulus. Lymph is not the defining route for any of the categories. Innervation would make the stimulus neural, and the hypothalamus is one site of sensing among many rather than a requirement.
questions.answerText: Humoral covers blood levels of ions and nutrients, not hormone on gland

questions.q: Blood glucose falls during a fast and the alpha cell secretes glucagon. Classify the stimulus and name what the gland is sensing.
options: Humoral, sensing the plasma Ca2+ concentration
Neural, sensing sympathetic activity to the pancreas
Humoral, sensing the plasma glucose concentration
Hormonal, sensing the fall in plasma insulin
questions.why: The alpha cell reads the nutrient level in blood directly, which is a humoral stimulus and lets the pancreas respond to fuel status without waiting for any other signal. Sympathetic input does modulate the islet during stress but is not the primary trigger during a simple fast. Falling insulin contributes but is not what the alpha cell is chiefly sensing, and Ca2+ is the humoral stimulus for the parathyroid rather than the alpha cell.
questions.answerText: Humoral, sensing the plasma glucose concentration

questions.q: Which pathway would still work in an animal whose nerves to the endocrine gland have all been cut, with everything else intact?
options: Suckling raising oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Cold air on the skin raising sympathetic output
A startle raising epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Low plasma Ca2+ raising parathyroid hormone
questions.why: A humoral pathway needs only the blood and the gland, so parathyroid hormone release continues when the nerve supply is gone. The startle response and the suckling reflex both begin with sensory nerves and end with neural drive to secretory cells, so cutting nerves abolishes them. Cold sensing and sympathetic output are neural from start to finish.
questions.answerText: Low plasma Ca2+ raising parathyroid hormone

questions.q: After a meal, glucose from the gut raises insulin, and gut derived GIP raises it further. Classify these two stimuli on the beta cell.
options: Glucose is a humoral stimulus and GIP is a hormonal stimulus
Glucose is a hormonal stimulus and GIP is a neural stimulus
Both glucose and GIP are neural stimuli
Both glucose and GIP are humoral stimuli
questions.why: One gland can receive more than one category of stimulus, and here the beta cell senses a nutrient directly, which is humoral, while GIP is a hormone from another endocrine tissue acting on it, which is hormonal. Calling GIP humoral misses that the category depends on what kind of signal arrives, not on the fact that it traveled in blood. Glucose is a nutrient rather than a hormone, and neither signal involves a nerve ending.
questions.answerText: Glucose is a humoral stimulus and GIP is a hormonal stimulus

questions.q: Trace the full pathway from a frightening sight to epinephrine in the blood, and name the stimulus category at the gland.
options: Brain to hypothalamic releasing hormone to pituitary to adrenal medulla, a hormonal stimulus
Brain to sympathetic preganglionic neuron to adrenal medullary cell, a neural stimulus
Rising plasma glucose to adrenal medullary cell, a humoral stimulus
Brain to ACTH to adrenal medullary cell, a hormonal stimulus
questions.why: The medulla is innervated directly by sympathetic preganglionic fibers, so the signal never leaves the nervous system until acetylcholine triggers catecholamine exocytosis, which is why the response takes seconds. The hypothalamic pituitary route is the cortisol pathway and is far slower. Glucose does not drive medullary secretion, and ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex rather than the medulla.
questions.answerText: Brain to sympathetic preganglionic neuron to adrenal medullary cell, a neural stimulus

questions.q: Trace the pathway from a low blood Ca2+ to a corrected Ca2+, and identify the stimulus category and the feedback sign.
options: Low Ca2+ triggers TSH, which raises PTH, and the rise in Ca2+ raises PTH further
Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the thyroid, calcitonin raises Ca2+, and the rise shuts off calcitonin
Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the parathyroid, PTH raises Ca2+, and that shuts off PTH
Low Ca2+ acts neurally on the parathyroid, PTH lowers Ca2+, and the fall shuts off PTH
questions.why: The chief cell reads plasma Ca2+ directly, PTH pulls Ca2+ from bone and kidney and gut, and the restored Ca2+ removes the stimulus, which is a simple negative feedback loop with a humoral trigger. PTH raises rather than lowers Ca2+, and the parathyroid is not driven by nerves. TSH controls the thyroid, not the parathyroid, and calcitonin lowers Ca2+ rather than raising it.
questions.answerText: Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the parathyroid, PTH raises Ca2+, and that shuts off PTH

questions.q: An experimental animal has its pituitary stalk cut, blocking hypothalamic hormones from reaching the anterior pituitary. Which secretion is least affected, and why?
options: Thyroid hormone, because the thyroid is controlled by a neural stimulus
Sex steroids, because the gonads respond to plasma glucose
Cortisol, because the adrenal cortex is directly innervated
Insulin, because it is driven by a humoral stimulus alone
questions.why: Cutting the stalk removes the hormonal drive to the anterior pituitary, which cripples every three tier axis, but insulin secretion depends on the beta cell sensing glucose and is untouched. Cortisol falls because ACTH falls, and the cortex is not driven by nerves. The thyroid depends on TSH rather than nerves, and the gonads respond to LH and FSH rather than to glucose.
questions.answerText: Insulin, because it is driven by a humoral stimulus alone

questions.q: A person eats a meal that is high in protein. Insulin and glucagon both rise. Classify the stimulus for each and explain why raising both makes sense.
options: Both are humoral responses to amino acids, and the pair protects blood glucose
Insulin is humoral and glucagon is neural, and the pair raises blood glucose sharply
Both are neural responses to gastric stretch, and the pair slows digestion
Both are hormonal responses to a gut trophic hormone that raises glucose
questions.why: Amino acids in the blood are sensed directly by both islet cell types, so both signals are humoral, and glucagon offsets the hypoglycemia that a large insulin release without carbohydrate would otherwise cause. Gut hormones such as GIP amplify insulin release but are not the main trigger here and do not raise glucose. Glucagon secretion is not primarily neural, and gastric stretch does not account for the amino acid response.
questions.answerText: Both are humoral responses to amino acids, and the pair protects blood glucose

questions.q: How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary?
options: By diffusion across the blood brain barrier
Through the hypophyseal portal veins
Through the general systemic circulation from the heart
Down the axons of hypothalamic neurons into the anterior lobe
questions.why: A portal system carries blood from a capillary bed in the hypothalamus straight to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary, so tiny amounts of releasing hormone arrive undiluted. Going through the systemic circulation would dilute them past usefulness. Axonal transport into the lobe describes the posterior pituitary, and these hormones do not need to cross the blood brain barrier on this route.
questions.answerText: Through the hypophyseal portal veins

questions.q: In a three tier axis, which tier is the peripheral gland?
options: The first tier, the hypothalamus and its releasing neurons
The second tier, the anterior pituitary and its trophic cells
The third tier, such as the thyroid or adrenal cortex
The posterior pituitary, which stores hypothalamic hormones
questions.why: The axis runs hypothalamus, then anterior pituitary, then peripheral gland, and it is the peripheral gland that makes the hormone with the widespread effects on body tissues. The hypothalamus is tier one and releases the releasing hormone. The anterior pituitary is tier two and releases the trophic hormone, and the posterior pituitary is not part of a three tier axis at all.
questions.answerText: The third tier, such as the thyroid or adrenal cortex

questions.q: Which hormone does the anterior pituitary release in response to TRH?
options: ACTH
Calcitonin
Thyroxine
TSH
questions.why: TRH from the hypothalamus drives thyroid stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary, which then drives the thyroid. Thyroxine is the third tier hormone from the thyroid gland itself. ACTH is the trophic hormone for the adrenal cortex and is driven by CRH, and calcitonin comes from thyroid parafollicular cells outside this axis.
questions.answerText: TSH

questions.q: Trace the adrenal axis in the correct order.
options: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol
CRH, then cortisol, then ACTH
ACTH, then cortisol, then CRH
ACTH, then CRH, then cortisol
questions.why: Corticotropin releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus, drives ACTH from the anterior pituitary, and ACTH drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Putting ACTH first reverses the top two tiers. The other two orders place the peripheral hormone before its own trophic hormone, which would mean the gland acts before being told to.
questions.answerText: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol

questions.q: What is long loop negative feedback in a three tier axis?
options: The trophic hormone inhibits the hypothalamus one tier above it
The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary
The releasing hormone inhibits its own hypothalamic neurons
The peripheral gland hormone stimulates more trophic hormone
questions.why: Long loop means the signal travels the full length of the axis, from the third tier back up to tiers one and two, which is what keeps the peripheral hormone near its set point. A trophic hormone acting back on the hypothalamus is the short loop, a shorter journey. Releasing hormone acting on its own neurons is an ultrashort loop, and a stimulating effect from the third tier would be positive rather than negative feedback.
questions.answerText: The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary

questions.q: What is short loop negative feedback in a three tier axis?
options: The releasing hormone inhibits the peripheral gland
The peripheral hormone inhibits the anterior pituitary corticotrophs
The trophic hormone from the pituitary inhibits the hypothalamus
The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus
questions.why: The short loop skips the peripheral gland, with tier two feeding back on tier one so the pituitary can restrain its own drive. Any answer in which the peripheral hormone inhibits a tier above it describes long loop feedback instead. Releasing hormone acting on the peripheral gland is not a feedback path, since portal blood delivers it to the pituitary rather than to the periphery.
questions.answerText: The trophic hormone from the pituitary inhibits the hypothalamus

questions.q: Which pair correctly names a hypothalamic hormone and the anterior pituitary hormone it controls?
options: CRH and TSH
GHRH and ACTH
TRH and cortisol
GnRH and LH
questions.why: Gonadotropin releasing hormone drives the gonadotropins LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary, which then act on the gonads. CRH drives ACTH rather than TSH, and GHRH drives growth hormone rather than ACTH. Cortisol is a peripheral gland hormone and is not released by the pituitary at all.
questions.answerText: GnRH and LH

questions.q: Why is the posterior pituitary not the middle tier of a three tier axis?
options: It releases hormones that hypothalamic neurons made and sent down axons
It receives releasing hormones through the portal system
It is controlled by long loop feedback from the adrenal cortex
It makes its own trophic hormones that drive peripheral glands
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin are synthesized in hypothalamic cell bodies and travel down axons to be released from the posterior lobe, so there is no separate gland taking orders and no trophic step. The posterior lobe synthesizes no hormones of its own. The portal system serves the anterior lobe, and the adrenal cortex feeds back on the CRH and ACTH pathway rather than on the posterior pituitary.
questions.answerText: It releases hormones that hypothalamic neurons made and sent down axons

questions.q: A drug destroys the hypophyseal portal vessels without damaging either the hypothalamus or the pituitary. Predict the effect on ACTH secretion.
options: ACTH rises, because feedback from cortisol is removed
ACTH falls, because CRH can no longer reach the corticotrophs
ACTH is unchanged, because CRH travels down axons to the pituitary
ACTH rises, because the pituitary secretes freely without hypothalamic input
questions.why: The anterior pituitary depends entirely on portal delivery of hypothalamic hormones, so cutting that supply starves it of CRH and ACTH output drops. Cortisol feedback is not removed here, since cortisol falls once ACTH falls. Axonal delivery serves the posterior lobe, and the corticotroph does not release much ACTH without CRH drive.
questions.answerText: ACTH falls, because CRH can no longer reach the corticotrophs

questions.q: Thyroid hormone rises well above normal in a healthy person given an injection. Predict what happens to TSH and to TRH.
options: TSH rises and TRH falls, because feedback acts only on the hypothalamus
Both rise, because more substrate is available for the axis
Both fall, because long loop feedback inhibits both tiers above
TSH falls and TRH rises, because only the pituitary senses thyroid hormone
questions.why: Long loop feedback from the third tier reaches both upstream tiers, so a rise in thyroid hormone suppresses TRH and TSH together and secretion of new thyroid hormone slows. A rise in all three would be positive feedback, which is not how this axis works. The two split answers each assume feedback lands on only one tier, but the long loop targets both.
questions.answerText: Both fall, because long loop feedback inhibits both tiers above

questions.q: A tumor secretes ACTH continuously and is not part of the pituitary. Predict what happens to CRH from the hypothalamus.
options: CRH is unchanged, since the tumor is outside the axis
CRH rises, because the adrenal gland is being overdriven
CRH rises to match the ACTH output
CRH falls, suppressed by both the high cortisol and ACTH
questions.why: High ACTH drives cortisol up, and cortisol suppresses the hypothalamus by long loop feedback while ACTH itself suppresses it by short loop feedback, so CRH is doubly inhibited. Rising CRH would require the feedback signals to be stimulatory. The tumor is outside the normal axis but its hormone is not, so the loops still respond.
questions.answerText: CRH falls, suppressed by both the high cortisol and ACTH

questions.q: A patient takes a high dose of a synthetic glucocorticoid for months. Predict the state of CRH, ACTH, and the adrenal cortex.
options: CRH and ACTH are low and the adrenal cortex atrophies
CRH is high, ACTH is low, and the cortex is normal
CRH and ACTH are low and the adrenal cortex enlarges
CRH and ACTH are high and the adrenal cortex enlarges
questions.why: The drug acts on the same receptors as cortisol, so the axis reads it as an excess and shuts down both upper tiers, and without ACTH the cortex loses its trophic support and shrinks. High CRH and ACTH would require the axis not to recognize the drug. A cortex cannot enlarge while its trophic hormone is suppressed, since ACTH is what maintains its mass.
questions.answerText: CRH and ACTH are low and the adrenal cortex atrophies

questions.q: Which observation would be evidence of short loop feedback rather than long loop feedback?
options: Infusing cortisol lowers ACTH release from the anterior pituitary corticotrophs
Infusing ACTH into the hypothalamus lowers CRH with cortisol held constant
Removing the adrenal glands raises ACTH
Infusing cortisol lowers CRH release from the hypothalamus
questions.why: Short loop feedback is the trophic hormone acting on the tier above it, so showing an effect of ACTH on CRH while cortisol is clamped isolates that loop. Infusing cortisol and watching either ACTH or CRH tests the peripheral hormone acting upstream, which is the long loop. Removing the adrenals raises ACTH by removing cortisol feedback, which is again the long loop.
questions.answerText: Infusing ACTH into the hypothalamus lowers CRH with cortisol held constant

questions.q: GnRH is given as a steady continuous infusion instead of in pulses, and LH output falls after a few days. What best explains the fall?
options: GnRH becomes an antagonist when given continuously
The hypothalamus stops making GnRH by short loop feedback
Continuous exposure down regulates GnRH receptors on the gonadotroph
Continuous exposure destroys the hypophyseal portal vessels over time
questions.why: The gonadotroph needs a pulsatile signal, and unrelenting stimulation causes receptor down regulation so the same hormone level does progressively less, which is the basis of using GnRH analogs to suppress the axis. The portal vessels are not damaged by hormone exposure. GnRH does not change into an antagonist, and suppressing hypothalamic GnRH would not matter when GnRH is being infused from outside.
questions.answerText: Continuous exposure down regulates GnRH receptors on the gonadotroph

questions.q: Growth hormone acts partly through IGF-1 made in the liver. Which molecule provides the long loop negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary in this axis?
options: Somatostatin
Insulin
GHRH
IGF-1
questions.why: IGF-1 is the peripheral product of the axis, so it plays the role cortisol or thyroid hormone plays elsewhere and inhibits both GHRH release and growth hormone release. GHRH is the tier one releasing hormone rather than a feedback signal. Somatostatin is an inhibiting hormone from the hypothalamus, part of the control rather than the feedback from the periphery, and insulin belongs to a different regulatory system.
questions.answerText: IGF-1

questions.q: A researcher cuts the pituitary stalk in an animal. Predict what happens to cortisol and to antidiuretic hormone over the following week.
options: Cortisol falls with the loss of ACTH drive, and antidiuretic hormone release is impaired too
Cortisol is unchanged and antidiuretic hormone falls, since only the posterior lobe uses the stalk
Cortisol falls and antidiuretic hormone rises, since the posterior lobe is released from inhibition
Both cortisol and antidiuretic hormone rise, since feedback pathways are cut
questions.why: The stalk carries both the portal vessels to the anterior lobe and the axons to the posterior lobe, so one cut interrupts hormonal delivery on one side and neural delivery on the other. Neither hormone can rise, since both depend on structures the cut removes. The anterior lobe is not spared, because its entire hypothalamic input arrives through those portal vessels.
questions.answerText: Cortisol falls with the loss of ACTH drive, and antidiuretic hormone release is impaired too

questions.q: Both adrenal glands are removed from an animal. Predict CRH, ACTH, and skin pigmentation over the following weeks, and explain the link.
options: CRH and ACTH fall, and the skin becomes pale from low ACTH
CRH and ACTH rise as feedback is lost, and high ACTH darkens the skin
CRH rises and ACTH falls, and pigmentation is unchanged
CRH and ACTH are unchanged, since the axis senses only the pituitary
questions.why: Cortisol is what normally restrains the upper two tiers, so removing its source releases both from inhibition and ACTH climbs, and because ACTH is derived from the same precursor as melanocyte stimulating hormone it darkens the skin at high levels. A fall in the upper tiers would require more cortisol, not less. CRH and ACTH move together here, since the same feedback loss reaches both.
questions.answerText: CRH and ACTH rise as feedback is lost, and high ACTH darkens the skin

questions.q: An animal is given a drug that blocks the glucocorticoid receptor everywhere. Predict CRH, ACTH, and plasma cortisol after several days.
options: CRH and ACTH fall while cortisol rises, because feedback is amplified
All three fall, because the receptor block prevents hormone release
All three rise, because the axis cannot sense the cortisol that is present
CRH and ACTH rise while cortisol falls, because the adrenal is blocked too
questions.why: Feedback works only if the upstream tiers can detect the hormone, so blocking the receptor makes cortisol invisible to the hypothalamus and pituitary and they drive the axis harder, raising all three measured values. A fall in all three would follow extra feedback rather than none. The adrenal cortex itself is not blocked, so it responds to the rising ACTH by making more cortisol.
questions.answerText: All three rise, because the axis cannot sense the cortisol that is present

questions.q: TRH is infused into a healthy person for one hour. Predict the sequence of changes in TSH and thyroid hormone, and what finally limits the response.
options: TSH and thyroid hormone rise together and stay high until the infusion ends
TSH falls while thyroid hormone rises, because TRH inhibits the pituitary
Thyroid hormone rises first, then TSH follows, and TRH runs out
TSH rises first, thyroid hormone follows, and the rise then shuts off TSH
questions.why: Signals move down the axis in order, so the pituitary responds within minutes and the thyroid takes longer, and once the peripheral hormone is up it uses long loop feedback to restrain TSH even while TRH is still arriving. The peripheral hormone cannot lead its own trophic hormone. A sustained plateau would require feedback to be absent, and TRH stimulates the pituitary rather than inhibiting it.
questions.answerText: TSH rises first, thyroid hormone follows, and the rise then shuts off TSH

questions.q: In endocrine disease, what does the word primary tell you about where the defect is?
options: The defect is in the peripheral gland itself
The defect is in the anterior pituitary
The defect is in the target tissue receptor
The defect is in the hypothalamus
questions.why: Primary points to the last tier of the axis, the gland that makes the hormone with the body wide effects, so the tiers above it are healthy and still responding to feedback. A pituitary defect is called secondary and a hypothalamic defect is called tertiary. A receptor defect in the target tissue is hormone resistance, which is a separate category from primary and secondary.
questions.answerText: The defect is in the peripheral gland itself

questions.q: In endocrine disease, what does the word secondary tell you about where the defect is?
options: The defect is in the peripheral gland, so the trophic hormone is abnormal
The defect is in the anterior pituitary, so the trophic hormone is abnormal
The defect is in the target tissue, so the receptor is abnormal
The defect is in the carrier protein, so the free fraction is abnormal
questions.why: Secondary names a problem one tier up from the peripheral gland, at the anterior pituitary, so the trophic hormone is the thing that is wrong and the peripheral gland is merely following orders. A defect in the peripheral gland itself is primary. Receptor and carrier protein problems change how hormone acts or travels rather than which tier of the axis is broken.
questions.answerText: The defect is in the anterior pituitary, so the trophic hormone is abnormal

questions.q: What happens to TSH in primary hypothyroidism?
options: It is normal
It is undetectable
It is high
It is low
questions.why: The thyroid gland is failing, so thyroid hormone is low, and low thyroid hormone removes the long loop inhibition on the pituitary, which pushes TSH up. Low or undetectable TSH would mean the pituitary is the failing tier, which is secondary hypothyroidism. A normal TSH with a low thyroid hormone is not what an intact feedback loop produces.
questions.answerText: It is high

questions.q: What happens to TSH in secondary hypothyroidism?
options: It is high, because feedback is lost
It is normal, because only the thyroid is abnormal
It is high, because the thyroid is not responding
It is low, because the pituitary is the failing tier
questions.why: In secondary disease the pituitary cannot make enough TSH, so the thyroid is understimulated and thyroid hormone falls with it, leaving both tiers low. A high TSH with low thyroid hormone is the primary pattern, in which the pituitary is healthy and shouting at a broken gland. Saying only the thyroid is abnormal describes primary disease, not secondary.
questions.answerText: It is low, because the pituitary is the failing tier

questions.q: What happens to ACTH when an adrenal tumor secretes cortisol on its own?
options: It is suppressed
It is unchanged
It rises and then plateaus
It is elevated
questions.why: The tumor makes cortisol without waiting for orders, and the high cortisol feeds back on the pituitary and hypothalamus, so ACTH is pushed down even while cortisol is high. Elevated ACTH with high cortisol would mean the pituitary is the source of the problem. Feedback is intact here, so ACTH cannot stay unchanged or drift upward.
questions.answerText: It is suppressed

questions.q: What happens to ACTH when a pituitary tumor secretes ACTH on its own?
options: It is low, and cortisol is high
It is high, and cortisol is high too
It is high, and cortisol is low
It is low, and cortisol is low as well
questions.why: The tumor is at the trophic tier, so it floods the adrenal cortex with ACTH and the cortex responds by making more cortisol, leaving both tiers high. Low ACTH with high cortisol is the adrenal source pattern. High ACTH with low cortisol would mean the adrenal cannot respond, and both low is pituitary failure rather than a secreting tumor.
questions.answerText: It is high, and cortisol is high too

questions.q: Why is measuring the peripheral gland hormone alone not enough to classify a disorder as primary or secondary?
options: The peripheral hormone is bound to protein, so it cannot be measured
The peripheral hormone is too unstable to measure accurately in plasma
Both patterns give the same peripheral level, so the trophic hormone decides
The peripheral hormone changes only in secondary disease, never in primary
questions.why: A low thyroid hormone looks identical whether the thyroid failed or the pituitary failed, so the tier above is what tells you which one broke, which is why these values are always read as a pair. The peripheral hormone can be measured reliably, and protein bound hormones are routinely assayed as free or total. The peripheral hormone changes in both primary and secondary disease, which is exactly the problem.
questions.answerText: Both patterns give the same peripheral level, so the trophic hormone decides

questions.q: What does the term hypersecretion mean in this classification scheme?
options: The target tissue is unable to respond to a normal hormone level
The hormone is released at the wrong time of day
Too little hormone is being released from the peripheral gland
Too much hormone is being released, whatever tier is at fault
questions.why: Hypersecretion and hyposecretion describe the direction of the abnormality, while primary and secondary describe its location, so a full classification uses one term from each pair. Too little hormone is hyposecretion, the opposite direction. Failure of the target tissue to respond is resistance, and abnormal timing is a separate problem from the amount released.
questions.answerText: Too much hormone is being released, whatever tier is at fault

questions.q: A patient has a low free T4 with a high TSH. Classify the disorder.
options: Primary hyposecretion
Secondary hypersecretion
Secondary hyposecretion
Primary hypersecretion
questions.why: Low peripheral hormone sets the direction as hyposecretion, and the high trophic hormone shows that the pituitary is healthy and pushing hard on a gland that cannot answer, which places the defect in the thyroid itself. Secondary hyposecretion would show a low TSH alongside the low T4. Both hypersecretion answers are ruled out because the peripheral hormone is low, not high.
questions.answerText: Primary hyposecretion

questions.q: A patient has a high free T4 with a suppressed TSH. Classify the disorder.
options: Secondary hyposecretion
Primary hypersecretion
Secondary hypersecretion
Primary hyposecretion
questions.why: High peripheral hormone sets the direction as hypersecretion, and the suppressed trophic hormone shows the pituitary is responding normally by shutting down, so the thyroid must be making hormone on its own. Secondary hypersecretion would show TSH high or inappropriately normal despite the high T4. Both hyposecretion answers are ruled out because the peripheral hormone is high.
questions.answerText: Primary hypersecretion

questions.q: A patient has a high free T4 together with a high TSH. Classify the disorder.
options: Secondary hyposecretion
Primary hypersecretion
Secondary hypersecretion
Primary hyposecretion
questions.why: Hormone is high, so the direction is hypersecretion, and the striking finding is that TSH is high when feedback should have shut it off, which means the pituitary is driving the thyroid rather than obeying it. Primary hypersecretion would show a suppressed TSH, since the healthy pituitary would respond to the excess. Both hyposecretion answers contradict the high peripheral hormone.
questions.answerText: Secondary hypersecretion

questions.q: A patient has a low free T4 together with a low TSH. Classify the disorder.
options: Primary hyposecretion
Secondary hypersecretion
Primary hypersecretion
Secondary hyposecretion
questions.why: Low peripheral hormone gives the direction, and a low trophic hormone in the face of it is the giveaway, since a healthy pituitary would have raised TSH sharply. Both tiers falling together points to failure at the pituitary. Primary hyposecretion would show a high TSH. The hypersecretion options do not fit a low peripheral hormone.
questions.answerText: Secondary hyposecretion

questions.q: A patient has a low morning cortisol with a markedly elevated ACTH. Where is the defect and in which direction?
options: The adrenal cortex, with hyposecretion
The adrenal cortex, with hypersecretion
The anterior pituitary, with hypersecretion
The anterior pituitary, with hyposecretion
questions.why: Cortisol is low, so the direction is hyposecretion, and the elevated ACTH proves the pituitary is working and being ignored, which places the failure in the cortex itself. A pituitary defect would leave ACTH low along with cortisol. Neither hypersecretion answer is possible when the peripheral hormone is low.
questions.answerText: The adrenal cortex, with hyposecretion

questions.q: A pituitary tumor destroys the corticotrophs while sparing the adrenal glands. Predict the ACTH and cortisol levels and classify the result.
options: ACTH high and cortisol low, primary hyposecretion
Both low, secondary hyposecretion
ACTH low and cortisol high, primary hypersecretion
Both high, secondary hypersecretion
questions.why: Losing the cells that make ACTH removes the trophic drive, and an adrenal cortex that is intact but unstimulated makes very little cortisol, so both tiers read low and the defect is one tier above the gland. High ACTH with low cortisol would require a healthy pituitary and a failing adrenal. The two options with a high hormone contradict the loss of secretory cells.
questions.answerText: Both low, secondary hyposecretion

questions.q: Which pair of values is impossible in a patient whose feedback loop is intact and whose only problem is in the peripheral gland?
options: Low peripheral hormone with a trophic hormone at the top of its range
Low peripheral hormone with high trophic hormone
High peripheral hormone with high trophic hormone
High peripheral hormone with low trophic hormone
questions.why: If the pituitary is healthy it must suppress the trophic hormone when the peripheral hormone is high, so seeing both high means the trophic tier is the driver and the problem is not confined to the peripheral gland. Low peripheral with high trophic and high peripheral with low trophic are the two normal responses of an intact pituitary to a failing or overactive gland. A trophic hormone at the top of its range alongside a low peripheral hormone is simply an early or mild primary deficiency.
questions.answerText: High peripheral hormone with high trophic hormone

questions.q: Two patients both have a plasma cortisol far above normal. Patient A has a suppressed ACTH and patient B has a high ACTH. Classify each and name the tier at fault.
options: Both have primary hypersecretion, since cortisol is high in each
Both have secondary hypersecretion, since ACTH controls cortisol in each
Patient A has secondary hypersecretion from the pituitary, patient B has primary hypersecretion from the adrenal cortex
Patient A has primary hypersecretion from the adrenal cortex, patient B has secondary hypersecretion from the pituitary
questions.why: An identical peripheral value carries opposite meanings depending on the tier above it, so the ACTH is what separates the two: suppressed ACTH means the pituitary is correctly reacting to an adrenal source, while high ACTH means the pituitary is the source and the adrenal is obeying. Reversing the two is the commonest error and comes from reading the peripheral hormone alone. Grouping them together ignores the trophic values entirely.
questions.answerText: Patient A has primary hypersecretion from the adrenal cortex, patient B has secondary hypersecretion from the pituitary

questions.q: An animal has a low thyroid hormone level. Exogenous TSH is given and thyroid hormone rises normally. Which tier was at fault, and what would the result have been in the other case?
options: The pituitary was at fault, since the gland responds when stimulated. A failing thyroid would not
The hypothalamus was at fault, since TSH bypasses the pituitary and the thyroid alike
Neither tier was at fault, since exogenous hormone always raises the level
The thyroid was at fault, since the gland needed extra stimulation. A failing pituitary would not have responded
questions.why: Supplying the missing trophic hormone tests whether the peripheral gland is capable, so a normal rise proves the thyroid is healthy and the shortage was upstream, which is secondary hyposecretion. A gland destroyed by primary disease would stay flat no matter how much TSH arrived. TSH does bypass the hypothalamus, but a hypothalamic defect would also have left TSH low before the test, so this result alone does not point there, and saying that exogenous hormone always raises the level ignores that a damaged gland cannot respond.
questions.answerText: The pituitary was at fault, since the gland responds when stimulated. A failing thyroid would not

questions.q: A patient has low cortisol with low ACTH, low thyroid hormone with low TSH, and low sex steroids with low LH. What single lesion explains all three axes, and how do you know it is not three separate gland failures?
options: Three separate peripheral gland failures, because each peripheral hormone is low
One anterior pituitary lesion, since three failed glands would each raise their trophic hormone
One peripheral gland lesion, because the pituitary controls all three glands from one cell type
A carrier protein deficiency, because all the measured hormones travel bound
questions.why: Every trophic hormone is low alongside its peripheral partner, which is the pattern of a pituitary that cannot drive any axis, and it is the low trophic values rather than the low peripheral values that make the call. If the three glands had each failed on their own, feedback would have pushed TSH, ACTH, and LH high. One peripheral lesion cannot explain three different glands, and carrier protein loss would not lower the trophic hormones.
questions.answerText: One anterior pituitary lesion, since three failed glands would each raise their trophic hormone

questions.q: A young athlete takes large doses of a synthetic androgen. Predict the plasma testosterone, the LH, and the size of the testes, and explain the pattern.
options: Androgen activity is high, LH is unchanged, and the testes are unchanged
Androgen activity is high, LH is high, and the testes enlarge
Androgen activity is high, LH is suppressed, and the testes shrink
Androgen activity is low, LH is suppressed, and the testes are unchanged
questions.why: The drug acts on androgen receptors, so the hypothalamus and pituitary read the axis as oversupplied and shut down LH, and without LH the testis loses its trophic support and atrophies, which reproduces the high peripheral with low trophic pattern of a source outside the axis. High LH alongside high androgen would mean the pituitary was driving the excess. LH cannot stay unchanged with an intact feedback loop, and the androgen effect is clearly high rather than low.
questions.answerText: Androgen activity is high, LH is suppressed, and the testes shrink

questions.q: Why is the posterior pituitary classified as neural tissue rather than glandular tissue?
options: It is a downgrowth of the hypothalamus made of axon terminals
It is an outpocketing of the roof of the developing mouth
It is a cluster of secretory epithelial cells fed by a portal system
It is a modified sympathetic ganglion with chromaffin cells
questions.why: The posterior pituitary forms as a downward extension of the developing brain, so it contains axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons plus supporting glia rather than gland cells. An outpocketing of the roof of the mouth describes the anterior pituitary, which is true glandular epithelium. Secretory epithelial cells fed by a portal system also describes the anterior lobe. A modified sympathetic ganglion with chromaffin cells describes the adrenal medulla.
questions.answerText: It is a downgrowth of the hypothalamus made of axon terminals

questions.q: Where are antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin actually synthesized?
options: In secretory cells of the posterior pituitary itself
In cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons
In the median eminence capillary bed
In corticotropes of the anterior pituitary
questions.why: Both peptides are made in neuron cell bodies of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, then travel down axons to be stored in the posterior lobe until release. The posterior pituitary itself contains no cells that synthesize hormone, only the nerve terminals. The median eminence is where hypothalamic releasing hormones enter the portal blood for the anterior lobe. Corticotropes make ACTH, an anterior pituitary product.
questions.answerText: In cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons

questions.q: What is the main target of antidiuretic hormone?
options: The glomerular capillary wall
The loop of Henle thin descending limb
The collecting duct of the kidney
The wall of the urinary bladder
questions.why: ADH binds receptors on collecting duct principal cells, which is where the final adjustment of water reabsorption is made. The glomerular capillary wall filters plasma and is not hormone gated for water. The thin descending limb is already freely permeable to water without hormonal control. The bladder stores urine and does not change its composition.
questions.answerText: The collecting duct of the kidney

questions.q: How does antidiuretic hormone increase water reabsorption?
options: It opens sodium channels that drag water along with them
It pumps water directly across the wall of the tubule
It increases the filtration rate at the glomerulus instead
It inserts aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane
questions.why: ADH triggers the insertion of stored aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane, so water can follow the medullary osmotic gradient out of the tubule. Sodium channels move Na+, and although water follows solute, that is not the hormone specific step ADH controls here. ADH does not act on filtration rate. No pump moves water directly, since water always moves down its own osmotic gradient.
questions.answerText: It inserts aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane

questions.q: What is the strongest ordinary stimulus for antidiuretic hormone release?
options: A rise in plasma osmolarity
A fall in plasma potassium
A rise in plasma calcium
A fall in plasma glucose
questions.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors fire when plasma osmolarity climbs even a percent or two, and that is the most sensitive trigger for ADH release. Plasma potassium is a stimulus for aldosterone, not ADH. Plasma calcium is monitored by the parathyroid glands. Plasma glucose drives insulin and glucagon secretion from the islets.
questions.answerText: A rise in plasma osmolarity

questions.q: Which two tissues does oxytocin act on in a nursing mother?
options: Kidney collecting duct and uterine smooth muscle
Uterine smooth muscle and breast myoepithelial cells
Breast alveolar secretory cells and liver
Ovarian follicle cells and uterine endometrium
questions.why: Oxytocin contracts uterine smooth muscle during labor and squeezes the myoepithelial cells wrapped around the milk alveoli, which is what ejects milk already made. The collecting duct is the ADH target, not the oxytocin target. Alveolar secretory cells make milk under prolactin, but they do not contract. Ovarian follicle cells respond to FSH and LH from the anterior lobe.
questions.answerText: Uterine smooth muscle and breast myoepithelial cells

questions.q: What stimulus triggers oxytocin release during breastfeeding?
options: A rise in plasma prolactin
Stretch of the milk ducts by stored milk
Suckling at the nipple
A fall in plasma estrogen after delivery
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors in the nipple fire during suckling and send that signal to the hypothalamic neurons that release oxytocin, which is a neuroendocrine reflex. Prolactin drives milk synthesis but does not itself trigger oxytocin. Duct stretch does not cause release, and in fact unremoved milk suppresses further production. Falling estrogen permits lactation to begin but is not the moment to moment trigger.
questions.answerText: Suckling at the nipple

questions.q: What is the other name for antidiuretic hormone?
options: Angiotensin II
Aldosterone
Atrial natriuretic peptide
Vasopressin
questions.why: ADH is called vasopressin because at high concentrations it also constricts arterioles and raises blood pressure. Aldosterone is an adrenal steroid that conserves sodium rather than water alone. Atrial natriuretic peptide does the opposite, promoting salt and water loss. Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor but it is generated in plasma, not released from the pituitary.
questions.answerText: Vasopressin

questions.q: A student drinks two liters of water quickly. What happens to antidiuretic hormone release?
options: It falls, because plasma osmolarity drops
It rises, because plasma volume increased
It rises, because the kidney must handle more water
It is unchanged, since only sodium intake affects it
questions.why: Diluting the plasma lowers osmolarity, the osmoreceptors quiet down, ADH release falls, and the collecting duct removes aquaporins so a large dilute urine is passed. Increased volume does not raise ADH, it lowers it through the low pressure stretch receptors. The kidney handles the extra water by making less ADH, not more. Water alone changes osmolarity, so sodium intake is not the only input.
questions.answerText: It falls, because plasma osmolarity drops

questions.q: A hiker has gone eight hours without water on a hot day. What is her urine like?
options: Large in volume and dilute
Small in volume and concentrated
Large in volume and concentrated
Small in volume and dilute
questions.why: Water loss raises plasma osmolarity, ADH rises, aquaporins go into the collecting duct, and water is reclaimed so the urine is scant and concentrated. Large and dilute is the water loaded response, when ADH is low. Large and concentrated happens only when a solute such as glucose forces an osmotic diuresis. Small and dilute is not physiologically possible as a normal response, since low volume comes from reclaiming water.
questions.answerText: Small in volume and concentrated

questions.q: Alcohol suppresses antidiuretic hormone secretion. What does that predict about urine output?
options: Urine volume falls and osmolarity rises
Urine volume is unchanged but sodium loss rises
Urine volume rises above the volume of fluid drunk
Urine volume falls because plasma volume falls first
questions.why: With ADH suppressed the collecting duct stays water impermeable, so water that would normally be reclaimed is lost and the person can excrete more fluid than they drank, which is why alcohol dehydrates. Falling volume with rising osmolarity is the high ADH pattern. ADH controls water rather than sodium handling, so a pure sodium loss is not the prediction. Plasma volume falls as a consequence here, not as the cause.
questions.answerText: Urine volume rises above the volume of fluid drunk

questions.q: A patient loses posterior pituitary function after surgery. What pattern of urine do you predict?
options: Very small volumes of concentrated urine
Very large volumes of concentrated urine
Normal volume with glucose present
Very large volumes of dilute urine
questions.why: Without ADH the collecting duct cannot insert aquaporins, so water passes straight through and the person makes many liters of dilute urine each day, the picture called diabetes insipidus. Small concentrated volumes require ADH to be present and working. Glucose in the urine points to diabetes mellitus, a different problem entirely. Large volumes of concentrated urine would require a filtered solute load, which is not the case here.
questions.answerText: Very large volumes of dilute urine

questions.q: During nursing, suckling causes oxytocin release, which causes milk ejection, which encourages more suckling. What kind of control is this?
options: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward control
Tonic inhibition
questions.why: The response amplifies the original stimulus rather than shutting it off, which is the defining feature of positive feedback, and the loop ends when the infant stops feeding. Negative feedback would mean milk ejection reduces oxytocin release. Feedforward means anticipating a change before it happens, such as insulin rising at the sight of food. Tonic inhibition describes a steady brake, not an amplifying loop.
questions.answerText: Positive feedback

questions.q: Plasma osmolarity rises from 290 to 300 mOsm/L. What happens at the collecting duct?
options: Aquaporins are withdrawn and far more water is excreted instead
More aquaporins are inserted and more water is reabsorbed
Sodium pumps are inhibited and more sodium is excreted
Filtration rate rises so much more urine is formed
questions.why: A ten milliosmole rise is a large osmotic signal, so ADH release climbs sharply and drives aquaporin-2 insertion, reclaiming water to bring osmolarity back down. Withdrawing aquaporins is what happens when osmolarity falls. Sodium handling in this segment is aldosterone territory, not the osmoreceptor pathway. Filtration rate is regulated at the glomerulus and is not the target of this reflex.
questions.answerText: More aquaporins are inserted and more water is reabsorbed

questions.q: A trauma patient has lost a liter of blood. Besides osmolarity, what else drives antidiuretic hormone release here?
options: Reduced plasma potassium sensed by the adrenal cortex
Increased firing from hypothalamic thermoreceptors
Reduced firing from arterial and atrial stretch receptors
Increased carbon dioxide sensed by central chemoreceptors
questions.why: A large volume loss unloads baroreceptors and atrial stretch receptors, and their reduced firing releases the brake on ADH, so ADH rises to conserve water and support pressure. Thermoreceptors drive sweating and skin blood flow, not ADH. Potassium sensing by the adrenal cortex governs aldosterone. Central chemoreceptors adjust ventilation rather than pituitary output.
questions.answerText: Reduced firing from arterial and atrial stretch receptors

questions.q: A patient after a head injury makes 9 L of dilute urine per day. Plasma sodium is high and plasma osmolarity is 310 mOsm/L. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Antidiuretic hormone is being released in great excess
Filtered glucose has exceeded the tubular transport maximum here
Aldosterone is being released in excess, wasting both salt and water
Antidiuretic hormone release has failed, so water is not reclaimed
questions.why: High plasma osmolarity should be a maximal ADH stimulus, so a dilute high volume urine in the face of that stimulus means the ADH signal itself is missing, which fits injury to the hypothalamus or posterior lobe. Excess ADH would give concentrated urine and low plasma sodium. Excess aldosterone retains sodium and does not produce dilute high volume urine. Filtered glucose above the transport maximum would give large volumes but the urine would carry glucose and osmolarity would not be dilute.
questions.answerText: Antidiuretic hormone release has failed, so water is not reclaimed

questions.q: A patient secretes antidiuretic hormone continuously regardless of plasma osmolarity. Predict plasma sodium and urine osmolarity.
options: Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is high
Plasma sodium rises and urine osmolarity is high
Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is low
