Plasma sodium rises and urine osmolarity is low
questions.why: Unregulated ADH keeps aquaporins in place, so water is retained and dilutes the plasma, dropping sodium, while the small urine that is passed is concentrated. Rising sodium with concentrated urine would mean water is being lost, not retained. Falling sodium with dilute urine is the pattern of drinking far too much water with ADH properly suppressed. Rising sodium with dilute urine is the picture of absent ADH.
questions.answerText: Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is high

questions.q: The pituitary stalk is cut, separating the hypothalamus from both pituitary lobes. Why does antidiuretic hormone secretion stop even though the neurons that make it are intact?
options: The releasing hormone can no longer reach the portal blood
The axons that carry the hormone to its release site are severed
The hypothalamic neurons lose their osmoreceptor input
The posterior lobe cells can no longer synthesize the peptide
questions.why: ADH reaches the circulation only by traveling down hypothalamic axons to terminals in the posterior lobe, so cutting the stalk cuts the delivery route even though the cell bodies survive. Portal blood delivery of releasing hormones is how the anterior lobe is controlled, a separate pathway. Osmoreceptors sit in the hypothalamus itself and are not disconnected by a stalk cut. The posterior lobe never synthesized the peptide, so losing synthesis there cannot be the reason.
questions.answerText: The axons that carry the hormone to its release site are severed

questions.q: A woman is severely dehydrated and also nursing. Both hormones of the posterior pituitary are elevated. Which pairing of effects do you predict?
options: Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk synthesis increases
Sodium reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk synthesis increases
Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast
Sodium reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast
questions.why: ADH acts on the collecting duct to reclaim water, and oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells to eject milk that has already been made, so those two effects appear together. Sodium reabsorption is the job of aldosterone, not either posterior pituitary hormone. Milk synthesis is driven by prolactin from the anterior lobe, so it is not part of the oxytocin response. Water reabsorption paired with milk ejection is the only combination that matches the actual targets of these two hormones.
questions.answerText: Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast

questions.q: Which structure secretes growth hormone?
options: The hypothalamus
The anterior pituitary
The posterior pituitary
The liver
questions.why: Somatotropes in the anterior pituitary make and release growth hormone into the general circulation. The hypothalamus supplies the releasing and inhibiting signals but does not make growth hormone itself. The posterior pituitary stores only ADH and oxytocin. The liver responds to growth hormone by making IGF-1, so it is a target rather than the source.
questions.answerText: The anterior pituitary

questions.q: Which organ produces most of the circulating insulin like growth factor 1?
options: The kidney
The anterior pituitary
The liver
The epiphyseal plate
questions.why: Growth hormone binds hepatocytes and the liver releases IGF-1 into the blood, which is how most of the growth promoting effect is actually delivered. The kidney makes erythropoietin and activates vitamin D, not IGF-1. The anterior pituitary makes growth hormone itself, one step earlier in the chain. The epiphyseal plate is the tissue IGF-1 acts on, and its local production is small compared with hepatic output.
questions.answerText: The liver

questions.q: What is the direct effect of growth hormone on adipose tissue?
options: It blocks fatty acid entry into mitochondria
It increases triglyceride storage in fat cells
It converts fatty acids into glucose
It increases lipolysis and releases fatty acids
questions.why: Growth hormone acts directly on fat cells to break down stored triglyceride, freeing fatty acids as an alternative fuel so glucose is spared for other tissues. Increasing storage is the effect of insulin, which is the opposing signal. Fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose in humans, so that option is not a real pathway. Blocking mitochondrial entry of fatty acids would prevent their use, the opposite of what growth hormone accomplishes.
questions.answerText: It increases lipolysis and releases fatty acids

questions.q: What is the direct effect of growth hormone on plasma glucose?
options: It raises plasma glucose
It lowers plasma glucose
It leaves plasma glucose unchanged
It lowers plasma glucose only during exercise
questions.why: Growth hormone opposes insulin in muscle and fat, reducing glucose uptake while the liver adds glucose to the blood, which is why it is described as having a diabetogenic action. Lowering glucose is the job of insulin. Glucose does not stay unchanged, since the anti insulin effect is measurable within hours. Exercise does not reverse the direction of the effect.
questions.answerText: It raises plasma glucose

questions.q: Which growth hormone action is carried out mainly through insulin like growth factor 1?
options: Release of fatty acids from stored adipose tissue
Lengthening of long bones at the epiphyseal plate
Reduction of glucose uptake by skeletal muscle
Increased hepatic output of glucose to the blood
questions.why: IGF-1 is the mediator that drives cartilage cell division and matrix production at the growth plate, along with general protein synthesis, so linear growth is the classic indirect action. Lipolysis, reduced glucose uptake, and hepatic glucose output are the direct metabolic actions of growth hormone on its own receptors. Splitting the actions this way is the point of the distinction between direct and mediated effects.
questions.answerText: Lengthening of long bones at the epiphyseal plate

questions.q: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits growth hormone release?
options: Growth hormone releasing hormone
Corticotropin releasing hormone
Somatostatin
Thyrotropin releasing hormone
questions.why: Somatostatin from the hypothalamus is the brake on somatotropes, and growth hormone output reflects the balance between it and the releasing hormone. Growth hormone releasing hormone is the accelerator, not the brake. Corticotropin releasing hormone drives ACTH and the cortisol axis. Thyrotropin releasing hormone drives TSH and the thyroid axis.
questions.answerText: Somatostatin

questions.q: Excess growth hormone in a child whose epiphyseal plates are still open produces which condition?
options: Cretinism
Acromegaly
Pituitary dwarfism
Gigantism
questions.why: Open plates can still add length, so excess growth hormone before closure produces an unusually tall person with roughly normal proportions. Acromegaly is the same hormone excess after the plates have closed. Pituitary dwarfism is growth hormone deficiency in childhood. Cretinism results from untreated thyroid hormone deficiency in infancy, a different hormone entirely.
questions.answerText: Gigantism

questions.q: Excess growth hormone in an adult whose epiphyseal plates have closed produces which condition?
options: Acromegaly
Pituitary dwarfism
Gigantism
Myxedema
questions.why: With the plates closed no further length is possible, so bone grows by thickening and the hands, feet, and jaw enlarge, which is acromegaly. Gigantism requires open plates and therefore childhood onset. Pituitary dwarfism is the deficiency state, not the excess. Myxedema is severe adult hypothyroidism and has nothing to do with growth hormone.
questions.answerText: Acromegaly

questions.q: A child produces almost no growth hormone from infancy. What do you predict about his adult stature and body proportions?
options: Short with a normal trunk and very short limbs
Short with roughly normal proportions
Tall with unusually long limbs
Normal height with enlarged hands and jaw
questions.why: Growth hormone deficiency slows growth at every plate at once, so the child ends up small but proportioned, the picture of pituitary dwarfism. Short limbs with a normal trunk is the pattern of a cartilage disorder such as achondroplasia, not a hormone deficiency. Tall with long limbs points to excess growth hormone or delayed plate closure. Normal height with enlarged hands and jaw is acromegaly, an adult onset excess.
questions.answerText: Short with roughly normal proportions

questions.q: A 45 year old finds that his ring size and shoe size have both increased over three years and his jaw has become more prominent. Which hormone problem does this fit?
options: Growth hormone deficiency in adulthood
Growth hormone excess before epiphyseal closure
Growth hormone excess after epiphyseal closure
Insulin like growth factor 1 deficiency
questions.why: After the plates close, extra growth hormone can only thicken bone and expand soft tissue, so hands, feet, and facial bones enlarge without any gain in height. Deficiency in adulthood reduces lean mass and bone density rather than enlarging the extremities. Excess before closure would have made him unusually tall as well. IGF-1 deficiency would blunt growth, not exaggerate it.
questions.answerText: Growth hormone excess after epiphyseal closure

questions.q: A person with a defective growth hormone receptor has high plasma growth hormone but very low IGF-1. What do you predict about growth?
options: Growth is excessive, because growth hormone is high
Growth is normal until the plates close, then slows
Growth is normal, because growth hormone acts directly on bone
Growth is poor, because the mediator is missing
questions.why: Linear growth depends on IGF-1, so a broken receptor upstream means the liver never releases the mediator and the child grows poorly no matter how high the growth hormone level climbs. High growth hormone cannot drive growth if the signal cannot be received. Growth hormone does not lengthen bone by acting directly on the plate to any meaningful degree. Growth failure is present from early childhood, not delayed until closure.
questions.answerText: Growth is poor, because the mediator is missing

questions.q: What happens to growth hormone secretion during a prolonged fast, and why does that make metabolic sense?
options: It rises, mobilizing fat and sparing glucose
It falls, reducing the demand for fuel
It falls, allowing insulin to store the remaining glucose
It rises, increasing glucose uptake into muscle
questions.why: Fasting increases growth hormone secretion, which frees fatty acids for muscle and other tissues while limiting glucose uptake so the brain keeps its supply. A fall would remove that fuel switching signal at the moment it is most needed. Insulin secretion falls during a fast, so there is little glucose storage to permit. Growth hormone reduces rather than increases glucose uptake into muscle.
questions.answerText: It rises, mobilizing fat and sparing glucose

questions.q: An adult with closed epiphyseal plates is given growth hormone. What effect on height do you predict?
options: A gain of several centimeters of height over a year
No increase in height, since no plate cartilage remains
A gain in height only if plasma IGF-1 also rises
A loss of height from increased bone resorption
questions.why: Lengthening requires proliferating cartilage at the epiphyseal plate, and once that plate has been replaced by bone the substrate for length is simply gone. A gain of centimeters is impossible for the same reason. Raising IGF-1 does not help, because IGF-1 needs plate cartilage to act on. Growth hormone does not cause height loss, since it favors bone formation rather than resorption.
questions.answerText: No increase in height, since no plate cartilage remains

questions.q: A patient with a growth hormone secreting tumor is found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 130 mg/dL. Which growth hormone action explains this?
options: Its IGF-1 mediated action on cartilage
Its stimulation of insulin secretion by beta cells
Its direct anti insulin action in muscle and fat
Its inhibition of hepatic glucose output
questions.why: Growth hormone directly opposes insulin, cutting glucose uptake into muscle and fat while the liver keeps releasing glucose, so fasting glucose drifts upward. The IGF-1 mediated action is on growth, not on glucose handling. Beta cells actually work harder to compensate here, but that is a response to the high glucose rather than the cause. Growth hormone raises hepatic glucose output rather than inhibiting it.
questions.answerText: Its direct anti insulin action in muscle and fat

questions.q: A child grows poorly. Growth hormone is normal or high, IGF-1 is very low, and liver function is severely impaired. What best explains the growth failure?
options: The pituitary is not secreting enough growth hormone at all
The epiphyseal plates have already closed prematurely
Somatostatin is suppressing the epiphyseal plates directly in the bone
The damaged liver cannot generate IGF-1 in response to the hormone
questions.why: Growth hormone works on bone through hepatic IGF-1, so liver failure breaks the chain at the mediator step and growth stalls even with plenty of hormone upstream. Inadequate pituitary secretion is ruled out by the normal or high growth hormone level. Somatostatin acts on the pituitary to reduce growth hormone release and does not act on plates. Premature plate closure would show as an advanced bone age with the plates gone, not as a low IGF-1.
questions.answerText: The damaged liver cannot generate IGF-1 in response to the hormone

questions.q: A patient with acromegaly is treated with a drug that mimics somatostatin. Trace the expected changes in growth hormone, IGF-1, and soft tissue swelling.
options: Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone rises, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 rises, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 is unchanged, and soft tissue swelling increases
questions.why: Somatostatin inhibits the somatotropes, so growth hormone drops, hepatic IGF-1 drops with it because it is downstream, and the soft tissue enlargement driven by both hormones recedes. IGF-1 cannot rise while its driver is falling. Growth hormone cannot rise under a somatostatin like drug, which is inhibitory. Unchanged IGF-1 with worsening swelling would mean the drug had no effect at all.
questions.answerText: Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases

questions.q: Two people have the same growth hormone secreting tumor. One developed it at age 10 and one at age 40. How will their presentations differ?
options: The adult becomes very tall, and the child only becomes thick boned instead
The child becomes very tall as well as thick boned, the adult only thick boned
Both become very tall, but only the adult has a high plasma glucose level
Both become thick boned, and neither of them gains any height at all
questions.why: Open epiphyseal plates at age 10 allow length to be added, so the child grows tall and also thickens, while the adult with closed plates can only thicken. The adult cannot gain height because the plate cartilage is gone. The anti insulin effect on glucose occurs at either age, so it does not separate them. Saying neither gains height ignores the open plates in the ten year old.
questions.answerText: The child becomes very tall as well as thick boned, the adult only thick boned

questions.q: A patient with growth hormone excess has elevated glucose and elevated insulin at the same time. What does that combination tell you?
options: The beta cells have been destroyed, so glucose cannot be cleared
Insulin is being secreted normally and the glucose reading is an error
The tissues are resisting insulin, so beta cells are compensating
Growth hormone is directly stimulating hepatic glycogen storage
questions.why: High insulin alongside high glucose means insulin is present but not working well, which is exactly the anti insulin state growth hormone creates in muscle and fat, and the beta cells raise output to keep up. Destroyed beta cells would give high glucose with low insulin. Two abnormal values that fit a known mechanism are not an error. Growth hormone opposes storage and raises hepatic glucose release rather than promoting glycogen storage.
questions.answerText: The tissues are resisting insulin, so beta cells are compensating

questions.q: Which element must be trapped by the thyroid gland to build thyroid hormone?
options: Iron
Zinc
Iodine
Selenium
questions.why: Thyroid follicular cells actively pump iodide from the blood and attach it to tyrosine residues, so iodine is built into the hormone molecule itself. Iron is required for hemoglobin and for cytochromes, not for thyroid hormone synthesis. Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes but is not incorporated into T3 or T4. Selenium is needed by the deiodinase enzymes that convert T4 to T3, a later step, but it is not part of the hormone.
questions.answerText: Iodine

questions.q: Which protein stores thyroid hormone in the follicular colloid?
options: Transthyretin
Thyroid binding globulin
Thyroid peroxidase
Thyroglobulin
questions.why: Thyroglobulin is the large protein in the colloid whose tyrosine residues are iodinated and coupled, so the gland stores months of hormone inside it. Thyroid binding globulin is the plasma carrier that transports hormone in the blood, outside the gland. Thyroid peroxidase is the enzyme that does the iodinating, not the storage scaffold. Transthyretin is another plasma transport protein.
questions.answerText: Thyroglobulin

questions.q: What does thyroid peroxidase do during hormone synthesis?
options: It oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues
It transports iodide into the follicular cell
It removes an iodine atom to convert T4 into T3
It splits hormone free from thyroglobulin in the cell
questions.why: Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes trapped iodide and adds it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin, then couples the iodinated tyrosines to form T3 and T4, which is why blocking it stops synthesis. Iodide transport into the cell is the job of the sodium iodide symporter. Removing an iodine from T4 is done by deiodinase enzymes in peripheral tissues. Lysosomal enzymes free the hormone from thyroglobulin after the colloid is taken back into the cell.
questions.answerText: It oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues

questions.q: Which thyroid hormone is the more potent form at the target cell?
options: T4, because it is secreted in greater amounts
T3
Both are equally potent
Neither is active until bound to thyroglobulin
questions.why: T3 binds the nuclear thyroid receptor with much higher affinity, so it is the form that actually drives gene transcription in the target cell. T4 is indeed secreted in far greater amounts, but it functions largely as a circulating reservoir that is converted to T3. Equal potency would make the conversion step pointless. Binding to thyroglobulin is a storage arrangement inside the gland, not an activation step in the target tissue.
questions.answerText: T3

questions.q: What do deiodinase enzymes in peripheral tissues do to T4?
options: They add one iodine to make T3
They bind T4 to a plasma carrier protein
They remove one iodine to make T3
They break the hormone down into free tyrosine
questions.why: Peripheral deiodinases strip a single iodine from T4 to yield the more active T3, which lets each tissue tune how much active hormone it gets. Adding iodine is backwards, since T4 already carries four iodine atoms and T3 carries three. Binding to a carrier protein happens in plasma and is not an enzymatic conversion. Complete breakdown to tyrosine is degradation, not activation.
questions.answerText: They remove one iodine to make T3

questions.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates the thyroid gland?
options: Thyrotropin releasing hormone
Growth hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone
Thyroid stimulating hormone
questions.why: TSH from the anterior pituitary drives iodide trapping, hormone synthesis, and release, and it also makes the gland grow when it is chronically elevated. Thyrotropin releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus and acts on the pituitary, one step earlier. ACTH drives the adrenal cortex. Growth hormone acts mainly through hepatic IGF-1 and does not stimulate the thyroid.
questions.answerText: Thyroid stimulating hormone

questions.q: What is the effect of thyroid hormone on basal metabolic rate?
options: It increases basal metabolic rate
It decreases basal metabolic rate
It has no effect on basal metabolic rate
It increases it only in skeletal muscle
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases the number of mitochondria and the activity of metabolic enzymes in nearly every tissue, so oxygen consumption and heat production rise. A decrease is what happens when the hormone is deficient. No effect would leave most of the signs of thyroid disease unexplained. The effect is body wide, not confined to skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: It increases basal metabolic rate

questions.q: Which thyroid cell type secretes T3 and T4?
options: Parafollicular C cells
Follicular cells
Chief cells
Chromaffin cells
questions.why: Follicular cells form the ring around the colloid, trap iodide, and secrete T3 and T4. Parafollicular C cells sit between the follicles and secrete calcitonin instead. Chief cells belong to the parathyroid glands and secrete parathyroid hormone. Chromaffin cells belong to the adrenal medulla and secrete catecholamines.
questions.answerText: Follicular cells

questions.q: A patient reports heat intolerance, a resting heart rate of 105, weight loss despite a good appetite, and tremor. What underlying rate of metabolism does this fit?
options: A normal metabolic rate with excess cortisol
A decreased metabolic rate from thyroid hormone deficiency
An increased metabolic rate from excess thyroid hormone
A decreased metabolic rate from iodine excess
questions.why: Every one of these signs follows from burning fuel faster, since extra heat must be shed, the heart is driven harder, and intake cannot keep up with expenditure. Deficiency produces the mirror image, with cold intolerance and weight gain. Excess cortisol tends to add central weight rather than cause loss. Iodine excess does not by itself lower metabolic rate in this pattern.
questions.answerText: An increased metabolic rate from excess thyroid hormone

questions.q: A patient reports feeling cold when others are comfortable, gaining weight on an unchanged diet, constipation, and a heart rate of 52. Which state does this describe?
options: Hyperthyroidism, with a raised metabolic rate
Hyperthyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate
Normal thyroid function with iron deficiency
Hypothyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate
questions.why: Slower metabolism means less heat produced, fewer calories burned, slower gut motility, and less stimulation of the heart, which is exactly this cluster. Hyperthyroidism gives the opposite picture in every one of those systems. Iron deficiency causes fatigue but not cold intolerance with slow bowels and bradycardia. Hyperthyroidism with a reduced metabolic rate is self contradictory.
questions.answerText: Hypothyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate

questions.q: A person's diet has contained almost no iodine for a year. Predict plasma T4, plasma TSH, and gland size.
options: T4 low, TSH high, gland enlarged
T4 low, TSH low, gland shrunken
T4 high, TSH low, gland enlarged
T4 normal, TSH normal, gland enlarged
questions.why: Without iodine the gland cannot make hormone, T4 falls, negative feedback is lost so TSH climbs, and sustained TSH stimulation makes the gland grow into a goiter. Low TSH with low T4 would point to a pituitary problem rather than a substrate shortage. High T4 is impossible without iodine. Normal values would not explain why the gland enlarged.
questions.answerText: T4 low, TSH high, gland enlarged

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle. What does this predict about the heart in hyperthyroidism?
options: The heart becomes largely insensitive to the catecholamines
The heart responds more strongly to a given level of catecholamines
Catecholamine secretion from the adrenal medulla falls sharply
The heart rate is set entirely by the thyroid hormone itself
questions.why: More receptors means the same plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine produce a larger effect, which is the permissive action that explains the tachycardia and tremor of hyperthyroidism. Insensitivity would follow from receptor loss, which is the hypothyroid direction. Adrenal medullary output is not reduced by thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormone amplifies the sympathetic signal rather than replacing it.
questions.answerText: The heart responds more strongly to a given level of catecholamines

questions.q: A drug blocks thyroid peroxidase. Predict the effect on plasma T4 over the next several weeks.
options: T4 falls immediately within an hour
T4 rises because stored colloid is released
T4 falls gradually as stored hormone is used up
T4 is unaffected because peripheral conversion continues
questions.why: Blocking peroxidase stops new synthesis, but the colloid holds weeks of ready made hormone, so the plasma level declines slowly as that reserve is released and cleared. An immediate fall would only happen if release rather than synthesis were blocked. Colloid release does not increase in response to the block. Peripheral conversion changes T4 into T3 and cannot create new hormone.
questions.answerText: T4 falls gradually as stored hormone is used up

questions.q: An infant with untreated thyroid hormone deficiency from birth develops which lasting problem?
options: Early puberty with unusually rapid bone maturation
Excessive linear growth with entirely normal intellect
Enlarged hands and jaw with normal adult height
Impaired nervous system development and stunted growth
questions.why: Thyroid hormone is required for normal brain development and for skeletal growth in the first years, so untreated deficiency causes both cognitive impairment and short stature, the condition called cretinism. Excessive linear growth is the opposite of what deficiency does. Enlarged hands and jaw with normal height is acromegaly, a growth hormone problem. Deficiency delays rather than accelerates bone maturation and puberty.
questions.answerText: Impaired nervous system development and stunted growth

questions.q: In a patient whose thyroid gland itself is overactive, what happens to TSH?
options: TSH falls, because high thyroid hormone suppresses the pituitary
TSH rises, because the gland is working harder
TSH stays normal, because the thyroid is not pituitary controlled
TSH rises first and then falls once the gland enlarges
questions.why: Thyroid hormone feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so when the gland overproduces on its own, TSH is driven down to a very low level. Rising TSH would be the cause of overactivity, not the response to it. The thyroid is under pituitary control, which is why the feedback works. There is no phase of high TSH in a gland that is autonomously overproducing.
questions.answerText: TSH falls, because high thyroid hormone suppresses the pituitary

questions.q: A patient has low plasma T4 and high plasma TSH. Where is the problem?
options: In the hypothalamus
In the thyroid gland itself
In the anterior pituitary
In the peripheral deiodinase enzymes
questions.why: A high TSH shows the pituitary is sensing low hormone and pushing hard, so the failure to respond must lie in the gland, which is what primary hypothyroidism means. A hypothalamic problem would lower TSH along with T4. A pituitary problem would also give a low TSH, since it could not produce the drive. A deiodinase problem would reduce T3 while leaving T4 normal or high.
questions.answerText: In the thyroid gland itself

questions.q: A different patient has low plasma T4 and low plasma TSH. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The thyroid gland has been destroyed by autoantibodies
Dietary iodine has been severely deficient in this patient
The pituitary is not producing enough TSH to drive the gland
Excess thyroid hormone is being taken by mouth daily
questions.why: When hormone is low, TSH should be high, so a low TSH means the drive itself has failed and the problem sits above the gland in the pituitary or hypothalamus. Destruction of the gland or iodine deficiency would both leave the pituitary intact and TSH would be high. Excess hormone taken by mouth would suppress TSH but plasma T4 would be high, not low.
questions.answerText: The pituitary is not producing enough TSH to drive the gland

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number and activity of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps throughout the body. Trace how that raises body temperature.
options: The pumps generate heat by moving ions against friction in the membrane
The pumps raise plasma sodium, which raises the hypothalamic set point
The pumps constrict skin arterioles and trap heat in the core
More ATP is hydrolyzed by the pumps, and that energy leaves as heat
questions.why: Running more pumps consumes more ATP, cells burn more fuel and use more oxygen to replace it, and much of the energy released in that cycle appears as heat. Ion movement through a channel does not generate meaningful frictional heat. Skin arteriole tone is a vascular response controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, not by the pumps. Plasma sodium is held nearly constant and the hypothalamic set point is not raised by thyroid hormone.
questions.answerText: More ATP is hydrolyzed by the pumps, and that energy leaves as heat

questions.q: A person has been taking too much thyroid hormone for months. Predict oxygen consumption, appetite, and body weight together.
options: Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight down
Oxygen consumption up, appetite down, weight down
Oxygen consumption down, appetite up, weight up
Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight up
questions.why: A raised metabolic rate burns more oxygen and more fuel, hunger rises in response, but intake usually fails to keep pace with expenditure so weight still falls. Appetite going down does not fit a high metabolic demand. Falling oxygen consumption is the hypothyroid pattern. Weight gain would require intake to exceed the increased expenditure, which is not the usual outcome.
questions.answerText: Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight down

questions.q: Which hormone is secreted by the zona glomerulosa?
options: Cortisol
Epinephrine
Dehydroepiandrosterone
Aldosterone
questions.why: The outermost cortical zone, the glomerulosa, is the only tissue with the enzyme needed to finish aldosterone, so it is the sole source of that hormone. Cortisol comes from the middle zone, the fasciculata. Dehydroepiandrosterone comes from the innermost cortical zone, the reticularis. Epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla, which is not cortex at all.
questions.answerText: Aldosterone

questions.q: Which hormone is secreted by the zona fasciculata?
options: Cortisol
Norepinephrine
Aldosterone
Androstenedione
questions.why: The broad middle zone, the fasciculata, is the main source of cortisol and it is the zone that grows under ACTH stimulation. Aldosterone is made in the outer glomerulosa. Norepinephrine is a medullary catecholamine, not a cortical steroid. Androstenedione is an adrenal androgen from the inner reticularis.
questions.answerText: Cortisol

questions.q: Which hormones are secreted by the zona reticularis?
options: The mineralocorticoids
The adrenal androgens
The catecholamines
The glucocorticoids only
questions.why: The innermost cortical zone, the reticularis, secretes weak androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone that are converted to stronger androgens in peripheral tissue. Mineralocorticoids means aldosterone, which is a glomerulosa product. Catecholamines come from the medulla. Glucocorticoid production belongs mainly to the fasciculata, although the reticularis contributes some.
questions.answerText: The adrenal androgens

questions.q: What is the primary action of aldosterone?
options: It increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by adding aquaporins
It increases plasma glucose by driving hepatic gluconeogenesis in the liver
It increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron
It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule of the nephron
questions.why: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct to add sodium channels and pumps, so sodium is retained and potassium is lost into the urine. Direct control of water permeability is the job of ADH, although water does follow the retained sodium. Driving gluconeogenesis is a cortisol action. Calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule is stimulated by parathyroid hormone.
questions.answerText: It increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron

questions.q: What is the primary metabolic action of cortisol?
options: It lowers plasma glucose by increasing muscle uptake
It raises plasma calcium by stimulating bone resorption
It raises plasma sodium by acting on the distal nephron
It raises plasma glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis
questions.why: Cortisol supplies the liver with amino acids and turns on the gluconeogenic enzymes, so plasma glucose is defended during stress and fasting. Lowering glucose by increasing muscle uptake is the action of insulin, the opposing signal. Sodium retention is the aldosterone action, although very high cortisol can spill over onto that receptor. Raising plasma calcium through bone resorption is parathyroid hormone territory.
questions.answerText: It raises plasma glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis

questions.q: From what molecule are all three classes of adrenal cortical hormone built?
options: Cholesterol
Tyrosine
Tryptophan
A chain of amino acids
questions.why: Aldosterone, cortisol, and the adrenal androgens are all steroids, and every steroid begins as cholesterol before enzymes in each zone modify it. Tyrosine is the precursor of the catecholamines and of thyroid hormone. Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin and melatonin. A chain of amino acids describes peptide hormones such as insulin and ADH.
questions.answerText: Cholesterol

questions.q: Which two signals are the main regulators of aldosterone secretion?
options: ACTH and plasma sodium concentration
Angiotensin II and plasma potassium
ADH and total plasma osmolarity
Renin and the plasma glucose level
questions.why: The zona glomerulosa responds mainly to angiotensin II generated when blood pressure or volume falls, and directly to a rise in plasma potassium. ACTH has only a small permissive effect on this zone, and plasma sodium is a weak signal compared with these two. ADH and osmolarity control water handling through a separate pathway. Renin acts upstream by generating angiotensin, and plasma glucose is not an input here.
questions.answerText: Angiotensin II and plasma potassium

questions.q: Which cortical zones are the main targets of ACTH?
options: The zona glomerulosa acting alone
All three cortical zones equally
The zona fasciculata and zona reticularis
The zona glomerulosa and the medulla
questions.why: ACTH drives cortisol from the fasciculata and androgens from the reticularis, which is why both fall together when ACTH is lost. The glomerulosa keeps working largely without ACTH because it answers to angiotensin II and potassium. Equal control of all three zones would mean losing ACTH also abolishes aldosterone, which does not happen. The medulla is controlled by sympathetic preganglionic neurons, not by ACTH.
questions.answerText: The zona fasciculata and zona reticularis

questions.q: Plasma aldosterone rises sharply. What happens to plasma potassium?
options: It rises, because potassium follows sodium into the blood
It falls, because potassium is shifted into bone
It is unchanged, because aldosterone only moves sodium
It falls, because more potassium is secreted into the urine
questions.why: Aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion at the same site, so more aldosterone means more potassium lost in the urine and a lower plasma level. Potassium moves opposite to sodium here, not with it. Aldosterone handles both ions, so no change is not the outcome. Bone is a calcium and phosphate store and does not buffer potassium in this way.
questions.answerText: It falls, because more potassium is secreted into the urine

questions.q: A person loses blood volume during surgery. Trace the change to the zona glomerulosa.
options: Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and aldosterone secretion increases
Renin falls, angiotensin II falls, and aldosterone secretion increases
ACTH rises and aldosterone secretion increases with cortisol
Plasma potassium falls and aldosterone secretion increases
questions.why: Reduced renal perfusion makes the kidney release renin, angiotensin II is generated, and it stimulates the glomerulosa to release aldosterone so sodium and therefore water are conserved. Falling renin cannot raise aldosterone, since it is the first step of the pathway. ACTH is not the main driver of the glomerulosa. Falling potassium reduces aldosterone rather than increasing it.
questions.answerText: Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and aldosterone secretion increases

questions.q: The entire adrenal cortex is destroyed by autoimmune disease. Predict plasma sodium, plasma potassium, and blood pressure.
options: Sodium high, potassium low, blood pressure high
Sodium low, potassium high, blood pressure low
Sodium low, potassium low, blood pressure high
Sodium high, potassium high, blood pressure low
questions.why: Losing aldosterone means sodium is wasted in the urine and potassium is retained, and the sodium loss takes water with it so volume and pressure fall. High sodium with low potassium is the pattern of aldosterone excess, the opposite problem. Low potassium cannot occur when the hormone that excretes it is gone. High sodium with high potassium does not fit a single failing pathway.
questions.answerText: Sodium low, potassium high, blood pressure low

questions.q: A patient has had very high ACTH for months. Which change in the adrenal gland do you predict?
options: The zona glomerulosa thickens and aldosterone output rises
The adrenal medulla enlarges and epinephrine output rises
The zona fasciculata thickens and cortisol output rises
The whole gland shrinks from overuse
questions.why: ACTH is both a secretory signal and a growth signal for the fasciculata, so chronic elevation makes that zone hypertrophy while cortisol output climbs. The glomerulosa is driven by angiotensin II and potassium, so it grows little under ACTH. The medulla answers to sympathetic nerves, not to ACTH. Glands enlarge under chronic trophic stimulation rather than shrinking.
questions.answerText: The zona fasciculata thickens and cortisol output rises

questions.q: A seven year old girl has adrenal androgen secretion many times the normal level. What do you predict?
options: Weight gain with a low blood glucose between meals
Delayed puberty with short stature and absent pubic hair
Salt wasting with a low blood pressure and a high plasma potassium
Early appearance of pubic hair and other androgen driven features
questions.why: Adrenal androgens are weak but at high concentration they produce the androgen dependent changes of puberty, so signs appear years early. Delayed puberty would follow from too little sex steroid, not too much. Salt wasting comes from aldosterone deficiency, a different zone. Weight gain with low glucose does not fit an androgen excess.
questions.answerText: Early appearance of pubic hair and other androgen driven features

questions.q: A small tumor of the zona glomerulosa secretes aldosterone continuously. Predict blood pressure and plasma potassium.
options: Blood pressure high and potassium low
Blood pressure low and potassium high
Blood pressure high and potassium high
Blood pressure normal and potassium low
questions.why: Continuous aldosterone retains sodium and water, raising volume and pressure, while potassium is steadily secreted into the urine and falls. Low pressure with high potassium is the deficiency picture. Potassium cannot rise while the hormone that excretes it is in excess. Blood pressure does not stay normal when sodium retention is sustained for weeks.
questions.answerText: Blood pressure high and potassium low

questions.q: A drug blocks the aldosterone receptor in the distal nephron. Predict urinary sodium and urinary potassium.
options: Sodium excretion falls and potassium excretion rises
Sodium excretion rises and potassium excretion falls
Both sodium and potassium excretion rise
Both sodium and potassium excretion fall
questions.why: Blocking the receptor removes the signal to reabsorb sodium and to secrete potassium, so sodium leaves in the urine while potassium is retained in the body. Falling sodium excretion with rising potassium excretion is what aldosterone itself does, not what a blocker does. The two ions move in opposite directions at this site, so both cannot rise or both fall.
questions.answerText: Sodium excretion rises and potassium excretion falls

questions.q: A patient has high plasma aldosterone and very low plasma renin. What does the renin value tell you?
options: The kidney is driving aldosterone secretion through angiotensin II release
The patient is volume depleted and the kidney is compensating for that
The adrenal gland is secreting on its own rather than responding to the kidney
The pituitary is secreting excess ACTH and driving the entire cortex hard
questions.why: If the kidney were driving the gland, renin would be high, so a suppressed renin with high aldosterone means the adrenal source is autonomous and the resulting volume expansion has shut renin off. Angiotensin II driven secretion requires high renin by definition. Volume depletion raises renin rather than suppressing it. Excess ACTH would raise cortisol and androgens rather than aldosterone.
questions.answerText: The adrenal gland is secreting on its own rather than responding to the kidney

questions.q: An inherited enzyme defect blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis. Trace what happens to ACTH and to the adrenal androgens.
options: ACTH falls and adrenal androgen output falls with it
ACTH is unchanged because cortisol is not its only signal
ACTH rises and all three steroid classes fall together
ACTH rises without feedback restraint and androgens increase
questions.why: Cortisol is the negative feedback signal, so if it cannot be made, ACTH climbs, the cortex is driven hard, and the precursors that accumulate are pushed down the androgen pathway that is still intact. ACTH cannot fall when its inhibitor is missing. Androgens rise rather than fall because their pathway is not blocked. Cortisol is the dominant feedback signal for ACTH, so the level does change.
questions.answerText: ACTH rises without feedback restraint and androgens increase

questions.q: A patient with primary adrenal failure has darkened skin creases. Trace the connection.
options: Low cortisol removes feedback, ACTH rises, and ACTH acts on pigment cells
Low aldosterone raises plasma potassium, which darkens the skin creases
High cortisol thins the skin and makes surface vessels more visible
Low adrenal androgens allow melanin to accumulate in skin creases
questions.why: When the gland cannot make cortisol, the pituitary loses its brake and pours out ACTH, which acts on melanocytes and deepens pigmentation in creases and scars. Potassium has no effect on skin pigment. High cortisol thins skin but that is the excess state, not adrenal failure. Adrenal androgens do not restrain melanin production.
questions.answerText: Low cortisol removes feedback, ACTH rises, and ACTH acts on pigment cells

questions.q: Two patients each lack one cortical hormone. Patient A lacks aldosterone only, patient B lacks cortisol only. Which finding separates them?
options: Patient A has low fasting glucose, patient B has high plasma potassium
Patient A has high plasma potassium, patient B has low fasting glucose
Both have high plasma potassium but only A has low glucose
Both have low fasting glucose but only B has high potassium
questions.why: Aldosterone controls sodium and potassium handling, so losing it raises plasma potassium, while cortisol defends glucose during fasting, so losing it lets fasting glucose fall. The reversed pairing assigns each problem to the wrong hormone. Neither patient should show both defects, because each lacks only one hormone and the two zones act on different systems.
questions.answerText: Patient A has high plasma potassium, patient B has low fasting glucose

questions.q: What does cortisol do to hepatic gluconeogenesis?
options: It increases it
It decreases it
It leaves it unchanged
It increases it only when insulin is also high
questions.why: Cortisol turns on the liver enzymes that build glucose from amino acids and glycerol, which is how it defends plasma glucose during a prolonged stress or fast. Decreasing gluconeogenesis is what insulin does. Leaving it unchanged would remove the main metabolic reason cortisol matters. High insulin opposes the effect rather than being required for it.
questions.answerText: It increases it

questions.q: What is the effect of cortisol on skeletal muscle protein?
options: It builds protein and increases muscle mass
It breaks protein down and releases amino acids
It has no effect on muscle protein
It traps amino acids inside muscle cells
questions.why: Cortisol is catabolic in muscle, freeing amino acids that travel to the liver as raw material for glucose synthesis. Building muscle protein is what growth hormone and insulin do. No effect would leave the muscle wasting of chronic cortisol excess unexplained. Trapping amino acids inside the cell is the opposite of the export that gluconeogenesis requires.
questions.answerText: It breaks protein down and releases amino acids

questions.q: What is the effect of cortisol on the immune response?
options: It enhances it
It has no effect on it
It suppresses it
It enhances it only during acute stress
questions.why: Cortisol reduces circulating lymphocytes, damps cytokine production, and blunts inflammation, which is why glucocorticoid drugs are used to control immune reactions. Enhancing immunity is the opposite of the observed effect. No effect would make glucocorticoids useless as anti inflammatory agents. Even acute stress cortisol suppresses rather than enhances the response.
questions.answerText: It suppresses it

questions.q: How does cortisol support blood pressure?
options: It directly constricts arterioles on its own without help
It causes the adrenal medulla to release more epinephrine
It increases the heart rate through beta receptors it activates itself
It permits vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines
questions.why: Cortisol is permissive, meaning it maintains the receptors and signaling that let norepinephrine and epinephrine constrict vessels, so without it the same catecholamine level produces a much weaker response. Cortisol does not itself bind vascular receptors to constrict. It does not activate beta receptors on the heart. Medullary catecholamine release is driven by sympathetic nerves rather than by cortisol.
questions.answerText: It permits vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines

questions.q: At what time of day is plasma cortisol normally highest?
options: Early morning, around waking
Late evening, before sleep
Immediately after the largest meal
It is constant throughout the day
questions.why: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm with a peak just before and around waking, which prepares fuel mobilization for the day ahead. Late evening is the trough, when levels are lowest. Meals influence insulin and glucagon far more than cortisol. A constant level would mean there was no rhythm, which is not the case.
questions.answerText: Early morning, around waking

questions.q: What is the correct order of the hormones in the stress axis?
options: ACTH, then CRH, then cortisol
CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol
CRH, then cortisol, then ACTH
ACTH, then cortisol, then CRH
questions.why: The hypothalamus releases corticotropin releasing hormone into the portal blood, the anterior pituitary responds with ACTH, and the adrenal cortex responds with cortisol. Any ordering that puts ACTH before CRH reverses the brain to pituitary step. Cortisol is always the final output, since it comes from the target gland at the end of the chain.
questions.answerText: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol

questions.q: Where does cortisol exert its negative feedback?
options: On the cells of the adrenal cortex itself
On the posterior pituitary and its terminals
On the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary
On the liver and on skeletal muscle cells
questions.why: Cortisol inhibits CRH release from the hypothalamus and ACTH release from the anterior pituitary, closing the loop at both levels above the gland. Feedback onto the adrenal cortex itself is not the main mechanism, since the cortex only responds to the ACTH it receives. The posterior pituitary handles ADH and oxytocin. Liver and muscle are target tissues for the metabolic actions, not feedback sites.
questions.answerText: On the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary

questions.q: What does cortisol do to adipose tissue?
options: It blocks fatty acid release during fasting
It promotes triglyceride storage in the limbs
It converts fat cells into muscle cells
It promotes lipolysis and releases fatty acids
questions.why: Cortisol frees fatty acids from stored triglyceride so tissues can burn fat while glucose is reserved, which is part of its fuel mobilizing role. Storage in the limbs is not a cortisol effect, and chronic excess actually thins the limbs. Fat cells cannot become muscle cells. Blocking fatty acid release during fasting would work against the purpose of the hormone.
questions.answerText: It promotes lipolysis and releases fatty acids

questions.q: A person has eaten nothing for 36 hours. How does cortisol help keep plasma glucose from falling?
options: By supplying amino acids from muscle for hepatic glucose synthesis
By increasing glucose uptake into muscle and fat tissue
By stimulating insulin release from the pancreatic beta cells
By preventing the brain from taking up glucose from the blood
questions.why: Cortisol breaks down muscle protein and the released amino acids become substrate for gluconeogenesis, so the liver can keep glucose in the blood well past the point where glycogen runs out. Increasing muscle uptake would lower plasma glucose, which is backwards. Insulin release falls during a fast rather than being stimulated by cortisol. Brain glucose uptake is insulin independent and is not blocked.
questions.answerText: By supplying amino acids from muscle for hepatic glucose synthesis

questions.q: A patient takes high dose glucocorticoid medication daily for a year. Predict plasma ACTH and adrenal size.
options: ACTH high and the adrenal cortex enlarged
ACTH low and the adrenal cortex atrophied
ACTH low and the adrenal cortex enlarged
ACTH high and the adrenal cortex atrophied
questions.why: The drug acts like cortisol at the feedback sites, so ACTH is suppressed, and without its trophic signal the fasciculata shrinks over months. High ACTH would require the feedback signal to be absent. An enlarged cortex needs ACTH stimulation, which is exactly what is missing. High ACTH with an atrophied cortex would describe a gland that cannot respond, not a suppressed axis.
questions.answerText: ACTH low and the adrenal cortex atrophied

questions.q: Why do patients on long term high dose glucocorticoids get infections more easily?
options: Cortisol reduces the number of red blood cells in the circulation
Cortisol thins the blood and spreads the bacteria more quickly
Cortisol suppresses lymphocyte function and the inflammatory response
Cortisol lowers body temperature so that bacteria grow much better
questions.why: Fewer and less active lymphocytes plus a blunted inflammatory response mean an invading organism meets weaker resistance and infections both start more easily and are noticed later. Red cell number is not meaningfully reduced by cortisol. Cortisol does not change blood viscosity in a way that spreads infection. Body temperature is not lowered enough to favor bacterial growth.
questions.answerText: Cortisol suppresses lymphocyte function and the inflammatory response

questions.q: How does chronic cortisol excess affect bone?
options: Bone density rises because dietary protein is redirected to bone
Bone density falls because parathyroid hormone secretion stops entirely
Bone density is unchanged because bone is not a cortisol target tissue
Bone density falls because formation is suppressed and absorption drops
questions.why: Cortisol inhibits osteoblasts and reduces intestinal calcium absorption while increasing urinary calcium loss, so the balance tips toward bone loss over months. Bone gain would require an anabolic signal, and cortisol is catabolic. Bone is very much a cortisol target, which is why osteoporosis is a well known consequence. Parathyroid hormone does not stop, and if anything it rises in response to the calcium losses.
questions.answerText: Bone density falls because formation is suppressed and absorption drops

questions.q: A patient with chronic cortisol excess has thin arms and legs but increased fat over the trunk and face. Which cortisol action explains the thin limbs?
options: Breakdown of skeletal muscle protein in the limbs
Reduced blood flow to the muscles of the limbs
Loss of subcutaneous fat only from the limbs
Failure of growth hormone secretion from the pituitary
questions.why: Cortisol is catabolic in skeletal muscle, and since the limbs are mostly muscle they visibly waste while fat is redistributed toward the trunk and face. Blood flow to the limbs is not meaningfully reduced by cortisol. Fat loss alone would not produce the weakness that goes with this pattern. Growth hormone secretion is somewhat blunted but muscle catabolism is the direct explanation.
questions.answerText: Breakdown of skeletal muscle protein in the limbs

questions.q: What does cortisol do to glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and how does that interact with insulin?
options: It increases uptake, adding to the insulin effect
It reduces uptake, so insulin has to work against it
It has no effect on uptake but blocks insulin secretion
It reduces uptake by destroying the insulin receptor permanently
questions.why: Cortisol makes muscle and fat less responsive to insulin, so glucose is left in the blood for the brain, and the beta cells must secrete more insulin to achieve the same effect. Adding to the insulin effect would lower glucose, which is the opposite of what cortisol does. Cortisol does not block insulin secretion, and beta cells usually increase output. The receptor is not destroyed, and the resistance reverses when cortisol falls.
questions.answerText: It reduces uptake, so insulin has to work against it

questions.q: A patient is given a glucocorticoid for a severe inflammatory reaction. What change in the inflamed tissue do you predict?
options: More swelling as fluid is drawn into the tissue
No change, because cortisol acts only on metabolism
Less swelling, redness, and immune cell infiltration
Faster wound closure with stronger scar tissue
questions.why: Glucocorticoids reduce cytokine production and limit the migration of immune cells into tissue, so the visible signs of inflammation subside. More swelling would be the response to a pro inflammatory signal. Cortisol has broad immune actions in addition to metabolic ones. Healing is actually slowed and scar tissue weakened, which is a cost of the treatment.
questions.answerText: Less swelling, redness, and immune cell infiltration

questions.q: A patient on daily glucocorticoids for a year stops the drug abruptly and becomes hypotensive and hypoglycemic. Trace the mechanism.
options: The drug is still circulating and is blocking the cortisol receptors
Aldosterone is lost first, and cortisol levels stay entirely normal
ACTH secretion rises too fast and overwhelms the adrenal gland
The suppressed adrenal cortex has atrophied and cannot supply cortisol
questions.why: A year of feedback suppression shrinks the fasciculata, so when the outside supply is removed the gland cannot restart in time, and the loss of cortisol removes both the permissive support for blood pressure and the drive for gluconeogenesis. A stopped drug is cleared rather than left blocking receptors. Rising ACTH is the recovery signal, not the cause of collapse. Aldosterone comes from the glomerulosa, which is not suppressed by the drug in the same way.
questions.answerText: The suppressed adrenal cortex has atrophied and cannot supply cortisol

questions.q: A student sleeps poorly and is under heavy pressure for months. Predict the combined effect on plasma glucose, infection risk, and blood pressure.
options: Glucose higher, infection risk higher, blood pressure higher
Glucose lower, infection risk higher, blood pressure lower
Glucose higher, infection risk lower, blood pressure higher
Glucose lower, infection risk lower, blood pressure lower
questions.why: Sustained cortisol raises glucose through gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, suppresses immune defense so infections take hold more easily, and supports vascular tone so pressure drifts upward. Lower glucose would require cortisol to act like insulin. Reduced infection risk contradicts the immune suppression. All three moving downward describes cortisol deficiency instead.
questions.answerText: Glucose higher, infection risk higher, blood pressure higher

questions.q: A healthy person is given a small dose of a synthetic glucocorticoid at night. What is measured the next morning, and why?
options: Cortisol is high, because the drug adds to the normal morning peak
Cortisol is low, because the drug fed back on the pituitary
Cortisol is unchanged, because feedback needs several days to act
ACTH is high, because the drug directly stimulates the pituitary
questions.why: The synthetic steroid is read by the feedback receptors as cortisol, so CRH and ACTH are shut down overnight and the adrenal makes little cortisol of its own by morning. The drug does not add to measured cortisol, since the assay reports the natural hormone. Feedback works within hours, not days. ACTH is suppressed rather than stimulated by a glucocorticoid.
questions.answerText: Cortisol is low, because the drug fed back on the pituitary

questions.q: A patient with adrenal insufficiency has normal plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine but still has a low blood pressure that responds poorly to those hormones. Explain.
options: The catecholamines are being broken down before they reach the vessels
The vessels are already maximally constricted, so no further effect is possible
Without cortisol the vessels lose their permissive support and respond weakly
Aldosterone is normal, so the low pressure must be a measurement error
questions.why: Cortisol maintains the receptors and signaling machinery that let catecholamines constrict arterioles, so when it is missing a normal catecholamine level produces an abnormally small response, which is what permissive means. Accelerated breakdown would show up as low measured catecholamine levels. Maximal constriction would give a high pressure, not a low one. Aldosterone is usually low as well in adrenal insufficiency, and the low pressure is real.
questions.answerText: Without cortisol the vessels lose their permissive support and respond weakly

questions.q: Which cells sense a fall in plasma calcium and respond by secreting a hormone?
options: Thyroid follicular cells
Parathyroid chief cells
Parafollicular C cells
Adrenal glomerulosa cells
questions.why: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands carry a calcium sensing receptor, and when plasma calcium drops they increase parathyroid hormone secretion within minutes. Thyroid follicular cells make T3 and T4 and do not monitor calcium. Parafollicular C cells sense a rise in calcium and release calcitonin instead. Adrenal glomerulosa cells respond to angiotensin II and potassium.
questions.answerText: Parathyroid chief cells

questions.q: What is the overall effect of parathyroid hormone on plasma calcium?
options: It raises plasma calcium only when vitamin D is absent
It lowers plasma calcium
It raises plasma calcium
It has no direct effect on plasma calcium
questions.why: Parathyroid hormone is the main defender of plasma calcium and raises it by acting on bone, kidney, and indirectly on intestine. Lowering plasma calcium is what calcitonin does. Vitamin D assists rather than opposes the hormone, so its absence weakens the response rather than being required for it. The effect on plasma calcium is the reason the hormone exists.
questions.answerText: It raises plasma calcium

questions.q: What does parathyroid hormone do in bone?
options: It increases osteoblast activity, adding new calcium to the bone
It blocks calcium from leaving the bone matrix altogether
It converts cartilage into bone at the epiphyseal growth plate
It increases osteoclast resorption, releasing calcium into the blood
questions.why: Parathyroid hormone drives bone resorption, and osteoclasts dissolve mineral and release both calcium and phosphate into the blood, which is the fastest large store the body can draw on. Increasing osteoblast deposition would remove calcium from the plasma instead. Endochondral growth at the plate is driven by growth hormone and IGF-1. Blocking calcium exit from bone would defeat the purpose of the hormone.
questions.answerText: It increases osteoclast resorption, releasing calcium into the blood

questions.q: What does parathyroid hormone do to calcium handling in the kidney?
options: It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule
It increases calcium excretion into the urine instead
It increases calcium filtration at the glomerulus
It has no action on calcium anywhere in the nephron
questions.why: Parathyroid hormone makes the distal tubule reclaim more filtered calcium, so less is lost in the urine and plasma calcium is defended. Increasing excretion would work against the hormone's purpose. Filtration at the glomerulus depends on the plasma concentration and pressure, not on this hormone. The renal action is one of the three arms of the response, so it cannot be absent.
questions.answerText: It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule

questions.q: What does parathyroid hormone do to phosphate handling in the kidney?
options: It increases phosphate reabsorption along with that of calcium
It decreases phosphate reabsorption, so more is excreted
It has no effect at all on renal phosphate handling
It decreases phosphate excretion, raising plasma phosphate
questions.why: Parathyroid hormone inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so plasma phosphate falls even while calcium rises, which keeps the two ions from precipitating together in tissue. Reabsorbing both would raise the calcium phosphate product and risk deposits. No effect would leave the low plasma phosphate of hyperparathyroidism unexplained. Reduced excretion is the opposite of what the hormone does.
questions.answerText: It decreases phosphate reabsorption, so more is excreted

questions.q: Which organ carries out the final activation step that produces calcitriol?
options: The liver
The small intestine
The kidney
The parathyroid gland
questions.why: The kidney holds the 1 alpha hydroxylase enzyme that converts the inactive precursor into calcitriol, and parathyroid hormone turns that enzyme on. The liver performs an earlier hydroxylation but not the activating step. The small intestine is the target of calcitriol rather than its source. The parathyroid gland makes the hormone that triggers the conversion, not the vitamin itself.
questions.answerText: The kidney

questions.q: What is the main action of calcitriol?
options: It increases calcium secretion into the gut lumen
It increases calcium loss in the urine
It stops osteoclasts from resorbing bone
It increases calcium absorption from the intestine
questions.why: Calcitriol acts on intestinal cells to build the transport proteins that carry dietary calcium into the blood, which is the only route by which the body gains new calcium. Increasing urinary loss would lower plasma calcium. Stopping osteoclasts is closer to what calcitonin does. Secretion into the gut lumen is the opposite direction from absorption.
questions.answerText: It increases calcium absorption from the intestine

questions.q: Which cells secrete calcitonin, and what does it do?
options: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it lowers plasma calcium
Parathyroid chief cells, and it lowers plasma calcium
Thyroid follicular cells, and it raises plasma calcium
Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it raises plasma calcium
questions.why: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular C cells scattered between thyroid follicles and it inhibits osteoclasts, which lowers plasma calcium. Chief cells of the parathyroid secrete parathyroid hormone, the opposing signal. Follicular cells make T3 and T4. Calcitonin lowers rather than raises plasma calcium, which is the point of having it.
questions.answerText: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it lowers plasma calcium

questions.q: Plasma calcium falls from 10 to 8 mg/dL. What happens to parathyroid hormone secretion?
options: It decreases within minutes
It increases within minutes
It is unchanged until calcium falls below 6 mg/dL
It increases only after calcitriol rises first
questions.why: The calcium sensing receptor on chief cells detects small drops and releases the brake on secretion, so parathyroid hormone rises quickly and begins correcting the fall. A decrease would let the fall continue unopposed. The system responds to small deviations rather than waiting for a severe one. Calcitriol rises as a result of parathyroid hormone, not before it.
questions.answerText: It increases within minutes

questions.q: Parathyroid hormone raises intestinal calcium absorption even though the intestine has no parathyroid hormone receptors. How?
options: It reaches the intestine through the portal vein at higher concentration
It stimulates the liver to release calcium binding protein into the gut
It stimulates the kidney to make calcitriol, which acts on the intestine
It stimulates calcitonin, which then acts on the intestine
questions.why: The intestinal arm of the response is indirect, since parathyroid hormone turns on renal 1 alpha hydroxylase and it is calcitriol that induces the intestinal calcium transporters. The liver does not release a calcium binding protein into the gut for this purpose. Portal blood carries absorbed nutrients away from the gut, not hormone toward it. Calcitonin opposes parathyroid hormone and does not mediate its actions.
questions.answerText: It stimulates the kidney to make calcitriol, which acts on the intestine

questions.q: The parathyroid glands are removed. Predict plasma calcium and the effect on nerve and muscle.
options: Calcium rises and nerve and muscle become less excitable
Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become less excitable
Calcium rises and nerve and muscle become more excitable
Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become more excitable
questions.why: Without parathyroid hormone plasma calcium falls, and low extracellular calcium makes voltage gated sodium channels open more readily, so nerves fire spontaneously and muscles go into tetany. Reduced excitability with low calcium is the opposite of what is observed. Calcium cannot rise when the hormone that defends it is gone. High calcium is what makes tissue less excitable, and that is the other end of the range.
questions.answerText: Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become more excitable

questions.q: A person gets almost no vitamin D and little sunlight for two years. Predict intestinal calcium absorption and the state of bone.
options: Absorption falls and bone becomes poorly mineralized
Absorption rises and the bone becomes denser
Absorption falls and the bone becomes denser
Absorption is unchanged and bone mineral is unaffected
questions.why: Without calcitriol the intestine cannot take up dietary calcium efficiently, so parathyroid hormone rises and draws calcium out of bone to hold the plasma level, leaving bone soft and undermineralized. Absorption cannot rise when the hormone that drives it is missing. Bone loses mineral rather than gaining it under this pressure. No change would contradict the requirement for vitamin D in calcium uptake.
questions.answerText: Absorption falls and bone becomes poorly mineralized

questions.q: A patient in chronic kidney failure cannot make calcitriol. What happens to plasma calcium and parathyroid hormone?
options: Calcium rises and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone rises
Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcium rises and parathyroid hormone rises
questions.why: Losing calcitriol cuts intestinal calcium uptake, plasma calcium drifts down, and the parathyroid glands respond by secreting more hormone in a sustained attempt to correct it. Rising calcium would require the intestinal arm to be intact. Parathyroid hormone cannot fall while calcium is low, because the calcium sensing receptor drives it up. Calcium and parathyroid hormone rising together would point to an autonomous gland, not to kidney failure.
questions.answerText: Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone rises

questions.q: Plasma calcium rises well above normal after a large calcium infusion. What happens to calcitonin?
options: Calcitonin secretion is unchanged
Calcitonin secretion decreases
Calcitonin secretion increases
Calcitonin is converted to parathyroid hormone
questions.why: Parafollicular C cells respond to a high plasma calcium by releasing calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts and slows calcium entry into the blood. A decrease would be the response to low calcium. No change would leave the C cells without a function. Calcitonin and parathyroid hormone are different peptides from different glands and are not interconverted.
questions.answerText: Calcitonin secretion increases

questions.q: Why does a person with very low plasma calcium develop muscle spasms?
options: Low extracellular calcium raises the resting membrane potential above threshold
Low extracellular calcium increases calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Low extracellular calcium prevents muscle relaxation after contraction
Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for firing an action potential
questions.why: Extracellular calcium normally stabilizes the membrane by making sodium channels harder to open, so when it falls the channels open at less depolarization and nerves fire on their own, driving the muscle into spasm. Sarcoplasmic reticulum stores are not increased by low plasma calcium. Relaxation depends on pumping calcium back into the reticulum and is not what fails here. The resting potential is not driven above threshold, since the change is in threshold rather than in the resting value.
questions.answerText: Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for firing an action potential

questions.q: A patient has a parathyroid tumor secreting hormone continuously. Predict plasma calcium, plasma phosphate, and the state of bone.
options: Calcium high, phosphate low, bone resorbed
Calcium high, phosphate high, bone resorbed
Calcium low, phosphate high, bone dense
Calcium high, phosphate low, bone dense
questions.why: Continuous parathyroid hormone drives bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption so plasma calcium climbs, while the same hormone blocks phosphate reabsorption so phosphate is wasted in the urine and falls. High phosphate would require the renal phosphate action to be absent. Low calcium contradicts an excess of the hormone that raises it. Bone cannot become denser while resorption is being driven hard.
questions.answerText: Calcium high, phosphate low, bone resorbed

questions.q: Plasma calcium falls after a low calcium meal. Trace the full corrective response through all three target organs.
options: Calcitonin rises, bone resorption rises, and intestinal calcium absorption rises
Parathyroid hormone rises, bone resorption and renal reabsorption rise, and calcitriol aids absorption
Parathyroid hormone rises, bone formation rises, and renal calcium excretion rises steadily as well
Calcitriol rises first, which then stimulates parathyroid hormone release and bone resorption in turn
questions.why: The corrective loop has three arms, all triggered by parathyroid hormone: calcium is pulled from bone within hours, less is lost in the urine, and over a day or two calcitriol made in the kidney increases uptake from food. Calcitonin lowers calcium and would worsen the fall. Increasing bone formation and urinary excretion would both remove calcium from plasma. Calcitriol is produced in response to parathyroid hormone, so it does not come first.
questions.answerText: Parathyroid hormone rises, bone resorption and renal reabsorption rise, and calcitriol aids absorption

questions.q: A woman eats a calcium poor diet for years yet her plasma calcium stays normal at every check. What has been sacrificed to keep it there?
options: Intestinal transport proteins, which have been used up
Renal filtration, which has been reduced to save calcium
Bone mineral, which has been resorbed to supply the plasma
Parathyroid tissue, which has been exhausted by long use
questions.why: Plasma calcium is defended tightly because nerve and muscle depend on it, and the skeleton is the reservoir the body draws on, so a normal plasma value over years of poor intake usually means bone has been mined. Transport proteins are made continuously under calcitriol and are not depleted. Filtration rate is not reduced to conserve calcium. The parathyroid glands enlarge under chronic demand rather than becoming exhausted.
questions.answerText: Bone mineral, which has been resorbed to supply the plasma

questions.q: Two days after a thyroid operation a patient has tingling around the mouth and cramping in the hands. Which mechanism explains this best?
options: Thyroid hormone was removed, so metabolic rate fell
Plasma phosphate fell, which made nerves fire spontaneously
Calcitonin secretion rose sharply after the operation
The parathyroid glands were injured, so plasma calcium fell
questions.why: The parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid and are easily damaged during thyroid surgery, and losing parathyroid hormone drops plasma calcium enough to cause the tingling and tetany of increased nerve excitability. A low metabolic rate from lost thyroid hormone develops over weeks and causes sluggishness rather than tetany. Calcitonin is lost rather than raised when thyroid tissue is removed. A low phosphate does not by itself produce tetany, and here phosphate would rise as parathyroid hormone falls.
questions.answerText: The parathyroid glands were injured, so plasma calcium fell

questions.q: Which islet cell secretes insulin?
options: The alpha cell
The delta cell
The beta cell
The acinar cell
questions.why: Beta cells make up the bulk of each pancreatic islet and are the only source of insulin. Alpha cells secrete glucagon, the hormone that opposes insulin. Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which damps both. Acinar cells are exocrine and release digestive enzymes into the duct system rather than hormones into the blood.
questions.answerText: The beta cell

questions.q: Which islet cell secretes glucagon?
options: The parafollicular cell
The beta cell
The delta cell
The alpha cell
questions.why: Alpha cells sit at the periphery of the islet and release glucagon when plasma glucose falls. Beta cells release insulin, which acts in the opposite direction. Delta cells release somatostatin. Parafollicular cells belong to the thyroid and secrete calcitonin, so they are not part of the pancreas at all.
questions.answerText: The alpha cell

questions.q: What is the main stimulus for insulin secretion?
options: A rise in plasma glucose
A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma potassium
A fall in plasma amino acids
questions.why: Beta cells take up and metabolize glucose, and the resulting rise in ATP closes potassium channels and triggers insulin release, so plasma glucose is the direct stimulus. A fall in glucose is the signal for glucagon instead. Plasma potassium regulates aldosterone. Amino acids stimulate insulin when they rise, not when they fall.
questions.answerText: A rise in plasma glucose

questions.q: What is the main stimulus for glucagon secretion?
options: A rise in plasma glucose
A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma insulin alone
A rise in plasma calcium
questions.why: Alpha cells respond to a falling plasma glucose by releasing glucagon so the liver can put glucose back into the blood. A rising glucose suppresses glucagon and stimulates insulin. Insulin does inhibit alpha cells, but it is the glucose level rather than insulin alone that is the primary signal. Plasma calcium is monitored by the parathyroid glands.
questions.answerText: A fall in plasma glucose

questions.q: What does insulin do to liver glycogen?
options: It converts glycogen into fatty acids directly
It promotes glycogen breakdown into glucose
It promotes glycogen synthesis and storage
It blocks glucose from entering the liver at all
questions.why: Insulin activates glycogen synthase and inhibits the breakdown enzymes, so after a meal the liver packs glucose away as glycogen. Breaking glycogen down is the glucagon action. Glycogen is not converted straight into fatty acids, although surplus glucose can be used for fat synthesis by a separate route. Hepatic glucose entry is not insulin dependent, which is what lets the liver sense glucose directly.
questions.answerText: It promotes glycogen synthesis and storage

questions.q: What does glucagon do to liver glycogen?
options: It stores glucose as glycogen for later use by the body
It moves glycogen from the liver to skeletal muscle
It converts glycogen into muscle protein for storage
It breaks glycogen down and releases glucose into the blood
questions.why: Glucagon activates glycogen phosphorylase in hepatocytes, and because the liver can release free glucose into the blood, plasma glucose rises within minutes. Storing glycogen is the insulin action. Glycogen cannot become protein. Glycogen is not transported between tissues, since each tissue keeps its own store.
questions.answerText: It breaks glycogen down and releases glucose into the blood

questions.q: Which glucose transporter does insulin recruit into the membrane of muscle and fat cells?
options: GLUT4
GLUT2
GLUT1
SGLT1
questions.why: Insulin causes vesicles carrying GLUT4 to fuse with the membrane of muscle and adipose cells, which is how it increases glucose uptake in those tissues. GLUT1 provides basal uptake in many cells and is not insulin regulated. GLUT2 is the high capacity transporter in liver and beta cells that lets them sense glucose. SGLT1 is a sodium coupled transporter in the intestine and kidney.
questions.answerText: GLUT4

questions.q: Which hormone lowers plasma glucose?
options: Glucagon
Insulin
Cortisol
Growth hormone
